items.name: Climeworks/Svante structured-laminate amine sorbent (Gen 2 -> Gen 3), DOE field pilot DE-FE0031952
items.mechanism: Climeworks amine sorbent formed into thin Svante laminate sheets with printed spacers; temperature-vacuum swing with direct low-grade steam heating; fast cycles (20-30 min adsorption) instead of multi-hour packed-bed cycles.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Published KPI targets (per kg laminate, real California air, 2022-23): Gen 2 equilibrium cyclic capacity 0.8-1.0 mol/kg, fast-cycle 0.5-0.7 mol/kg, uptake rate 0.05-0.07 mol/kg/min; Gen 3 1.1-1.6 mol/kg equilibrium, 0.8-1.0 mol/kg fast-cycle, 0.08-0.1 mol/kg/min. Slides state Gen 2 targets met or exceeded in cyclic field operation and Gen 3 targets 'nearly all met' (Gen 3 data not shown). Pre-tests at 30-90% RH on 360x360 mm beds. OptiLex calc: 0.9 mol/kg at a 40-min cycle = 1.43 kg CO2/kg/day vs about 0.22 for a 5-cycle/day packed bed.
items.regeneration: Direct steam, vacuum-temperature swing; no absolute energy published. Pressure-drop targets 800-1000 Pa (Gen 2) and 400-700 Pa (Gen 3). OptiLex fan calc at 75% capture, 60% fan efficiency: 400-700 Pa = 1.18-2.06 GJ/t (327-572 kWh/t); 800-1000 Pa = 2.35-2.94 GJ/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Lifetime targets: <10% (Gen 2) and <5% (Gen 3) average capacity loss in about 1 year. Durability runs >3,000 cycles (Gen 2) and >5,000 cycles (Gen 3) using accelerated cycling; pressure drop stable, laminates mechanically intact. Post-test FTIR confirmed oxidation, stronger on the air-inlet side than the steam-inlet side. Capacity retention was only shown graphically and depended on test weather (10 C/90% RH vs 15 C/50% RH).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4 -> 5; 30 kg CO2/day integrated test unit operated about 1 year (2022-23); basis of Climeworks Gen 3.
items.cost: Not disclosed; slides list cost versus packed beds under fast cycling as an open question.
items.bottleneck: Oxidative fade at single-digit % per year and a 400-700 Pa pressure drop; Gen 3 measured values still unpublished.

items.name: Climeworks Gen 2 packed-bed plants in the field (Orca 2021, Mammoth 2024)
items.mechanism: Amine-functionalised granular sorbent in structured packed-bed filter elements; temperature-vacuum swing at about 100 C using geothermal heat; multi-hour cycles.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Orca (Iceland): nameplate 4,000 t/y gross, about 3,000 t/y net by design. First-fill sorbent (2019 state of the art) was 10-20% below specification with up to 20% batch variation, giving 2,400-2,500 t/y achievable. Actual removal 487 t (2022) and 1,000 t (2023). Best 7-day run rate 1,900 t/y annualised in Q1 2024 on filter material more than 2 years old. Mammoth (nameplate 36,000 t/y, 72 containers, built out in stages): 105 t in first 10 months (press report), 119 t net in H1 2025, 675 t net in H1 2026; upgraded containers reach the design 1.37 t/container/day.
items.regeneration: Plant-derived LCA inputs (Deutz & Bardow 2021, as tabulated in the EES 2025 review): 700 kWh electricity + 11.9 GJ heat per t at 4 kt/y scale; 500 kWh + 5.4 GJ projected for 100 kt/y. OptiLex calc: 11.9 GJ at 100 C plus 700 kWh is about 9.5% second-law efficiency.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 1,900 of 2,400-2,500 t/y on 2-year-old filter implies an all-cause shortfall of 21-24%, so capacity fade is at most roughly 10-12% per year (upper bound; confounded by downtime and weather). Early operation vented up to 30% of captured CO2; later cut by about 90%.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8-9; about 41,000 t/y installed nameplate (Climeworks total), real output far lower so far.
items.cost: About $1,000/t at Mammoth (company statements, 2024-26); operating cost per tonne reported halved by Sept 2026.
items.bottleneck: Delivered output 33% of design at Orca in 2023; Mammoth H1 2026 output is 3.8% of half-year nameplate, but this is confounded by staged build-out and retrofits, so it is not a clean measure of sorbent performance.

items.name: Oxidative degradation of supported PEI: measured kinetics and the role of CO2 and humidity
items.mechanism: Radical autoxidation of the aminopolymer (hydroperoxide route to amides/imines, C-N cleavage). Chemisorbed CO2 acid-catalyses key steps, while heavy CO2 loading stiffens chains and slows radical propagation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 45 wt% branched PEI on gamma-alumina; capacity measured at 0.04% CO2, 30 C, dry, after 18 h ageing in air (21% O2) with 0, 0.04, 1 or 5% CO2 at 30-110 C (JACS 2024).
items.stability_and_lifetime: About 2% capacity loss after 18 h at 55 C but 15% at 60 C in dry 0.04% CO2/air; air-level CO2 accelerates oxidation more than 1-5% CO2 below about 90 C. Related results cited in the literature: 30 cycles at 70 C under 0.04% CO2/air lost 29% dry and 52% humid. Static storage at 23 C in ambient air lost under 13% in 12 months (ACS Omega 2026). OptiLex calc: at the 60 C rate, a 5% loss takes 5.7 h cumulative, i.e. about 1.6 s of hot-air exposure per cycle at 13,000 cycles/year. The 55 -> 60 C jump is not Arrhenius-like (apparent 379 kJ/mol), indicating an induction period, so extrapolation to ambient is unreliable.
items.regeneration: Implication: sorbent must be cooled below about 55 C before air readmission, or purged oxygen-free while hot.
items.trl_and_scale: Milligram TGA and in-situ IR; unstabilised model sorbent, not a commercial formulation.
items.bottleneck: No rate law has been validated against plant temperature/oxygen profiles.

items.name: Sorbent cost and replacement economics (NETL generic sorbent DAC case studies)
items.mechanism: Techno-economic model of a generic solid-sorbent DAC plant; sorbent price and lifetime varied as sensitivities.
items.cost: 2022 report: literature range $15-100/kg and 0.25-5 years; one amino-polymer entry at $16/kg and 3 years. Base case assumed $0.20/kg and 0.5-year life. Cost of capture rises from $702/t to $1,030/t at $15/kg and $2,910/t at $100/kg, which backs out to about 22 kg sorbent per tonne CO2. 2024 update poster (labelled preliminary): about $10/kg sorbent, $774-1,229/t net at 100,000 t/y, capital the largest contributor in gas-fired cases; shortening the cycle from 60 to 20 min cuts cost 20-30%. OptiLex calc for a fast-cycle laminate (0.9 mol/kg, 36 cycles/day): $29/t at $15/kg with 1-year life, $10/t with 3-year life; packed bed at 5 cycles/day: $187/t and $62/t.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Assumed 1.2 mol/kg, 60% capture fraction, 100 C desorption.
items.regeneration: Assumed 4.3 GJ/t sorbent regeneration energy.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Assumed 0.5 years 'due to lack of data'; cost flattens beyond about 2 years at the low base price, but not at realistic prices.
items.trl_and_scale: Paper study, 100,000 t/y net.
items.bottleneck: No audited commercial sorbent price or lifetime exists publicly; results swing by a factor of 4 on those two inputs.

items.name: Laminate-supported PEI/silica (ePTFE sheets, W.L. Gore) across climates
items.mechanism: PEI-impregnated silica held in expanded-PTFE sheets; carbamate formation when dry, water-assisted carbamic acid/enhanced amine efficiency when humid.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2, fixed bed, -20/5/35 C and 0-80% RH (JACS Au 2025). Pseudo-equilibrium capacity 0.41-1.8 mmol/g (30 wt% PEI), 0.61-2.8 (40 wt%), 0.44-3.5 (50 wt%). Dry at -20 C only 0.45-0.74 mmol/g. At 35 C humidity changes capacity by only -0.18 to +0.22 mmol/g. Amine efficiency 0.12-0.17 mol CO2/mol N at 35 C and 0.19-0.29 at 5 and -20 C when humid, i.e. 24-58% of the 0.5 carbamate limit. At 50 wt% PEI capacity fell from 3.38 (50% RH) to 2.89 mmol/g (80% RH).
items.regeneration: Temperature-programmed desorption only; no energy data.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not tested.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab fixed bed; laminate form factor is close to commercial structured sorbents.
items.bottleneck: Higher PEI loading raises capacity but slows uptake; the best loading changes with climate, so one formulation cannot be optimal everywhere.

items.name: Benchmark amine sorbent equilibrium data: Lewatit VP OC 1065 and amine-grafted alumina
items.mechanism: Primary benzylamine on polystyrene resin (Lewatit, considered close to early Climeworks sorbents) and aminosilane-functionalised gamma-alumina pellets; ammonium carbamate plus water-stabilised species.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Lewatit: 1.0 mmol/g at 0.04 kPa CO2, 298 K, dry; about 1.8 mmol/g near 55% RH (J. Chem. Eng. Data 2023, PMC10726313). Amine-alumina (3.6 mmol N/g; IECR 2025): Toth fit q_s 1.17 mmol/g at 308 K, heat of adsorption -77.8 kJ/mol; OptiLex evaluation of the fit gives 0.49 mmol/g dry at 42 Pa and 25 C (0.57 at 15 C, 0.41 at 35 C). Humidity enhancement plateaus near 40% RH (water monolayer); slight loss at 10% RH.
items.regeneration: Water uptake from the GAB fit: 3.2 mmol/g at 40% RH, 4.2 at 50%, 9.9 at 80%; water heat of adsorption about 45 kJ/mol. That is 6-9 mol water per mol CO2 at equilibrium for 40-50% RH. OptiLex cycle: each mol of water co-desorbed per mol CO2 adds 1.0 GJ/t (heat 4.0 GJ/t with none, 8.0 with 4, 12.0 with 8).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Lewatit (IECR 2017, PMC5384483): hydrothermally stable, significant oxidation above 70 C in air, urea formation above 120 C in concentrated dry CO2.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab isotherms and breakthrough on gram scale.
items.bottleneck: Water loading exceeds CO2 loading several-fold at ordinary humidity, so water management sets the heat demand.

items.name: Climeworks Gen 3 large-scale test and 2026 next-generation claims
items.mechanism: Svante structured adsorbent with Climeworks sorbent in cube-shaped collectors; 2026 upgrades changed sorbent formulation and production plus mechanical design.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Muttenz (Switzerland) test, May 2024 to Jan 2025: 1,300+ cycles, sub-freezing to warm, semi-arid to saturated air; double capacity versus Gen 2; results within +/-5% of predictions. Only relative figures; no absolute capacity given. 1,300 cycles in about 250 days is roughly 5 cycles/day, far slower than the 20-30 min adsorption steps of the earlier DOE pilot.
items.regeneration: Half the energy of Gen 2 (relative only; company declined to give absolute figures). Gen 2 reference from older reporting: about 2,000 kWh heat + 650 kWh electricity per t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Material 'designed' to last three times longer than Gen 2. Sept 2026: tenfold sorbent-lifetime improvement and fourfold process densification claimed in the lab; plant testing planned for early 2027.
items.trl_and_scale: Large-scale test module; first deployment planned for Project Cypress (Louisiana).
items.cost: Target $250-350/t capture cost by 2030 versus about $1,000/t today.
items.bottleneck: No independently verified absolute energy, capacity or lifetime numbers.

items.name: Stabilising amines against oxidation: epoxide functionalisation, chelators, and trace-metal sensitivity
items.mechanism: Converting primary amines to hydroxyalkyl-substituted secondary amines and poisoning ppm-level Fe/Cu that catalyse radical initiation; conversely, Cu/Fe contamination accelerates autoxidation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Nat. Commun. 2018 tested in flue-gas conditions, not air. Functionalisation costs capacity: reported 3.8 -> about 2 and 1.5 mmol/g at 15% CO2 for 0.37 and 0.54 epoxybutane per N (as summarised in a 2024 ACS Omega paper).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Epoxybutane-PEI on chelator-treated silica lost 8.5% working capacity after 30 days at 110 C in O2-containing flue gas, about 50 times slower than plain PEI/silica, which lost everything. Opposite direction (Environ. Sci. Technol. 2026, PMC13235560): after 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air the clean PEI/SBA-15 control kept 72% of capacity, a sample with about 4 ppm Cu kept 63%, and 1000:1 PEI:metal samples kept 25-50%; order Cu > Fe >> Ni.
items.regeneration: Not measured.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab; the stabilisation result has not been shown under 400 ppm, 21% O2 cycling for thousands of cycles in the open literature.
items.bottleneck: Stability gains so far trade away a large share of capacity, and ambient dust can keep supplying catalytic metals.

items.name: Thermal and CO2-induced (urea) degradation; accelerated testing of PEI-silica pellets
items.mechanism: At high temperature in dry CO2, carbamates dehydrate to ureas; in hot air, amines oxidise. Water vapour suppresses urea formation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 50 wt% PEI (Mw 800) on mesoporous silica, pelletised; about 1 mmol/g at 420 ppm CO2 in air.
items.stability_and_lifetime: About 94% capacity loss within 24 h at 120 C in ambient air. 100 h accelerated tests (33-100 cycle equivalents) at 80/100/120 C: dry-CO2 degradation 2-3 times that in nitrogen at 100 C and above; 75% RH reduces it. Authors place the optimum regeneration temperature at 80-100 C.
items.regeneration: Regeneration at 80 C leaves desorption incomplete; 120 C is stable only without oxygen.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab fixed bed, 100 h.
items.bottleneck: The safe regeneration window (80-100 C, oxygen-free, humid) is narrow and sits right where the thermodynamics need 90-100 C.

items.name: Global Thermostat (Zero Carbon Systems): PEI on ceramic monolith with direct steam
items.mechanism: PEI in a mesoporous alumina washcoat on cordierite honeycomb monoliths; parallel-channel flow at high air velocity; regeneration by condensing saturated steam that also sweeps CO2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Founder-authored preprint (2024): 5 m/s air, 0.15 m monolith depth, pressure drop under 150 Pa, more than half the CO2 removed; about 40 L CO2 collected per monolith in 15 min. OptiLex calc: 150 Pa at 50-75% capture = 0.44-0.66 GJ/t fan work.
items.regeneration: Steam at 70-100 C; about 4 GJ/t stated as achievable, steam-use efficiency about 90%; sensible heat of the monolith is the main load.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No lifetime data published; steam stability of the support is the known concern.
items.trl_and_scale: Colorado demonstration unit rated above 1,000 t/y operating since end-2022 (no public capture data); about 4,000 t/y installed per the EES 2025 review; acquired by Zero Carbon Systems in 2024.
items.cost: Claims under $50/t at maturity; not supported by published plant data.
items.bottleneck: Heavy inert monolith mass per unit of amine, and no independent performance or lifetime measurements.

items.name: Low-temperature-regenerable epoxide-functionalised PEI/TREN on silica
items.mechanism: Butylene-oxide substitution lowers the share of primary amines (to 24-33%), weakening CO2 binding so it desorbs at 40-45 C.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2 at 25 C; 180 min adsorption, 90 min desorption (Adv. Sci. 2026). Working capacity 1.95-1.99 mmol/g with 45 C desorption (PEI300 variant) and 1.37 mmol/g at 40 C (TREN variant) at 50% RH over 10 breakthrough cycles; unmodified PEI gives 1.41-1.58 mmol/g at 70 C.
items.regeneration: Desorption was into flowing pure nitrogen, which keeps CO2 partial pressure near zero and yields no concentrated product. OptiLex thermodynamics: a site strong enough to load at 420 ppm (about -70 kJ/mol) needs about 92 C to unload against 1 kPa CO2. The 40-45 C result therefore does not yet show low-temperature production of pure CO2. Authors' modelled heat 2.85-2.91 MJ/kg.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 2.8% and 0.6% loss over cycles 2-20 with air as balance gas; negligible loss over 100 dry cycles; 15-19% drop over the first 10 humid cycles before levelling.
items.trl_and_scale: Milligram TGA and small breakthrough column.
items.bottleneck: Must be re-tested under vacuum or steam at about 1 kPa CO2 and with minutes-scale cycles.

items.name: Rotary honeycomb PEI/silica adsorber with steam-assisted temperature swing (prototype in real humid air)
items.mechanism: PEI (Mw about 600) with silica sol coated on a glass-fibre honeycomb wheel (42 kg structured adsorbent) rotating between an air sector and a steam-purge sector.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Ambient air at 21-28 C and 52-81% RH; capture fraction 50-85%; product purity above 90% (98% in one case); productivity 0.235-0.352 kg CO2 per kg adsorbent per day (Adv. Sci. 2026).
items.regeneration: Steam at about 103-105 C. Modelled energy with heat recovery 7.41-9.64 MJ/kg; 2.50-3.14 MJ/kg only with a hypothetical better adsorbent.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: Single-rotor prototype described as having ton-scale potential.
items.bottleneck: Measured productivity is about a quarter of what the Climeworks/Svante Gen 3 targets imply, and energy stays above 7 GJ/t even with modelled heat recovery.

items.name: PEI/silica hollow-fibre sorbents cycled with hot water
items.mechanism: Polysulfone hollow fibres loaded with PEI-infused silica; an impermeable lumen barrier lets 86 C water flow through the bore to heat and 22 C water to cool, with no steam contact.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2 in nitrogen, 22 C, 45% RH: swing capacity 0.72 mmol per g fibre with 68% CO2 recovery in the final cycle (IECR 2026).
items.regeneration: 86 C water; 13 min desorption plus 2 min cooling under inert sweep before the feed returns, which also keeps hot sorbent away from oxygen.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only 10 cycles.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab module.
items.bottleneck: Low capacity per total fibre mass and no long-cycle or air-fed data.

bottlenecks: Oxidative lifetime. Commercial targets are under 5-10% capacity loss per year (Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot). Unstabilised PEI/alumina loses 15% in 18 h at 60 C in air with 0.04% CO2 and about 2% at 55 C; by OptiLex calculation that allows roughly 1.6 s of hot-air exposure per cycle at 13,000 cycles/year. Even static storage at 23 C costs up to 13% in a year. Pilot post-mortem found oxidation concentrated at the air-inlet side.

Sorbent replacement cost. NETL's model implies about 22 kg sorbent per tonne CO2 at a 0.5-year life, adding about $330/t at $15/kg. OptiLex calculation: a 5-cycle/day packed bed needs $187/t at $15/kg with a 1-year life; a 36-cycle/day laminate needs $29/t, or $10/t at 3 years. Fast cycling only helps if fade per cycle falls in proportion.

Regeneration heat. Plant-derived figures are 11.9 GJ heat plus 700 kWh electricity per tonne at 4 kt/y scale (about 9.5% second-law efficiency by OptiLex calculation); the literature median is 9 GJ/t heat. Reaction heat is only 1.6-2.7 GJ/t; the rest is sensible heat and co-adsorbed water.

Water co-adsorption. Measured water loading on an amine-alumina sorbent is 3.2-4.2 mmol/g at 40-50% RH against 0.5-1 mmol/g CO2, i.e. 6-9 mol water per mol CO2 at equilibrium. Each mol of water desorbed per mol CO2 adds 1.0 GJ/t.

Pressure drop. The Climeworks/Svante targets are 400-700 Pa (Gen 3) and 800-1000 Pa (Gen 2). At 75% capture and 60% fan efficiency that is 1.2-2.1 and 2.4-2.9 GJ/t of electricity, 4-10 times the 100 Pa figure in the OptiLex baseline and consistent with the 500-700 kWh/t reported for plants.

Productivity and capital. Packed beds run about 5 cycles/day (about 0.2 kg CO2/kg/day); a real-air rotary prototype measured 0.24-0.35; Gen 3 targets imply 1.0-1.4. Capital is the largest cost item in NETL's gas-fired cases ($774-1,229/t net, preliminary 2024), and Mammoth runs at about $1,000/t.

Amine efficiency. Laminate PEI/silica at 400 ppm reaches only 0.12-0.29 mol CO2 per mol N, 24-58% of the dry carbamate limit, so most of the nitrogen is dead mass that is heated every cycle and still oxidises.
Weather sensitivity. The same laminate sorbent ranges from 0.41 to 3.5 mmol/g between -20 and 35 C and 0-80% RH; dry cold air gives 0.45-0.74 mmol/g.

Field reliability and manufacturing. Orca's first sorbent fill was 10-20% below specification with 20% batch variation, up to 30% of captured CO2 was initially vented, and Orca removed 1,000 t in 2023 against a 3,000 t/y net design.
open_problems: An oxidation-resistant amine site without the capacity penalty. Epoxide functionalisation plus metal chelation slowed deactivation about 50-fold in flue-gas tests but roughly halves capacity; nothing public shows under 5% loss per year at 400 ppm, 21% O2, humid, over 10,000+ cycles. Candidate imports: radical-scavenging and metal-passivation chemistry from polymer and lubricant stabilisation.

A degradation rate law validated on real cycle profiles. None exists publicly. An executable verifier that integrates oxidation and urea kinetics over a cycle's temperature, oxygen, CO2 and humidity history would let the engine score process ideas (cool-before-air, oxygen-free purge, hot-water fibres) numerically. The sharp onset between 55 and 60 C suggests an induction period that a simple Arrhenius model will miss.

Keeping the humidity boost while rejecting bulk water. CO2 enhancement saturates at the water monolayer (about 40% RH) but water uptake keeps climbing to about 10 mmol/g at 80% RH. A support that stops at the monolayer could remove several GJ/t.

Low-temperature regeneration that still delivers concentrated CO2. Reported 40-45 C desorption used a nitrogen purge. The open question is whether cooperative or step-shaped binding can escape the single-site Langmuir window (about 92 C at 1 kPa for -70 kJ/mol), tested under vacuum or steam.

A contactor geometry that combines the Gen 3 uptake rate (0.08-0.1 mol/kg/min) with a pressure drop near 100-150 Pa instead of 400-700 Pa, at low inert thermal mass. Laminates, monoliths, hollow fibres and rotary honeycombs have never been compared on one basis with measured data.
Raising amine efficiency above 0.3 mol CO2 per mol N at 400 ppm without the slow diffusion that comes with high polymer loading.
Protection against airborne trace metals. About 4 ppm copper measurably speeds oxidation, and ambient dust is a continuing source; no field data quantify how fast metals accumulate on a sorbent.
Climate-specific formulations or a single sorbent that holds capacity in cold dry air and in hot saturated air.

Public long-run pilot data. Capacity versus cycle number under fixed reference conditions for any commercial-type amine sorbent over a year would settle whether lifetime or energy is the larger cost term.
An audited sorbent cost. Public figures span $10-16/kg (NETL, one literature entry) to $15-100/kg (literature range), and Climeworks reported 20% batch-to-batch variation in early production.

key_claims.claim: Oxidation is the life-limiting mechanism for the commercial-baseline sorbent at pilot scale, and the bar is single-digit percent per year. In the Climeworks/Svante DOE field pilot (30 kg CO2/day, California, about 1 year, >3,000 cycles Gen 2 and >5,000 cycles Gen 3) the stated targets were under 10% (Gen 2) and under 5% (Gen 3) capacity loss per year, and post-test FTIR confirmed oxidation, stronger on the air-inlet side than the steam side. Gen 3 measured results were not shown.

A higher-capacity material alone will not move the baseline. The 2025 Energy & Environmental Science review (with a Climeworks co-author) reports plant-derived energy of 700 kWh electricity plus 11.9 GJ heat per tonne at 4 kt/y scale, Orca removing 1,000 t in 2023 against a 3,000 t/y net design, a process governed mainly by heat and mass transfer, no material yet shown to beat amines in real process conditions, and that "there is no data in literature on how any DAC materials degrade" over long pilot or commercial operation.

surprises: Fan work is not small in real structured amine beds. The OptiLex brief assumed a 100 Pa contactor (0.29 GJ/t), but the Climeworks/Svante pressure-drop targets are 400-700 Pa for Gen 3 and 800-1000 Pa for Gen 2, which compute to 1.2-2.9 GJ/t of electricity at 75% capture. Passive or very low-resistance air contact is worth more than 'a few percent' against this baseline.

The pilot found oxidation mainly where air enters, not where steam enters. That points to air contact with warm sorbent (and long ambient exposure) rather than the regeneration step itself, so process fixes may matter as much as new chemistry.

Humid air is not benign for lifetime. Water suppresses urea formation in hot CO2, but cited cycling data for PEI/alumina at 70 C show 52% loss humid versus 29% dry, and air-level CO2 speeds oxidation below about 90 C. These are different mechanisms, not contradictory findings; Lewatit's benzylamine chemistry behaves differently again (CO2 and moisture were protective).

Climeworks has never published absolute Gen 3 energy or capacity numbers, only 'half' and 'double'. Its headline 'real-world' test logged 1,300+ cycles in about eight months (about 5 per day), while the earlier small DOE pilot ran over 5,000 cycles in a year.

NETL's 2022 base case priced sorbent at $0.20/kg, roughly 100 times below the literature range it cites; moving to $15/kg adds about $330/t at its assumed 0.5-year life. Many published cost figures hide this assumption.
Unstabilised PEI sorbent loses up to 13% of capacity in 12 months simply stored at room temperature in air, the same size as the whole annual fade budget for a commercial sorbent.
About 4 ppm of copper is enough to measurably accelerate amine oxidation, so sorbent purity and airborne dust become lifetime variables.

Mammoth's net removal was 675 t in the first half of 2026 against a 36,000 t/y nameplate. This is heavily confounded by staged build-out, retrofits and mechanical issues and should not be read as a verdict on amine chemistry; Orca's shortfalls trace partly to a 2019-vintage sorbent whose batch variation has since been fixed.

Climeworks said in September 2026 that it has shown a tenfold sorbent-lifetime gain in the lab, with plant tests from early 2027. If that holds in the field, lifetime stops being the binding constraint and energy, pressure drop and capital take over. It is an unverified company claim.

Sources I could not open: the Holmes et al. 2024 degradation-aware cost model (numbers not verified, only title and authors) and the Deutz & Bardow 2021 paper itself (energy figures taken from the EES 2025 review's table; adsorbent-consumption figures not verified). Calculations are in climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/amine_checks.py.

verifs.claim: Oxidation is the life-limiting mechanism for the commercial-baseline sorbent at pilot scale, and the bar is single-digit percent per year. In the Climeworks/Svante DOE field pilot (30 kg CO2/day, California, about 1 year, >3,000 cycles Gen 2 and >5,000 cycles Gen 3) the stated targets were under 10% (Gen 2) and under 5% (Gen 3) capacity loss per year, and post-test FTIR confirmed oxidation, stronger on the air-inlet side than the steam side. Gen 3 measured results were not shown.
verifs.corrected_claim: In the Electricore/Climeworks/Svante DOE field test (DE-FE0031952; TRL 5 "Integrated DAC System", design 30 kg CO2/day, California; 2023 NETL review slides, 29 Aug 2023), the BP2 cyclic-lifetime targets were <10% (Gen 2) and <5% (Gen 3) average capacity loss "in ~1 year". The sorbents were developmental Climeworks amine sorbents on Svante structured laminates (36 x 36 cm beds), not the commercial packed-bed baseline. The plant ran for about one year overall, but the Gen 2 durability run was accelerated cycling: >3,000 cycles in roughly 3.5 months (about Nov 2022 to late Feb 2023), treated as "~1 year equivalent"; Gen 3 reached >5,000 cycles. Measured Gen 2 result (before/after characterization at fixed air conditions, read off a bar chart): roughly 96-98% capacity retained under one air condition (target met) but only about 89% (20 min adsorption) and about 79% (30 min adsorption) under the other (target missed); the slide's wording is "Gen2 target can be met; air weather conditions have an impact". Post-test FTIR "confirms presence of oxidation, more significant on the air inlet side than steam inlet", with mitigation options said to be in development. The slides do not state that oxidation is the life-limiting mechanism, do not quantify its share of the loss, and give no Gen 3 durability results (analysis was still ongoing).
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the primary PDF (slides 4, 10, 17, 21-23, 25). The numbers in the claim are right (30 kg/day, California, <10% / <5% targets, >3,000 / >5,000 cycles, FTIR oxidation stronger on the air-inlet side, Gen 3 not reported), but four framings are not supported by the source.

1. **"Life-limiting mechanism" is an inference.** The slide only says FTIR confirmed oxidation was present. It gives no attribution of capacity loss to oxidation versus other causes such as amine leaching, steam or hydrothermal effects, or fouling. The air-side gradient is consistent with O2-driven degradation but does not establish it as the dominant mechanism.

2. **"Commercial-baseline sorbent" is wrong.** This was a TRL 4 to 5 development project testing new sorbent generations (Gen 2 "DAC sorbent for humid air", Gen 3 "weather-stable") on Svante laminates. Climeworks' commercial plants use structured packed beds.

3. **"Per year" and "about 1 year, >3,000 cycles" conflate two things.** The plant operated for about one year in total, but the Gen 2 durability line ran accelerated cycles over about 3.5 calendar months (slide 21 x-axis), labelled "~1 year equivalent". Oxidation depends on time at temperature with O2 exposure, so accelerated cycle count may under-represent calendar-time oxidative ageing. The target is a project KPI, not an industry "bar".

4. **The Gen 2 outcome is condition-dependent, and the claim omits that it was shown.** Under the less favourable characterization condition, retained capacity was about 79-89%, a loss of roughly 11-21%, which misses the <10% target. The bar values are my reading of the chart, not tabulated numbers. The slide text lists the two conditions as 10C/90%RH and 15C/50%RH; mapping "condition 1" (the worse one) to 10C/90%RH is my reading of the legend order, not stated explicitly.

Other context: capacities are per gram or kg of laminate, not of neat sorbent. Sorbent chemistry is not disclosed. Ambient CO2 concentration is not stated (outdoor air is presumed). This is a conference slide deck, not a peer-reviewed or final report; the final technical report (OSTI) would be the place to look for Gen 3 durability data. The deck itself prints two different award numbers (DE-FE0031952 on the title slide, DE-FE0031959 on the overview slide).

verifs.claim: A higher-capacity material alone will not move the baseline. The 2025 Energy & Environmental Science review (with a Climeworks co-author) reports plant-derived energy of 700 kWh electricity plus 11.9 GJ heat per tonne at 4 kt/y scale, Orca removing 1,000 t in 2023 against a 3,000 t/y net design, a process governed mainly by heat and mass transfer, no material yet shown to beat amines in real process conditions, and that "there is no data in literature on how any DAC materials degrade" over long pilot or commercial operation.
verifs.corrected_claim: Capacity is not the main lever, but the review does not say a better material cannot move the baseline. The 2025 Energy & Environmental Science review (van der Spek et al., DOI 10.1039/d5ee01732g; co-author John Young, Climeworks AG) lists in its LCA table (Table 8) 700 kWh electricity plus 11,900 MJ heat per tonne CO2 captured for a 4 kt/y sorbent DAC system. That row is cited from Deutz and Bardow (Nature Energy 2021), which the review describes as assessing Climeworks' real-world plants at Hinwil and Hellisheidi; the same study's 100 kt/y row is 500 kWh plus 5,400 MJ. The review reports Orca's "design removal capacity" as 3,000 t/y (2,500 t/y achievable with the current filter material; best weekly run rate equivalent to 1,900 t/y on two-year-degraded filter), with 1,000 t actually removed in 2023 and 487 t in 2022. On productivity it says adsorbent CO2 capacity is "somewhat important" but the process "is primarily driven by heat and mass transfer in the design space of amine functionalised materials", while still naming volumetric working capacity as one of two main productivity levers. It says no material has "proven to be significantly better than amine-functionalised in real process conditions", then adds that material-design breakthroughs "could lead to a step change in the cost". It also states "there is no data in literature on how any DAC materials degrade over an extended period in a pilot or commercial scale process".
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the full text from Europe PMC (the PMC page itself is behind a reCAPTCHA). Every number and the degradation quote are in the source; the corrections are about framing.

1. **Headline is an inference.** "A higher-capacity material alone will not move the baseline" is not stated in the review. The source says capacity is "somewhat important", lists working capacity as one of two productivity levers, and says a materials breakthrough on any Table 1 challenge (productivity, energy, lifetime, ambient variability) could give a step change in cost. The heat/mass-transfer statement is scoped to productivity within amine-functionalised materials, resting on two modelling references (74, 101), not plant data. The review also notes productivity estimates cover only seven real materials, all packed beds, and are missing for physisorbents and humidity-swing materials.

2. **Energy figure is second-hand and old.** The 700 kWh / 11.9 GJ pair is one row in a table of LCA study inputs, not the review's own measurement. It reflects first-generation Climeworks plants around 2020 and is per tonne captured, not net removed. I could not open Deutz and Bardow to confirm measured-vs-reported status (paywall, search budget exhausted). Other rows in the same table range from 180 to 1,500 kWh and 0 to 18,152 MJ, so this is not a consensus baseline.

3. **Orca wording.** The review says "design removal capacity", not "net". The Orca figures come from Climeworks' own disclosure (ref 89), not independent measurement. The shortfall is attributed to first-of-a-kind mechanical problems and filter degradation, so it is not evidence about sorbent capacity as such.

4. **"Beat amines" is stronger than the source.** The review's wording is "significantly better", with no stated conditions (CO2 concentration, humidity, cycle count) and no citation on that sentence; it is expert judgement.

5. **Degradation statement.** It appears in the solid-sorbent lifetime section and reflects literature to roughly 2024-25 (the plant table is dated August 2024). It concerns published long-duration pilot or commercial data; lab-scale degradation literature exists and is cited. The same section notes humidity-swing sorbent stability is shown only in lab tests of about 10 cycles.

title: MOFs, COFs and porous crystals for DAC

items.name: COF-999 (olefin-linked COF with covalently tethered polyamines; Zhou...Yaghi, Nature 635, 96, Oct 2024)
items.mechanism: Amine chemisorption (carbamic acid dry; carbamate + bicarbonate when humid) on polyethylenimine chains grown from covalently anchored initiators inside a hydrophobic, hydrolysis-proof C=C-linked framework. Conventional solid-amine chemistry plus one imported idea: covalent tethering in a crystalline all-organic scaffold.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2, 25 C: 0.96 +/- 0.03 mmol/g dry; 1.69 at 25% RH; 2.05 +/- 0.03 at 50% RH; 2.09 at 75% RH (breakthrough, simulated air). Single-gas isotherm 0.91 mmol/g at 0.4 mbar; Qst 53 kJ/mol (dry). Half capacity in 18.8 min, 80% in 61.7 min. Outdoor Berkeley air (410-517 ppm, 28-51% RH, Jan-Feb 2024): mean 1.28 mmol/g per cycle (max 1.48, min 1.03), i.e. 62% of the lab humid figure. Water uptake 0.09 g/g at 50% RH.
items.regeneration: 60 C, but under flowing N2 (a purge, so product CO2 is dilute); 80% desorbed in 44 min at 60 C, 22 min at 80 C, 16 min at 100 C. OptiLex calc (Clausius-Clapeyron with the paper's Qst): equilibrium CO2 pressure over the loaded sorbent at 60 C is only ~3.8 mbar; Langmuir fit gives zero working capacity at 60 C against 1 kPa CO2, 0.64 mol/kg at 0.1 kPa. Concentrated CO2 at 60 C therefore needs deep vacuum or steam; ~100 C needed at 1 kPa.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 100 temperature-swing cycles over 20 days in outdoor air; isotherm, breakthrough, FT-IR, SEM unchanged afterwards. The 'full retention' claim rests on 12 selected cycles at 37 +/- 1% RH (1.2-1.3 mmol/g); per-cycle values otherwise move with humidity. No data beyond 100 cycles, none with hot O2 exposure, none with steam.
items.cost: Not reported. Multi-step route (azide-functional dialdehyde monomer, Staudinger reduction, aziridine ring-opening polymerisation) - paper itself lists scalability as a future priority. OptiLex calc: at 1.28 mol/kg, 100 demonstrated cycles = $3,550/t CO2 at $20/kg; $20/t requires 17,752 cycles at $20/kg or 177,516 cycles at $200/kg.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4: powder, gram-scale packed tube. No shaped contactor. No independent reproduction found as of Oct 2026 (follow-up structural study includes the Yaghi group).
items.bottleneck: Lifetime evidence (100 cycles vs >=18,000 needed) and regeneration under realistic CO2 back-pressure; water co-adsorption is still ~2.4 mol H2O per mol CO2 (latent heat ~2.4 GJ/t, the largest term in a 4.6 GJ/t powder-only heat budget).

items.name: COF-1000 (larger-pore successor; Zhou, Ma, Zhang, Sabeva, Yaghi, Nature Sustainability 9, 431-438, 2026)
items.mechanism: Same tethered-polyamine chemisorption as COF-999 with enlarged pores to raise amine density while keeping fast diffusion; the advance is kinetic (cycle rate), not thermodynamic.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2: 1.31 mmol/g dry, half capacity in 8.1 min; 2.19 mmol/g at 75% RH, half capacity in 6.8 min. Outdoor air: 50 cycles in 3 days, 22.1 mmol/g/day (= 0.97 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day; ~1.33 mmol/g per cycle at 16.7 cycles/day). Numbers from the journal abstract as returned by search; full text paywalled.
items.regeneration: 60 C (press material: full adsorption-desorption cycle in ~90 min). Desorption atmosphere not confirmed from primary text; if N2 purge as for COF-999 the same back-pressure caveat applies.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only 50 outdoor cycles (3 days) reported in abstract. At 16.7 cycles/day a 3-year life means ~18,000 cycles - 360x the demonstrated count.
items.cost: Not reported. Productivity cuts sorbent inventory to ~2.8 kg per t CO2/yr versus ~10 kg for a 1 mol/kg, 6 cycles/day amine reference (OptiLex calc), which attacks the dominant capital term rather than energy.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4 powder. Supported by Atoco (Yaghi start-up); Atoco statements of multi-ton production 'within a year' (Dec 2024) are company claims with no public verification found.
items.bottleneck: Faster cycling multiplies cycles per year, so the per-cycle fade tolerance tightens to ~0.001%/cycle; no long-run or shaped-contactor data.

items.name: Diamine-appended Mg2(dobpdc) family (mmen-, m-2-m-, e-2-, tetraamine variants): cooperative step-isotherm MOFs
items.mechanism: CO2 inserts into Mg-N bonds forming ammonium carbamate chains along the pore; cooperative, so the isotherm is a step. Promise: large working capacity from a small temperature swing.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Independent assessment (Farha group, Northwestern, Chem. Sci. 2023): mmen-Mg2(dobpdc) with 50-60% amine loading takes 1.5 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 25 C (dry isotherm); under humid CO2 (50% RH) 1.7 mmol/g CO2 plus 3 mmol/g H2O. Original report (McDonald 2012, via search snippet) 2.0 mmol/g at 0.39 mbar, 25 C. Water isotherm jumps at 40-50% RH to 40 mmol/g at 90% RH.
items.regeneration: Best at 120 C under dynamic vacuum or 150 C under N2; CO2 released at 90-100 C in TGA. Diamine fragments appear only above 200 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 50 cycles (pure or 15% CO2, not 400 ppm): 85-90% capacity retained dry; 80% when desorbed under CO2. Ten ambient-air cycles at 45-50% RH: 15% loss of total uptake. Accelerated ageing at 80% RH, 70 C for 12 h stripped the amine to trace and cut 400 ppm uptake from 1.5 to 0.07 mmol/g (recoverable by re-amination). Stated stable only up to 50% RH.
items.cost: Not reported for the appended material; parent MOF-74-type frameworks estimated $13-71/kg at scale depending on route (literature TEA, via search snippet).
items.trl_and_scale: Mosaic Materials (acquired by Baker Hughes 2022) announced DAC pilots with HIF Global (Chile, Texas) in 2023; no public performance data or 2025-26 status found. Tetraamine variant showed 1,000 humid flue-gas/steam cycles (Kim, Science 2020) - point source, not DAC.
items.bottleneck: Amine is held by a coordinate bond, so hot humid conditions displace it; plus oxidation and step-pressure limits (next two items).

items.name: Oxidative degradation of diamine-appended MOFs (Xiong...Long, JACS 147, 25761, 2025)
items.mechanism: O2 attacks the appended diamine via carbon-centred radicals (initiated by OH radical or trace metals), cleaving C-N bonds to aldehydes, imines, ethylamine; the framework itself stays intact. Same chemistry applies to any alkylamine sorbent, including PEI-in-COF.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Not an uptake study. e-2-Mg2(dobpdc): ~15% loss of CO2 capacity after 60 days in dry air at ~25 C. In 1 atm dry O2 at 100 C for 5 days, diamine loading fell from 100% to 52%; argon at 100 C for 10 days caused only minor change.
items.regeneration: Implication: any regeneration step that exposes hot sorbent to air is the main damage route; vacuum or steam purging of O2 before heating matters.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Fe-doped sample (~2,700 ppm Fe) fell from 90% to 22% diamine loading in 5 days O2 at 100 C - trace transition metals accelerate decay. Design fix shown: tmen (alpha-carbons fully substituted) in Mg2(olz) kept ~98% of the amine after 10 days O2 at 100 C, but only ~80% loading was reached in Mg2(dobpdc) and cooperativity/capacity trade-offs are flagged. OptiLex calc: 15%/60 days = 0.27%/day, half-life ~0.7 yr at ambient before any hot exposure.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3 mechanistic study, mg-g scale.
items.bottleneck: Oxidation rate sets sorbent life; accelerated tests are dry and O2-rich, so the rate under real humid 400 ppm cycling is still unmeasured.

items.name: Step-isotherm kinetics and capture-fraction ceiling for cooperative MOFs in DAC (Martell, Milner, Siegelman, Long, Chem. Sci. 2020; Darunte et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2019)
items.mechanism: A step isotherm adsorbs nothing below the step pressure, so the bed cannot polish air below p_step; near the step there is an induction period (nucleation-and-growth, Avrami kinetics).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Martell 2020 (TGA): most diamine variants show an induction period before peak uptake rate, most pronounced near the step temperature, and inverse-Arrhenius behaviour (faster when colder). It cites DAC breakthrough tests on m-2-m-Mg2(dobpdc) where CO2 broke through early, then outlet concentration fell again - delayed onset. A 2026 Jones-group study (RSC Industrial Chem. Mater., abstract via search only) reports amine-impregnated Mg2(dobpdc) at -20 to 25 C under dry 400 ppm showed no shock-wave breakthrough and did not reach 1 CO2 per diamine.
items.regeneration: Small swing is the selling point, but only if adsorption sits well above the step.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed.
items.cost: Not addressed.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab TGA and small fixed beds.
items.bottleneck: OptiLex calc (ceiling = 1 - p_step/p_feed, step enthalpy -71 kJ/mol): a step at 0.10 mbar at 25 C allows at most 75% capture at 25 C, 37% at 35 C and none at 45 C; a step at 0.05 mbar gives 88%, 68%, 24%. Hot-climate operation needs p_step(25 C) well below 0.05 mbar, which pushes regeneration temperature up.

items.name: Fluorinated ultramicroporous physisorbents: TIFSIX-3-Ni, SIFSIX-3-Ni/Cu, NbOFFIVE-1-Ni, SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta
items.mechanism: Physisorption in ~0.33-0.35 nm channels lined with MF6(2-) pillars; strong electrostatics give DAC-level affinity without amines (so no amine oxidation).
items.uptake_and_conditions: TIFSIX-3-Ni, independent re-measurement (Low, Danaci, Petit, Imperial, Energy & Fuels 2024): 1.11 mmol/g at 0.4 mbar, 25 C, dry, single-gas (original Kumar 2017: 1.05; Qst ~50 kJ/mol) - capacity reproduced. Batch-to-batch uptake varied 0.88-1.11 mmol/g on 4x scale-up. NbOFFIVE-1-Ni: 1.3 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 298 K dry (search snippet). Literature humid co-adsorption: ~60-70% CO2 capacity loss at 74-75% RH (measured at 3,000 ppm or pure CO2, not 400 ppm).
items.regeneration: Tested with 160 C desorption in air; lower-temperature inert/vacuum desorption suggested but not demonstrated. Authors judge steam desorption unlikely to be tolerated.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Original stability claim not reproduced: after 14 days at 40 C/75% RH air, 0.4 mbar uptake fell 0.88 to 0.51 mmol/g; after 6 months ambient air to 0.39; after 50 ambient-air TSA cycles pellets fell 0.94 to 0.44 mmol/g with 36% loss on the long-cycle check (OptiLex: ~0.9%/cycle, half capacity in ~78 cycles). Authors: "limited stability of the MOF under humid and oxidative conditions". SIFSIX-3-Ni shows the same water-driven degradation (Barsoum, JACS 2024).
items.cost: Not quantified; HF-forming fluorinated precursors raise safety and cost (noted in Chen et al. 2024).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3; pelletised binder-free at lab scale; previously sold by MOF Technologies (now Nuada).
items.bottleneck: Water: competitive adsorption plus irreversible framework hydrolysis above the water-isotherm step; would need pre-drying of air, which costs more than the capture step saves.

items.name: CALF-20 (Zn triazolate-oxalate; Lin...Shimizu, Science 374, 1464, 2021; Svante/BASF)
items.mechanism: Hydrophobic physisorbent; CO2 out-competes water below ~40% RH. The one MOF with proven industrial durability, but for flue gas.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 2.6 mmol/g at 0.15 bar, 298 K (2.47 at 0.1 bar); 4.07 at 1.2 bar, 293 K; heat of adsorption ~ -40 kJ/mol. Selective over water only below 40% RH; negligible CO2 uptake at 70% RH (search snippet). No measured 400 ppm value found; OptiLex Langmuir fit to the two points gives ~0.017 mmol/g at 0.4 mbar (dG -5.6 kJ/mol versus -19.2 needed for half filling), about 2% of COF-999's dry uptake.
items.regeneration: Low-pressure steam / rapid thermal swing on structured laminate (Svante rotary contactor).
items.stability_and_lifetime: >450,000 steam cycles and wet acid gas durability (Science abstract) - the lifetime benchmark any DAC framework should be compared against.
items.cost: ~$25-30/kg estimated at ton scale (as cited in Chen et al., Adv. Sci. 2024).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7-8 for point source: multi-kg batches in 2021, BASF commercial supply agreement 2023, Svante Redwood filter plant opened 2025 with a claimed capacity for 10 Mt CO2/yr of filters (company claim). Not a DAC sorbent.
items.bottleneck: Binding is ~14 kJ/mol too weak for 400 ppm; it shows durability and scale are achievable for MOFs, but not at DAC binding strength.

items.name: MOF-808-Lys / MOF-808-TAPA (amino-acid and polyamine functionalised Zr MOF; Chen...Yaghi, JACS 146, 2835, 2024)
items.mechanism: Amines bound to Zr6 nodes (amino acid carboxylate) or covalently to a chloro-functionalised linker; water switches the product to bicarbonate, 1 CO2 per amine.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2: MOF-808-Lys 0.612 mmol/g dry, 1.205 at 50% RH (+97%); MOF-808-TAPA 0.498 dry, 0.872 at 50% RH (+75%). Temperature-swing cycling of MOF-808-Lys at 400 ppm, 50% RH: mean working capacity 0.696 mmol/g per cycle (truncated 'quick scan' cycles).
items.regeneration: Temperature swing; cycles stopped at 20 ppm outlet CO2 (purge-type desorption).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Short cycling run only; no long-term or oxidative data. Zr-MOF backbone is hydrolytically robust.
items.cost: Not reported; Zr and trimesic acid are commodity-adjacent, but the node-capping step takes days.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3 powder.
items.bottleneck: Capacity about half of COF-999 at the same humidity; lifetime unknown. Same pattern as COF-999: humidity roughly doubles amine uptake, the opposite of physisorbents.

items.name: Amine-impregnated MOFs: TEPA/PEI in MIL-101(Cr) at sub-ambient temperature (Rim...Lively, Jones, JACS Au 2, 380, 2022) and TAEA@MIL-101(Cr) (2026)
items.mechanism: Liquid oligoamines physically loaded into large-pore MOFs - the conventional amine/support recipe with a MOF as support. Weak chemisorption sites become useful when the air is cold.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 30 wt% TEPA-MIL-101(Cr), 400 ppm: 0.39 mmol/g at 25 C rising to 1.12 mmol/g at -20 C; fixed-bed runs dry and at 70% RH. 2026 benchmark (abstract via search, unverified): TAEA@MIL-101(Cr) 3.12 mmol/g equilibrium at 298 K, 12.4 wt% dynamic dry, 9.7 wt% at 50% RH, regenerated at 50 C.
items.regeneration: Working capacity 0.72 mmol/g over 15 cycles with adsorption at -20 C and desorption at only 25 C - regeneration with ambient heat in cold climates.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 15 cycles shown. Impregnated (non-tethered) amines can leach or evaporate; Cr-based support is a toxicity/cost concern.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3; earlier process models used PEI-MIL-101(Cr) films on monoliths.
items.bottleneck: Only works where air is cold; amine volatility and oxidation unresolved; 15 cycles.

items.name: Carbonic-anhydrase-mimic Zn-OH MOFs: MFU-4l-(OH) (Wright...Dinca, Chem 4, 2894, 2018) and Zn(ZnOH)4(bibta)3 (Bien...Wade, JACS 2018)
items.mechanism: Biology import: CO2 inserts into a terminal Zn-OH bond to give Zn-bicarbonate, the carbonic anhydrase active-site reaction, at azolate-bound Zn nodes. Amine-free chemisorption, so the amine C-N oxidation route is absent.
items.uptake_and_conditions: MFU-4l-(OH), 25 C, dry single-gas: 0.86 mmol/g taken up below 17 Torr (first Zn-OH per node), 3.41 mmol/g at 800 Torr, matching 3.36 mmol/g of Zn-OH sites. Zero-coverage Qst 81 kJ/mol, falling to 62-35 for the second CO2 per node. No 400 ppm breakthrough or humid data in this paper. Bien et al. report strong trace-CO2 capture and mild regeneration for the bibta analogue (abstract only).
items.regeneration: Mild temperature claimed (abstract); with 81 kJ/mol the first site would need >140 C at 1 kPa by the OptiLex window, the later sites much less.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not cycled under humid air in the sources read. Water competes for Zn-OH and promotes isotope exchange (i.e. water is active at the site).
items.cost: Bistriazolate linkers are specialty chemicals; not costed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3.
items.bottleneck: Only one of four Zn-OH per node binds strongly, so DAC-relevant capacity is <=0.86 mmol/g with an 81 kJ/mol penalty; humid 400 ppm performance unmeasured.

items.name: Computational screening for DAC MOFs: Open DAC 2023 / 2025 and the EPFL correspondence (Jin, Garcia, Smit, ACS Cent. Sci. 11, 868, 2025)
items.mechanism: DFT binding energies of CO2 and H2O (plus N2, O2 in ODAC25) in thousands of MOFs with machine-learned potentials trained on them; 'promising' means CO2 bound more strongly than water and beyond ~50 kJ/mol.
items.uptake_and_conditions: ODAC23 flagged 135 of 5,961 pristine MOFs as promising. Independent recomputation (same PBE-D3 functional, different code, re-relaxed empty frameworks) found only 1 MOF (ASEJOZ01) meeting the criterion, and it was not on the ODAC list; recomputed CO2 binding energies fell in the -50 to -10 kJ/mol range.
items.regeneration: Not modelled.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not modelled - hydrolysis, oxidation and amine loss are outside the dataset.
items.cost: Free data; ODAC25 (arXiv 2508.03162): ~60-70 million DFT single points on ~15,000 MOFs including amine-functionalised and defective structures.
items.trl_and_scale: Dataset/benchmark; no ODAC-predicted DAC sorbent has a published humid 400 ppm measurement that I could find.
items.bottleneck: About 40% of the underlying CoRE-MOF 2019 structures were flagged as charged (missing H or wrongly removed ions), inflating binding energies; binding energy is a difference of two large numbers sensitive to framework relaxation. ODAC25 ships MOFChecker flags but its headline discussion uses the unfiltered set.

items.name: NUS-110 (dimeric butylamine linker MOF made mechanochemically; JACS 2025, doi 10.1021/jacs.5c12750)
items.mechanism: Alkylamine built into a rigid polycyclic linker (rather than appended or impregnated), giving a sigmoidal isotherm and sterically protected amines.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2: 0.89 mmol/g dry; 1.35 mmol/g at 30% RH; humid breakthrough shows faster kinetics.
items.regeneration: Not given in abstract.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Stable over 20 DAC cycles; oxidative stability claimed from steric protection (abstract only; full text not accessible).
items.cost: Solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis is a cost argument, not a costed figure.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3.
items.bottleneck: 20 cycles; capacity below COF-999; claims unverified beyond abstract.

items.name: Cheap aluminium MOFs: MIL-120(Al)-AP, Al-fumarate, MIL-160 (Chen...Serre, Adv. Sci. 2024)
items.mechanism: Physisorption on mu2-OH-lined 1-D channels of Al-carboxylate frameworks made in water at ambient pressure from commodity acids.
items.uptake_and_conditions: MIL-120(Al)-AP: 1.9 mmol/g at 0.1 bar, 298 K (flue-gas condition). No 400 ppm figure reported; physisorption of this strength gives a few hundredths of a mmol/g at 0.4 mbar by the same scaling as CALF-20.
items.regeneration: Pressure/vacuum or mild temperature swing (point source).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Hydrothermally robust; shaped and tested in humid breakthrough at flue-gas concentrations.
items.cost: Techno-economic estimate $12.94/kg (2022 prices) at ~1,000 t/yr - the lowest credible MOF cost found, versus $2,916/kg from lab-catalogue reagent prices.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4-5 for point source; Al-fumarate is already made at tonne scale industrially.
items.bottleneck: Not DAC-capable as is. Value to a DAC programme is as a $13/kg water-stable scaffold onto which a strong site could be grafted.

items.name: ZnH-MFU-4l (zinc hydride MOF for hot CO2; Rohde...Long, Science 386, 814, 2024)
items.mechanism: CO2 inserts reversibly into terminal Zn-H to give Zn-formate; binding strong enough to work at 300 C.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Captures CO2 at ~300 C from 20-30% CO2 streams (cement/steel) and down to ~4% (gas turbine). Not tested or intended for 400 ppm ambient air.
items.regeneration: Isothermal pressure/concentration swing at 300 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 508 isothermal cycles at 300 C with >96% capacity retained (press summary of the paper).
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3.
items.bottleneck: Irrelevant to ambient DAC directly (hydride site is water-reactive at ambient conditions); listed because it shows non-amine insertion chemistry can be cycled hundreds of times.

items.name: Scale-up and pilot status of framework sorbents for DAC, 2025-2026 (Airthena/AspiraDAC, Mosaic/Baker Hughes, Atoco)
items.mechanism: MOF-polymer nanocomposite or coated-laminate contactors with temperature-vacuum swing.
items.uptake_and_conditions: CSIRO Airthena pilot (as cited in Low et al. 2024): 8 kg CO2 captured from ambient air over 2,680 cycles; press figures of 6 kg/day and ~2 kWh electricity per kg CO2 (= 7.2 GJ/t electric). No peer-reviewed plant-scale 400 ppm humid dataset exists for any MOF or COF.
items.regeneration: Low-temperature (reported 80 C class) resistive/solar-thermal heating with vacuum for Airthena.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 2,680 cycles is the longest framework-sorbent DAC cycle count found, but capacity-fade data are not public.
items.cost: AspiraDAC sold 500 t to Stripe/Frontier at $1,000/t for delivery by 2027 (purchase price, not cost). CSIRO press claims of ~$100/t are unsubstantiated.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5-6 at best (Airthena); Mosaic DAC pilots with HIF announced 2023 with no published results; Atoco COF production plans are statements only; Svante's commercial MOF business is point-source.
items.bottleneck: No framework sorbent has public long-duration DAC field data; incumbents (amine resins, PEI/silica) keep the plant slots.

bottlenecks: Lifetime evidence gap. Best DAC frameworks are shown for 50-100 outdoor cycles (COF-1000, COF-999); OptiLex calc: at 1.28 mol/kg, $20/t sorbent cost needs 17,752 cycles at $20/kg, 44,379 at $50/kg, 177,516 at $200/kg. Keeping 80% capacity over 20,000 cycles allows 0.0011% fade per cycle; a 100-cycle test would show 0.11% loss, far below the ~3% scatter in reported cycle data, so current papers cannot confirm or refute the required lifetime.

Amine oxidation. Measured: e-2-Mg2(dobpdc) loses ~15% capacity in 60 days of dry air at 25 C (0.27%/day, half-life ~0.7 yr); diamine loading drops 100% to 52% in 5 days of O2 at 100 C, and 90% to 22% with ~2,700 ppm Fe. The mechanism (C-centred radicals at alpha-carbons) applies to every alkylamine sorbent including COF-999-type PEI; no humid 400 ppm long-run oxidation data exist for the COFs.

Regeneration under real CO2 back-pressure. The headline 60 C regeneration of COF-999 is under N2 purge. With the paper's Qst of 53 kJ/mol the equilibrium CO2 pressure at full DAC loading is ~3.8 mbar at 60 C, ~11 mbar at 80 C, ~29 mbar at 100 C; working capacity against 1 kPa CO2 is zero at 60 C and ~0.56 mol/kg at 100 C (dry Langmuir fit). Low-temperature claims therefore trade heat for vacuum work or steam.

Water. For amine frameworks water doubles uptake (COF-999 0.96 to 2.05 mmol/g; MOF-808-Lys 0.61 to 1.21) but co-adsorbs at ~2.4 mol H2O per mol CO2 in 'hydrophobic' COF-999 (0.09 g/g at 50% RH), a ~2.4 GJ/t latent load, the largest term in a 4.6 GJ/t powder-only heat budget. For physisorbents water is fatal: TIFSIX-3-Ni loses ~0.9% per ambient-air cycle; CALF-20 is selective only below 40% RH and binds ~14 kJ/mol too weakly for 400 ppm (~0.017 mmol/g estimated).

Step-isotherm limits for cooperative MOFs. Capture fraction cannot exceed 1 - p_step/p_feed: a step at 0.10 mbar (25 C) caps capture at 75% at 25 C, 37% at 35 C, 0% at 45 C; coordinated amines are stripped at 80% RH/70 C (1.5 to 0.07 mmol/g in 12 h); induction-period kinetics lower bed utilisation.

Cost and scale. Only physisorbent MOFs unsuited to DAC are at tonne scale (CALF-20 ~$25-30/kg, MIL-120(Al) ~$13/kg). No DAC-grade framework has a published cost; COF-999's route uses azide monomers and aziridine and its authors list scalability as future work. All DAC framework data are on powders at gram scale; shaped-contactor kinetics and thermal mass are unmeasured.

Reliability of computed and reported numbers. ODAC23's 135 'promising' MOFs shrank to 1 on independent recomputation, with ~40% of source structures mis-charged. Experimentally, TIFSIX-3-Ni capacity varied 0.88-1.11 mmol/g between batches and its published humidity stability was not reproduced; no independent reproduction of COF-999/COF-1000 was found. Calculations: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/mof_map_calc.py
open_problems: Oxidation-proof chemisorption site on a covalent tether: combine the COF-999 architecture (covalently anchored amines in a metal-free, hydrolysis-proof framework) with the Long-group rule that fully substituted alpha-carbons block radical degradation (tmen kept ~98% after 10 days O2 at 100 C). Testable by executed calculation (binding free energy must stay near -19 to -22 kJ/mol despite steric bulk) and by a small accelerated-O2 experiment.

A lifetime verifier: an accelerated-ageing protocol plus kinetic model (O2 pressure, temperature, humidity, trace-metal content) that predicts 20,000-cycle capacity from a few hundred hours of data, validated against the published Mg2(dobpdc) and TIFSIX datasets. No such standard exists; it would let any candidate be ranked on $/t rather than mmol/g.

Measure or model COF-999-class sorbents under true product conditions (1-10 kPa CO2, steam or vacuum, humid loading) to find the real regeneration temperature and energy; the humid isosteric heat (bicarbonate route) is unreported and decides whether 60-80 C is achievable.

Exploit the humidity dependence deliberately: amine frameworks hold ~2x more CO2 wet than dry, so a humidity or combined moisture-temperature swing could release CO2 with less heat. A patent on humidity control of step-shaped adsorbents exists, so prior-art search is needed before claiming novelty.

Cheap scaffold plus strong site: graft tethered, oxidation-resistant amines (or Zn-OH type sites) onto a $13/kg water-stable Al-MOF or other commodity porous support, aiming for COF-999-like uptake (about 2 mmol/g humid) at under $30/kg.

Amine-free chemisorption tuned into the DAC window: carbonic-anhydrase-style Zn-OH sites bind the first CO2 at 81 kJ/mol (too strong) and later ones at 35-62 (too weak). Design problem: node/linker electronics that put all sites near 60-70 kJ/mol with dS about -165 J/mol/K, and that tolerate water at the site.

Step-position engineering for hot climates: find diamine/framework pairs with p_step below 0.05 mbar at 35 C without pushing the desorption temperature past ~120 C, or mixed-amine materials with two steps; the OptiLex window calculation can pre-screen step enthalpy and entropy pairs.

An error-checked computational screen: rerun a DAC filter on the MOFChecker-clean subset of ODAC25 with re-relaxed empty frameworks, add water at open metal sites and a hydrolysis-stability proxy, and compare against the roughly dozen sorbents with measured humid 400 ppm data as a calibration set before trusting any new hit.

Contactor-level questions nobody has measured for frameworks: uptake kinetics and capacity after shaping (binder, laminate, monolith), and the added thermal mass; COF-1000's 16.7 cycles/day advantage only survives if the shaped form keeps the ~7-8 min half-time.

key_claims.claim: The strongest published framework result for DAC (COF-999) is 2.05 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2, 50% RH, 25 C, with 100 outdoor-air cycles over 20 days averaging 1.28 mmol/g per cycle - but regeneration at 60 C was done under flowing N2, and lifetime evidence stops at 100 cycles (COF-1000: 50 cycles). Economic viability needs roughly 18,000-180,000 cycles and desorption against real CO2 pressure, neither of which has been shown.

OpenDAC-style DFT screening is not yet a trustworthy source of DAC candidates: an independent recomputation found only 1 MOF meeting the 'promising' criterion versus 135 of 5,961 reported by ODAC23, and that one was not on the original list; about 40% of the underlying structures carried spurious net charge. Any screening pack must use structure-checked inputs and be calibrated on measured humid 400 ppm data.

surprises: The widely quoted '60 C regeneration' of COF-999 is a nitrogen-purge result. Using the paper's own 53 kJ/mol, the sorbent can only push CO2 out at about 3.8 mbar at 60 C, so making concentrated CO2 at that temperature needs deep vacuum or steam.

COF-999 is described as hydrophobic, yet at 50% RH it still holds ~5 mol water per kg against 2.05 mol CO2 (2.4 H2O per CO2) - similar to the 2:1 assumed for ordinary solid amines, so the water heat penalty is not removed.

Outdoor performance of COF-999 was 62% of the lab humid number (1.28 vs 2.05 mmol/g), and the 'no loss over 100 cycles' statement is supported by 12 selected cycles at matched humidity plus before/after isotherms, not by a flat 100-cycle trace.

A diamine-appended MOF lost ~15% of its capacity just sitting in dry room-temperature air for 60 days, and trace iron (0.27 wt%) more than doubled the high-temperature degradation - impurity control in synthesis may matter as much as amine choice.
An independent lab reproduced TIFSIX-3-Ni's capacity (1.11 vs 1.05 mmol/g) but not its published humidity stability: uptake roughly halved after 14 days at 40 C/75% RH or 50 air cycles.

COF-1000's real advance is cycle speed, not capacity or energy: ~0.97 kg CO2 per kg sorbent per day cuts sorbent inventory about 3.5x versus a 6-cycle/day amine reference, which targets the capital charge OptiLex already identified as dominant - but it also consumes cycle life 3x faster.

CALF-20, the only MOF with tonne-scale production and >450,000 demonstrated steam cycles, is useless for air capture: its binding free energy is about -5.6 kJ/mol against the -19.2 kJ/mol needed, giving roughly 2% of COF-999's dry uptake at 400 ppm.

Humidity has opposite effects on the two sorbent classes: it roughly doubles uptake for tethered-amine frameworks (bicarbonate formation) and destroys both capacity and structure in fluorinated physisorbents - so 'humid stability' screens must be class-specific.
No public long-duration DAC field data exist for any MOF or COF in 2026; the longest cycle count found is CSIRO's Airthena pilot (2,680 cycles, 8 kg CO2 total) with no published fade curve.

verifs.claim: The strongest published framework result for DAC (COF-999) is 2.05 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2, 50% RH, 25 C, with 100 outdoor-air cycles over 20 days averaging 1.28 mmol/g per cycle - but regeneration at 60 C was done under flowing N2, and lifetime evidence stops at 100 cycles (COF-1000: 50 cycles). Economic viability needs roughly 18,000-180,000 cycles and desorption against real CO2 pressure, neither of which has been shown.
verifs.corrected_claim: COF-999 (Zhou et al., Nature 635, 96-101, 2024) is the most prominent COF result for DAC, not demonstrably the strongest framework result. It measured 2.05 (+/-0.03) mmol/g by dynamic breakthrough in simulated air (400 ppm CO2, 50% RH, 25 C) on milligram-scale samples; dry capacity is 0.96 mmol/g. It ran 100 temperature-swing cycles on Berkeley outdoor air over 20 days, averaging 1.28 mmol/g per cycle. Those were deliberately partial cycles at lower humidity (RH 28.5-51%, mean 39%; CO2 410-517 ppm), so 1.28 against 2.05 is not degradation. Regeneration at 60 C (column wall temperature) used an N2 purge that released CO2 at sub-1000 ppm; no concentrated CO2 product was shown, and the regeneration energy (259 kJ/mol) is calculated, not measured. Outdoor-air lifetime evidence stops at 100 cycles (COF-999) and 50 cycles in 3 days (COF-1000, Nat. Sustain. 2026). COF-1000 also ran 200 simulated-air cycles with no loss, so the longest cycling evidence for the family is 200 cycles, not 100. The "18,000-180,000 cycles" requirement is not in either paper; it is an outside assumption that depends on cycle time (at the demonstrated 5-15 cycles/day, a 1-3 year sorbent life is about 2,000-16,000 cycles). The gap to commercial lifetime and to desorption into concentrated CO2 is real, but that range should be labelled an assumption.
verifs.caveats:
**What I could check.** The Nature main text is paywalled and the authors' read-only link sits behind a CAPTCHA, so I did not read it. I verified against the abstract, the publisher-hosted Supplementary Information, the peer review file, the Fig. 4 source-data spreadsheet, and the COF-1000 full text from the Yaghi group site.

**Confirmed**
- **Capacity:** 2.05 (+/-0.03) mmol/g at 50% RH and 400 ppm, quoted from the revised manuscript in the peer review file; SI Fig. 16 gives 25 C and 2.02 for a single batch. It is 1.69 at 25% RH and 2.09 at 75% RH.
- **Outdoor cycles:** the Fig. 4 source data has 100 cycles spanning 19.3 days, with mean uptake 1.283 mmol/g (range 1.03-1.48).
- **Measured, not simulated:** all capacity and cycling numbers are experimental. Only the regeneration energy is calculated, which a reviewer noted.

**Changes how the claim should be used**
- **1.28 is a partial-cycle figure.** SI Table 1 footnotes it as "Not cycling under full capacity"; SI Fig. 24 shows an adsorption cutoff at 300 ppm downstream and a desorption cutoff at 20 ppm.
- **Late-cycle uptake is lower.** The first 10 cycles average 1.32 mmol/g and the last 10 average 1.18. Uptake tracks ambient humidity (r = 0.85), and humidity fell from about 40-45% to about 35% in the second half. The authors report unchanged isotherm, breakthrough, FT-IR and SEM after cycling. So this is probably a humidity effect, but 100 cycles cannot exclude slow degradation.
- **N2 purge.** SI Fig. 21 states desorption "under N2 flow" at 60 C, and the desorption traces stay within a sensor range of 0.6-985 ppm. That the outdoor cycles specifically used N2 is inferred from the SI and from the COF-1000 methods, which state a 50-sccm N2 purge on the same type of setup.
- **60 C is a wall temperature.** The COF-1000 paper says a 60 C wall corresponds to a 41 C bed centre.
- **Scale is milligrams.** COF-999 desorption kinetics used 5 mg; COF-1000 outdoor cycling used 4 mg.
- **"Strongest framework result" is not supported.** COF-1000 reports 2.19 mmol/g at 75% RH with faster kinetics. The COF-999 SI's own comparison table lists a non-framework amine/silica sorbent at 3.36 mmol/g. Amine-appended MOFs with higher 400 ppm capacities exist, but that is from memory and was not checked here.
- **The 18,000-180,000 range is unsourced.** I could not trace it to a publication. It matches roughly 100 cycles/day for 0.5-5 years, or 24 cycles/day for 2-20 years.

**Sources**

verifs.claim: OpenDAC-style DFT screening is not yet a trustworthy source of DAC candidates: an independent recomputation found only 1 MOF meeting the 'promising' criterion versus 135 of 5,961 reported by ODAC23, and that one was not on the original list; about 40% of the underlying structures carried spurious net charge. Any screening pack must use structure-checked inputs and be calibrated on measured humid 400 ppm data.
verifs.corrected_claim: ODAC23's list of promising DAC MOFs is not reliable as published. Jin, Garcia and Smit (ACS Central Science 2025, 11, 868-871, a Correspondence) recomputed PBE-D3 binding energies for a filtered subset of about 714 CoRE MOF 2019 structures (uncharged, closed-shell, under 500 atoms) and found only one, ASEJOZ01, meeting ODAC23's criterion (CO2 binding stronger than 50 kJ/mol and stronger than H2O binding). ODAC23 had reported 135 of 5,961 pristine MOFs meeting it, and ASEJOZ01 was not among them. MOFchecker flagged about 40% of the underlying CoRE MOF structures as "charged" (2,052 of 5,168 in the authors' Zenodo table), usually from missing hydrogens or wrongly removed charged solvent. The authors attribute ODAC23's extreme binding energies to local-minimum artifacts in the empty-framework reference energy and say the ML models should be retrained. All of this is DFT single-molecule binding energy, not measured uptake at 400 ppm or under humidity. The requirement to calibrate on measured humid 400 ppm data is our own inference, not a statement in the source; the source supports structure-checked inputs and re-relaxed empty-framework references. ODAC25 (arXiv 2508.03162, Aug 2025) has since adopted both the re-relaxation fix and MOFChecker flags, so the critique applies to ODAC23 data and models, not automatically to ODAC25.
verifs.caveats:
The headline numbers match the primary source. PMC itself was behind a reCAPTCHA, so I read the same article's open-access full text via Europe PMC and checked the authors' Zenodo data (zenodo.org/records/14802658) directly. The SI PDF was not read.

Points that change how the claim should be used:
- **Denominators differ.** The "1" comes from about 714 recomputed structures (row count of the Zenodo binding_energy.csv; the main text gives no number), not from all 5,961. "1 versus 135" is not like-for-like, though the conclusion that ODAC23's list was mostly artifact stands: the discarded charged structures were the ones giving unrealistically high binding energies.
- **The one survivor is marginal.** ASEJOZ01 has CO2 binding of -51.4 kJ/mol, 1.4 kJ/mol past the threshold and within PBE-D3 error. The sibling entry ASEJOZ (same framework, different CSD refinement) gives H2O binding of -125.6 kJ/mol and fails. Do not treat ASEJOZ01 as a validated lead.
- **"Charged" is a MOFchecker flag, not a per-structure verification.** The ODAC25 authors dispute the reliability of the semi-empirical oxidation-state assignment and kept flagged MOFs in a "full" set alongside a "filtered" one. A further 779 of 5,168 are flagged geometrically wrong in the Zenodo table.
- **Everything is simulated.** These are 0 K, single-adsorbate DFT binding energies (CP2K versus ODAC23's VASP). The only experimental anchor is the remark that measured heats of adsorption typically fall between -50 and -10 kJ/mol. There are no 400 ppm, humidity or cycling data.
- **The source is narrower than "not trustworthy".** It is a short Correspondence about binding energies only. It praises ODAC23's flexible-framework relaxation and open data, and says the other DFT results are unaffected except where input structures are problematic. The authors also note their own method does not guarantee the global minimum.
- **ODAC23 is superseded.** ODAC25 (nearly 60M DFT calculations, 15,000 MOFs) re-relaxes the empty MOF after every adsorbate relaxation, uses the lowest-energy reference, corrects k-point errors (about 7% of ODAC23 calculations had errors well above 0.2 eV), and ships MOFChecker v0.9.6 flags. A screening pack should use ODAC25's filtered subset or CoRE MOF 2025 rather than ODAC23. ODAC25 still has no direct experimental validation of adsorption energies; only Henry coefficients are compared with experiment, so the need for measured humid 400 ppm calibration remains a sound design rule even though this source does not state it.

items.name: ASU outdoor moisture-driven DAC pilot (Purolite A501 beads on a conveyor into alkaline pond), Flory et al. 2025 preprint
items.mechanism: Strong-base quaternary-ammonium anion-exchange resin (carbonate/bicarbonate form) dries in wind, binds CO2; is then dipped in alkaline water where CO2 is released as dissolved bicarbonate. Passive air contact, no heat or vacuum in the capture step.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Effective CO2 capacity used in TEA 0.675 mmol/g (A501, outdoor-representative); wind tunnel 5 m/s, 15% RH, 25 C: 30 min drying before any CO2 binds, 80 min to 90% loading in thin mesh tubes vs 275 min in a mesh bag; ~90% of CO2 released within 15 min in 10 mM Na2CO3. Outdoor 7-day trial in Mesa AZ (mean 24.4 C, 16.7% RH): 782 g CO2 delivered (~112 g/day) from a 4.2 m2 raceway pond system; model predicted 762 g. Rates used in TEA: adsorption 0.08 umol/g/s, desorption 0.5 umol/g/s.
items.regeneration: Liquid-water/alkaline-solution wetting; product is CO2 dissolved in alkaline brine (not gas). Getting to 15 MPa gas needs a modelled thermal extraction + compression step (+$280/t practical, +$109/t aspirational). Electricity 490 kWh/t net (practical), 350 kWh/t (aspirational), mostly conveyor.
items.stability_and_lifetime: TEA assumes 5-year resin life (practical) and 10-year (aspirational) as assumptions, not measurements; see companion durability item which contradicts the 5-year assumption under biotic outdoor use.
items.cost: Authors' TEA (nth-of-a-kind, 100 kt/yr): practical $670/t into solution, $950/t net at 15 MPa (95% CI $530-1,500); aspirational $51/t into solution, $160/t at 15 MPa, requires 4.0 mmol/g capacity and 50 wt% water uptake (neither demonstrated together). Resin price range $7-100/kg (mean $54/kg); resin purchase+replacement ~ $200/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL ~4-5; ~100 g CO2/day outdoor, 7-day trial (2024-25). Largest openly reported measured moisture-swing field data found.
items.bottleneck: Water uptake 330 wt% (3.3 g/g) -> ~100 g water per g CO2, ~80x the 3:1 molar (1.2 kg/kg) limit stated in the paper body (abstract says 33-fold; my check 3.3 g/g / 29.7 mg CO2/g = 111 g/g supports the body). Drying, not CO2 uptake, sets cycle time (2 h day, 4 h night).

items.name: Outdoor durability of the same A501 resin over 302 days (Flory et al. 2025 companion preprint, cyanobacteria cultivation)
items.mechanism: Same moisture-driven resin packets cycled wet/dry outdoors in Mesa AZ across four seasons, partly immersed in live algae/cyanobacteria culture at pH ~10.
items.uptake_and_conditions: After 35 days (142 cycles, 33 days in culture): capacity ~25% of initial, restorable to ~70% by peracetic acid/bleach/HCl wash but with 3-4x slower kinetics. After 302 days (~1,380 wet/dry cycles, 78 days in culture, 1.8 MJ/m2 UV): capacity ~10% of initial, only ~35% restorable.
items.regeneration: Liquid immersion in alkaline culture medium.
items.stability_and_lifetime: FTIR and TGA show loss of quaternary ammonium groups after 190 and 302 days; beads fracture mechanically; ~90% of mesh packets damaged over summer. Authors cite Velazco-Medel et al.: QA polymers with bicarbonate counter-ion oxidise within four weeks of wet-dry cycling in air, faster than chloride form. CONFOUND: biofouling, pH 10 immersion and UV are mixed with pure wet/dry cycling, so this is an upper bound on degradation for an abiotic vapour-swing process, but permanent QA loss is chemical, not just fouling.
items.cost: My calc (sorbent.py): at $54/kg and 0.675 mmol/g, a 1,380-cycle life costs $1,317/t CO2 in sorbent alone; 14,600 cycles (5 yr x 8/day) gives $125/t; $7/kg and 14,600 cycles gives $16/t.
items.trl_and_scale: Small outdoor pilot (840 L pond, ~100 g CO2/day), March 2024 - February 2025.
items.bottleneck: Lifetime: measured cycles-to-failure (~10^3) are 10-30x short of the ~1.5-4 x 10^4 cycles needed for sorbent cost below ~$20-50/t.

items.name: IRA-900 resin, dynamic breakthrough at DAC conditions (Wang, Realff, Lively et al., ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2025)
items.mechanism: Macroporous polystyrene quaternary-ammonium resin in carbonate/bicarbonate form; humidity controls carbonate hydrolysis to hydroxide, which binds CO2 as bicarbonate.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 1.92 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2, 20-21% RH, 25 C (10-cycle average), i.e. >91% of available OH- sites; resin has 4.18 mmol N/g, so the carbonate-bicarbonate swing ceiling is ~2.09 mmol/g (0.5 CO2 per N+). Capacity at ~86.5% RH ~1.04 mmol/g. Maximum working capacity 1.27 mmol/g for a 20% -> 50% RH swing at 25 C with prompt CO2 removal. Water uptake 7.1 mmol/g at 20% RH, 28.4 mmol/g at 85% RH.
items.regeneration: Humid purge gas (dilute product) or vacuum with water vapour; in vacuum, CO2 release needed water vapour pressure of ~1.85 kPa (~65% RH equivalent). Heating raised peak desorption rate by 75% at similar RH. Product CO2 partial pressure not reported.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only 10 consecutive cycles shown; authors flag absence of long-term stability data.
items.cost: Not assessed. My calc: 1.27 mmol/g, $7/kg, 14,600 cycles -> $9/t sorbent; at $20/kg and 2,000 cycles (0.9 mmol/g) -> $252/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, gram-scale packed bed.
items.bottleneck: Kinetics controlled by internal (intraparticle) mass transfer in 614 um beads; water swing of ~21 mmol/g per ~0.9-1.3 mmol/g CO2 means 17-24 mol water cycled per mol CO2 (7-10 kg/kg) even with vapour only (my calc).

items.name: Vacuum moisture swing (VMS) process on IRA-900 (Sinyangwe, Wade et al., NAU, arXiv June 2026)
items.mechanism: Five-step cycle: air loading, evacuation to 0.5 kPa, water-vapour stripping from a ~27 C water reservoir boiling under vacuum, final pull to 1 kPa, compression of CO2 to 0.1 MPa. Replaces heat with low-temperature vapour; can use saline/brackish water.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured (TGA, 400 ppm, 25 C, 20<->95% RH, 3 cycles): CO2 working capacity 0.9 +/- 0.1 mmol/g on drying (~2 h) and 1.1 +/- 0.2 mmol/g release on wetting (~3 h); water swing 23-24 mmol/g. Measured LDF mass-transfer coefficients 14e-4 /s (drying) and 4.5e-4 /s (wetting), about 10x slower than the 20-90e-4 /s assumed in comparable DAC models. Modelled productivity 0.2-0.6 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day at 20% RH.
