items.regeneration: Modelled electricity 1-15 MJ/kg CO2 to deliver ~99% CO2 at 0.1 MPa; ~2.5 MJ/kg at 0.5 kg/kg/day. At the low-energy point, CO2 compression from ~1 kPa is ~0.47 MJ/kg. No external heat. Water loss to air 1.4-3.5 kg/kg CO2 (model assumes all stripping vapour is condensed and recovered).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not tested; authors state ambient stability of moisture-swing sorbents needs study.
items.cost: No TEA yet. My calc: 2.5 GJ/t electricity = 19% second-law efficiency vs 0.465 GJ/t floor; comparable to the amine reference cycle's 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent (25%), so the gain is 'no heat supply', not lower exergy.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3: process simulation with measured single-particle kinetics; no cyclic rig demonstrated.
items.bottleneck: Energy rises steeply with vapour-flow rate (1 -> 15 MJ/kg); humidity window: at fixed 5 MJ/kg, modelled productivity 0.55 / 0.50 / 0.44 / 0.28 kg/kg/day at 20 / 50 / 65 / 80% RH, zero near saturation.

items.name: CO2-water co-sorption isotherms on a moisture-swing resin (Guzzo, Wade, Schulze, Chem. Eng. J. 2025) and IRA-900 isotherm model (Lopez-Marques, Wade et al., ES&T 2026)
items.mechanism: Equilibrium CO2 loading as a joint function of CO2 partial pressure, RH and temperature on quaternary-ammonium anion exchangers.
items.uptake_and_conditions: At 15% RH the isotherm saturates by ~200 ppm CO2: 0.82 mmol/g at 25 C, 0.64 mmol/g at 45 C. At 80% RH maximum loading falls below 0.4 mmol/g and saturation needs ~60,000 ppm (6 kPa) CO2. Lopez-Marques: total uptake from OH- form matches ion-exchange capacity (1 CO2 per site); uptake rises with lower RH, lower T, higher pCO2.
items.regeneration: Implies equilibrium product partial pressure of order kPa when wetted at ambient temperature (consistent with Wang/Lackner 2011 'two orders of magnitude' and Flory's 'up to 500-fold' with liquid water, i.e. ~4-21 kPa ceiling from 42 Pa).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed.
items.cost: Not addressed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, dynamic column breakthrough, lab.
items.bottleneck: Climate window is thermodynamic: my calc gives minimum water evaporated per CO2 to reach 1 atm of 4.8 mol/mol (2.0 kg/kg) at 20% RH, 11.2 (4.6 kg/kg) at 50% RH, 35 (14 kg/kg) at 80% RH; free energy per mol water is only 4.0 / 1.7 / 0.55 kJ.

items.name: Carbon Collect MechanicalTree (Lackner/ASU licence): Gen-I 2022, Gen-II end-2025
items.mechanism: Passive wind-contacted sorbent discs on a 10 m column that retract into a base chamber for regeneration. Originally associated with Lackner's moisture-swing resin; the company now describes regeneration as low-temperature thermal-vacuum swing.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No measured capture rate published. Design claim ~90 kg CO2/day per tree (2022, ASU). June 2026 company release: Gen-II showed higher CO2 yields than Gen-I across 41 completed test cycles (ASU report, May 2026, not public); a PM Group analysis found temperature, humidity and wind significantly affect performance.
items.regeneration: Company: low-temperature thermal-vacuum regeneration 'well below 100 C'; not a pure moisture swing. NETL 2024 review lists its challenge as optimising water consumption and energy use.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No public data.
items.cost: No public cost data; $20M raise launched June 2026.
items.trl_and_scale: Company self-reports TRL 7 for Gen-II (single unit, Tempe AZ). As of mid-2025 only one tree had been installed. 1,000 t/yr system and Gen-IV FEED (due Sept 2026) planned; one tracker lists the DOE Southwest Regional DAC Hub as cancelled (secondary source, unconfirmed).
items.bottleneck: Four years after first unit: no published capture, energy, water or purity numbers; flagship moisture-swing commercialiser has added heat and vacuum, signalling the pure moisture swing did not deliver a usable product stream.

items.name: Avnos Hybrid DAC (water harvesting + moisture-swing CO2 sorbent)
items.mechanism: Inlet air is first dehumidified by a water sorbent bed; the dried air then passes a proprietary moisture-responsive CO2 sorbent; the harvested water is used to desorb CO2. Engineered dryness removes the climate dependence, at the cost of a dehumidification step.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No sorbent capacity, kinetics or product pressure published.
items.regeneration: Moisture from the upstream water bed, claimed 'no external heat input'; compression/vacuum details undisclosed. Company claims >50% lower energy than other DAC; no measured kWh/t found.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No public data.
items.cost: CEO targets (claims): <$250/t late 2020s, <$100/t early 2030s. >$100M raised.
items.trl_and_scale: Pilot ~30 t CO2/yr (Bakersfield, Nov 2023); Project Brighton 450 t/yr design entered operations Aug 2026 (New Jersey); Project Cedar 3,000 t/yr targeted early 2027. Largest moisture-swing-based deployment by nameplate.
items.bottleneck: Water co-product claims are inconsistent: 5 t/t (pilot), ~4.0 t/t (475,000 gal per 450 t, my calc), 2 t/t (Cedar), 10 t/t (CEO interview). All figures are design values; energy of regenerating the water bed is the undisclosed cost.

items.name: Kinetics spectrum: thin quaternised mesoporous resins (Wang et al., Sci. Rep. 2020) vs commercial sheets (Shi, Lackner et al., PLoS ONE 2017)
items.mechanism: Quaternary ammonium grafted onto pre-formed mesoporous polymer beads (QMPR) to shorten ion/water diffusion paths; compared with resin powder in polypropylene sheets (Excellion-type).
items.uptake_and_conditions: QMPR-2: 0.28 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 21% RH, 20 C; stable swing capacity 0.26 mmol/g (21% -> 100% RH); adsorption half-time 2.9 min; only ~60% of sites used. Commercial sheet (P-100, 100 um): 16.4 L/kg (~0.73 mol/kg) at 1,000 ppm; half-time 31.8 min at 400 ppm, 30% RH; water diffusivity in binder 6.5e-12 m2/s.
items.regeneration: 100% RH air or liquid water at ambient temperature.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 'Multiple cycles' only; no long-term data.
items.cost: Not assessed. My calc: 0.26 mmol/g at 72 cycles/day gives 0.82 kg/kg/day, above the amine reference 0.55, but sorbent cost $87/t at $20/kg even with 20,000 cycles.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, gram-scale.
items.bottleneck: Speed-capacity trade-off: 10x faster kinetics came with ~4-7x lower capacity. Diffusion scaling (my calc, L^2/D with D = 6.5e-12 m2/s): 6 min for 100 um sheet, ~230 min for 0.6 mm bead, so structures must be <=50-100 um thick.

items.name: Anion variants: phosphate, pyrophosphate, borate, silicate vs carbonate (Song et al. 2019; Hegarty/Dravid 2023 and 2026)
items.mechanism: Replace carbonate with higher-valency basic anions whose hydrolysis equilibrium shifts with hydration, producing hydroxide when dry.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Song et al. (Energy & Fuels 2019): phosphate-loaded resin moisture-swing capacity 80% larger than carbonate form, 15-35 C (absolute values not in abstract). Hegarty 2023 (ES&T): dibasic phosphate best per mass, pyrophosphate best per ion/charge; silicate and borate also swing. Hegarty 2026 (ES&T): 10 commercial resins, ambient CO2, 20-70% RH closed loop: macroporous beats gel only with intermediate, connected pores; Type I resins best with phosphate, Type II with carbonate; phosphate slows adsorption, carbonate slows desorption.
items.regeneration: Humidity increase at ambient temperature.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not reported; phosphate/silicate leaching and anion exchange with atmospheric acids untested.
items.cost: Not assessed; commercial resins.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, milligram-gram closed-loop cells.
items.bottleneck: Capacity gains are tied to a kinetic penalty (phosphate slows uptake); absolute capacities and 400 ppm working capacities not available from open sources here.

items.name: Non-resin 'platform' moisture-swing materials: carbonate/phosphate on activated carbon and metal oxides (Dravid 2025; Zheng et al. 2024)
items.mechanism: Basic anions confined in mesopores of cheap supports (activated carbon, nanostructured graphite, Al/Fe/Mn oxides); nanoconfined hydration shifts the carbonate/bicarbonate/hydroxide equilibrium as in resins.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Dravid group (ES&T April 2025): best swing capacity at pore sizes ~50-150 Angstrom; aluminium oxide and activated carbon fastest, iron oxide and nanostructured graphite highest capacity (values not in open sources). Zheng et al. 2024: K2CO3 on activated carbon 0.562 mmol/g at 25 C and 5% RH.
items.regeneration: Humid air / water at ambient temperature.
items.stability_and_lifetime: K2CO3/activated carbon lost ~40% capacity over 50 cycles from potassium leaching; recoverable by re-impregnation. Untethered salts migrate with liquid water.
items.cost: Supports are <$5/kg-class commodity materials (general knowledge, not from the papers).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3.
items.bottleneck: Leaching of the mobile salt (40% in 50 cycles) and the need for very dry air (5% RH) for the headline capacity.

items.name: Record-capacity claim: quaternised PET fabric, 6.08 mmol/g (Wang, Zhu et al., Sep. Purif. Technol. 2026)
items.mechanism: UV-induced grafting of quaternary ammonium groups onto PET fibre fabric; moisture-swing regeneration.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Abstract claims 6.08 mmol/g 'under ambient conditions', 1.64x a prior record of 3.71 mmol/g; CO2 concentration, RH and mass basis not stated in the abstract.
items.regeneration: Moisture swing, no heat or pressure input claimed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only three full cycles and ten short cycles.
items.cost: PET substrate is cheap; no cost analysis.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2.
items.bottleneck: Plausibility: carbonate-bicarbonate swing gives at most 0.5 CO2 per N+ and hydroxide-bicarbonate 1 per N+; a typical styrenic QA polymer holds ~4.2 mmol N+/g, so 6.08 mmol/g needs 6-12 mmol N+/g. Treat as unverified until conditions and basis are checked in the full paper (not accessible here).

items.name: Moisture-driven CO2 pump membrane (Wade et al., J. Membrane Science 2023)
items.mechanism: Continuous version: a commercial anion-exchange membrane (Fumasep FAA-3) with dry air on one side and saturated vapour on the other pumps CO2 uphill, driven only by the water-vapour gradient.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured CO2 flux 1.1 umol/m2/s (kinetically limited); modelled diffusion-limited potential 11 umol/m2/s; best feed humidity ~50% RH.
items.regeneration: None (steady state); product is CO2 in saturated water vapour at low partial pressure.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not reported.
items.cost: Authors identify water loss as the major cost of the separation.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, cm2 coupons.
items.bottleneck: Flux: 1.1 umol/m2/s is ~1.5 t CO2 per 1,000 m2 per year, so ~650,000 m2 of membrane per kt/yr (my arithmetic); water crossover dominates cost.

items.name: Comparator: same resin class with electrochemical pH-swing regeneration (Shu, Hamelers et al., ES&T 2022)
items.mechanism: Anion-exchange resin in hydroxide form captures CO2 from air in a column; regenerated by alkaline solution made in an electrochemical cell, CO2 released on the acid side.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 1.76 mmol/g dry resin at 394 ppm, 69% RH, 25 C (i.e. works in humid air); capture fell 22% from 33% to 84% RH.
items.regeneration: Electrochemical, room temperature: 537 kJ/mol CO2 at 20 mA/cm2 (12.2 GJ/t, my conversion); stated theoretical minimum 164 kJ/mol (3.7 GJ/t). Product >95% CO2 at atmospheric pressure.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 150 cycles with no apparent degradation.
items.cost: Not assessed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4 bench column.
items.bottleneck: Energy 5-6x a TVSA work-equivalent; water loss 6.65 g/g CO2 (humid air) to 18 g/g (dry air); 5 kPa bed pressure drop. Shows the resin itself tolerates humidity and 150 cycles when not relying on drying.

items.name: Quaternary-ammonium vs primary-amine resins: binding strength and thermal limits (Najaf Tomaraei, Wade et al., ACS AMI 2025)
items.mechanism: Side-by-side calorimetry, TGA and DFT on IRA-900 (quaternary ammonium) and Lewatit (primary amine).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Water heat of sorption at low loading ~58 kJ/mol on IRA-900 vs ~52 kJ/mol on Lewatit; IRA-900 takes up nearly double the water per active site. Lewatit shows no moisture-driven CO2 release; IRA-900 releases CO2 at 95% RH, 25 C.
items.regeneration: Thermal desorption from IRA-900 is slow (k = 0.008 /min at 100 C vs 0.24 /min for Lewatit) and needs ~100-180 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Quaternary ammonium decomposition begins above ~120 C, degradation onset 150-200 C; Lewatit stable to 350 C (inert-atmosphere thermal stability, not oxidative cycling).
items.cost: Not assessed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3 materials characterisation.
items.bottleneck: Quaternary ammonium binds CO2 too strongly for a clean thermal swing and too weakly-stable for high temperature, so it is locked into moisture (or mild heat + moisture) regeneration with its water and kinetics penalties.

items.name: Independent critical review: van der Spek et al., Energy Environ. Sci. 2025 (DAC review, part 1)
items.mechanism: Review classing humidity-swing ion-exchange sorbents among emerging adsorbents.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No new data.
items.regeneration: Notes the promise of low or zero regeneration heat.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Review states: "There is little data at all to show the stability of humidity swing adsorbents beyond short laboratory scale tests over 10 cycles."
items.cost: No humidity-swing cost or energy dataset available to the reviewers; TVSA thermal demand in literature 5-25 GJ/t, median 9.
items.trl_and_scale: Characterised as early-stage, lacking field studies.
items.bottleneck: Reviewers judge the class suited only to arid environments because water competes with CO2 at high humidity. (The 2025 Flory preprints add the first >1,000-cycle field data, after this review.)

bottlenecks: Water uptake and drying dominate, not CO2 chemistry. Commercial resin takes up 330 wt% water on liquid wetting, giving ~100 kg water per kg CO2 (244 mol/mol), ~80x the 1.2 kg/kg stoichiometric limit (Flory 2025, outdoor). Even vapour-only swings cycle 17-27 mol water per mol CO2 (7-11 kg/kg; my calc from Lively and Wade data). At 244 mol/mol, one pass of 20%->60% RH air that gives up half its CO2 can carry only ~60 mol water per mol CO2 (my calc), so the contactor must move >=4x more air for drying than for CO2 supply, and 30 of 80 min loading time is pure drying.

Slow intraparticle kinetics. Measured mass-transfer coefficients on IRA-900 are 4.5e-4 to 14e-4 /s (t90 = 27-85 min), ~10x slower than the 20-90e-4 /s assumed in DAC process models (Wade 2026). Real cycles are 2-5 h, giving 0.19-0.27 kg CO2/kg/day vs ~0.55 for the amine reference at 12 cycles/day (my calc). The one material with a 2.9 min half-time has only 0.26 mmol/g.

Capacity ceiling from stoichiometry. The carbonate-bicarbonate swing uses at most 0.5 CO2 per quaternary nitrogen: IRA-900 has 4.18 mmol N/g, ceiling 2.09, measured 1.92 mmol/g at 400 ppm/20% RH/25 C; working capacity 0.9-1.27 mmol/g in the lab and 0.675 mmol/g effective outdoors. The 4 mmol/g assumed in the $160/t aspirational TEA would need ~8 mmol N+/g in carbonate chemistry, beyond typical QA polymers.

Dilute, wet product. Wetting raises equilibrium CO2 pressure ~100x (Wang/Lackner 2011) to at most ~500x with liquid water (Flory), i.e. ~4-21 kPa ceiling and ~1-5 kPa in practice, mixed with ~3.2 kPa water vapour at 25 C. Reaching 1 atm costs 0.28-0.43 GJ/t at 60% pump efficiency and 150 bar another ~0.43 GJ/t (my calc); the full modelled VMS process needs 1-15 GJ/t electricity, ~2.5 GJ/t at useful productivity = 19% second-law efficiency, no better than the amine reference's 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent (25%). Moisture swing removes the heat supply, not the exergy bill.

Durability. Only field dataset: capacity down to ~10% after 302 days / ~1,380 outdoor wet-dry cycles, ~35% recoverable, with spectroscopic loss of quaternary ammonium groups (confounded by biofouling, pH 10 immersion, UV). At $54/kg and 0.675 mmol/g that lifetime is $1,317/t of sorbent; <$20/t needs roughly >=15,000 cycles and <=$7-10/kg (my calc). Lab papers show 3-50 cycles.

Climate window is thermodynamic. Free energy per mol water evaporated is 4.0 kJ at 20% RH, 1.7 kJ at 50%, 0.55 kJ at 80%; minimum water to deliver CO2 at 1 atm is 2.0 / 4.6 / 14 kg per kg CO2 (my calc). Measured capacity falls from 0.82 mmol/g (15% RH) to <0.4 mmol/g (80% RH); modelled productivity halves from 20% to 80% RH. The dry sites that work best have the least water; at 100 t/t water costs $30-150/t CO2, at 1.4-3.5 t/t only $0.4-5/t.

No plant-scale evidence. Largest openly measured system is ~100 g CO2/day for 7 days; its own TEA gives $950/t net with current data. Carbon Collect (one unit since 2022, Gen-II 2025) publishes no capture/energy numbers and now uses thermal-vacuum regeneration; Avnos (450 t/yr nameplate, 2026) publishes no measured energy.
open_problems: Decouple the few 'switching' waters from bulk swelling: design a quaternary-ammonium material that swings hydration by <=5-10 H2O per CO2 (vs 17-27 by vapour and ~270 by liquid wetting today) while keeping >=1 mmol/g. Verifiable target: water uptake <=50 wt% at ion-exchange capacity >=3 mmol/g; the ASU group reports sub-50 wt% only at lower ion content, and PVDF blending kept ~0.9 mmol/g.

Import ONE mechanism from alkaline fuel-cell/electrolyser membranes: oxidation- and hydroxide-stable cations (e.g. piperidinium/spirocyclic or ether-free aryl backbones developed for anion-exchange-membrane durability) into a moisture-swing sorbent. Test: abiotic wet/dry cycling in real air with bicarbonate counter-ion for >=5,000 cycles, tracking N content. Prior-art check needed; this is an inference, not a verified gap.

Structure for speed without losing capacity: diffusion scaling with D ~6.5e-12 m2/s says <=50-100 um solid thickness gives minute-scale kinetics (6 min at 100 um vs ~230 min for 0.6 mm beads). Thin coatings/fibres/hollow shells of high-IEC resin on a hydrophobic scaffold; target k >= 20e-4 /s at >=1 mmol/g, which no reported material reaches.

Raise product pressure cheaply: hybrid moisture + mild heat (40-60 C, waste or solar heat) or staged/counter-current wetting to approach the ~3 waters per CO2 limit (5 kPa at 20% RH). Guzzo data show a temperature lever at low RH (0.82 -> 0.64 mmol/g from 25 to 45 C). Needs measured CO2 partial pressure vs loading, which open literature barely reports.

Avoid compression altogether: couple the kPa-level or dissolved-bicarbonate product directly to mineralisation, alkaline electrolytic conversion, algae or greenhouse use. The ASU TEA shows $670 -> $51/t into solution in the aspirational case; the open question is a large sink that accepts dilute CO2.

A standard accelerated durability protocol and public dataset for moisture-swing sorbents (abiotic, real air, >=1,000 cycles, separated stressors: O2, UV, wet/dry mechanical stress, salts/Cl- poisoning). Currently one confounded field dataset exists.

Engineered dryness vs siting: quantify with executed thermodynamics whether upstream dehumidification (Avnos-style) pays back, i.e. desiccant regeneration energy per tonne CO2 vs the productivity gain from 20% RH operation, across real climate data. No measured numbers are public.

Higher-valency or non-carbonate anions that beat the 0.5 CO2 per N+ ceiling without the kinetic penalty seen for phosphate, and tethered (non-leaching) versions of the cheap salt-on-carbon/oxide platforms that lost 40% in 50 cycles.

Negative guidance for the engine: kinetics here are limited by water/ion diffusion in the polymer (measured), not by CO2 hydration chemistry, so importing carbonic-anhydrase-type catalysis is unlikely to help this sorbent class (inference from the mass-transfer data).

key_claims.claim: With measured outdoor performance (Arizona, ~17% RH, 2024-25) a commercial moisture-swing resin delivers an effective 0.675 mmol CO2/g, takes up 330 wt% water (~100 g water per g CO2, ~80x the stoichiometric limit) and its authors' own TEA gives $950 per net tonne at 15 MPa; the $160/t aspirational case requires 4 mmol/g and 50 wt% water uptake, which no material has shown together.

The only field durability dataset shows the resin at ~10% of initial CO2 capacity after 302 days (~1,380 wet/dry cycles) outdoors, only ~35% recoverable by cleaning, with measured loss of quaternary ammonium groups; this is confounded by biofouling, pH ~10 immersion and UV, but implies ~$1,300/t sorbent cost at $54/kg unless lifetime improves >10x.

surprises: Carbon Collect, the company commercialising Lackner's 'mechanical tree', now describes its regeneration as low-temperature thermal-vacuum swing (well below 100 C), not moisture swing, and after four years has published no capture or energy numbers.

Moisture swing is not an exergy win: the best modelled vacuum-moisture-swing process needs ~2.5 GJ/t of electricity (19% second-law), about the same as the amine reference cycle's 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent (25%). Its real advantage is needing no heat source; the ambient air still supplies 3.4-8.5 GJ/t of latent heat for free.

Measured mass-transfer coefficients on the standard resin are roughly ten times slower than the values routinely assumed in DAC process models, so earlier optimistic productivity estimates for this class are likely overstated.

The humid-climate limit is set by thermodynamics, not only materials: at 80% RH each mol of water yields 0.55 kJ, so at least 14 kg of water must evaporate per kg CO2 delivered at 1 atm, versus 2 kg at 20% RH.

A 2026 'record' capacity of 6.08 mmol/g for a quaternised PET fabric exceeds what site stoichiometry allows for typical quaternary-ammonium polymers (ceiling ~2-4 mmol/g) and rests on 3 full cycles; another instance of headline numbers needing a primary-source check.

The same resin family holds 1.76 mmol/g at 69% RH and survives 150 cycles when regenerated electrochemically, so humidity sensitivity and fragility belong to the drying-based swing, not to the resin's CO2 chemistry as such.

Avnos turns the climate constraint around by harvesting water upstream and claims to be water-positive, but its own published water ratios range from 2 to 10 t per t CO2 and no measured energy figure is public.

The key ASU preprint is internally inconsistent on water (abstract: 33-fold over the limit; body: ~80-fold); an independent check from its own uptake and capacity numbers gives ~111 g/g, supporting the larger figure.

verifs.claim: With measured outdoor performance (Arizona, ~17% RH, 2024-25) a commercial moisture-swing resin delivers an effective 0.675 mmol CO2/g, takes up 330 wt% water (~100 g water per g CO2, ~80x the stoichiometric limit) and its authors' own TEA gives $950 per net tonne at 15 MPa; the $160/t aspirational case requires 4 mmol/g and 50 wt% water uptake, which no material has shown together.
verifs.corrected_claim: In Flory et al. (arXiv:2508.02650v1, Aug 2025, ASU preprint, not peer reviewed), the commercial anion-exchange resin Purolite A501 in hydrophilic mesh packets takes up ~330 wt% water (lab-measured; TEA uses 3 g/g), i.e. ~100 g water per g CO2, which the body text puts at ~80x the 3:1 molar (1.2:1 mass) theoretical limit (the abstract says ~33-fold). The authors' modeled nth-of-a-kind TEA "practical scenario" uses an effective CO2 binding capacity of 675 umol/g (= 90% loading threshold on a ~0.75 mmol/g capacity from lab/wind-tunnel data at ~15% RH, 22-25 C; not an outdoor-measured value) and gives $950 per net tonne compressed to 15 MPa ($670 capture into alkaline solution + $280 extraction/purification/compression; Monte Carlo 95% range $530-1,500, median $930). The outdoor evidence is a single 7-day pilot trial (1-8 May 2024, Mesa AZ, mean 24.4 C / 16.7% RH) that delivered 782 g CO2 (~100 g/day) into a 4.2 m2 raceway pond. The $160/net tonne aspirational case ($51 + $109) assumes 4 mmol/g effective capacity and 50 wt% water uptake, and also a 10-year resin lifetime (vs 5), faster adsorption/desorption rates (0.125 and 2 vs 0.08 and 0.5 umol/g-s) and ~1 h dry/load; the paper cites no material combining these (their own <50 wt% AERs had lower ion-exchange capacity; Wang et al. ~3.4 mmol/g reached only ~1 mmol/g in 1 h; Dong et al. PVDF-doped AER ~0.9 mmol/g).
verifs.caveats: All headline numbers (0.675 mmol/g, 330 wt%, ~100 g/g, ~80x, $950, 15 MPa, $160, 4 mmol/g, 50 wt%) do appear in the primary source; the errors are in attribution and conditions. (1) Measured vs modeled: 0.675 mmol/g is a TEA input in Table S1 (675 umol/g, oddly referenced to X. Wang rather than 'Experiment'; main text says 0.75 mmol/g), derived from lab/wind-tunnel loading data, not from the outdoor trial. The outdoor trial only validated a wind-speed loading model (762 g predicted vs 782 g measured). $950 and $160 are modeled nth-of-a-kind costs, not demonstrated costs. (2) Date/scale: the outdoor trial is 1-8 May 2024 only (not '2024-25'), seven days, ~100 g CO2/day, 376 packets of ~1-2 g resin; no multi-hundred-cycle durability data for A501 is reported (resin lifetime of 5 years is an assumption). (3) Internal inconsistency in the source: abstract says water use is '~33-fold higher than the thermodynamic limits' while the body says '~80 fold higher' than the 3:1 molar limit; arithmetic (100 / 1.2 = 83) supports ~80x. (4) The 330 wt% figure is for resin plus hydrophilic mesh packet, not bare resin. (5) The system releases CO2 by liquid-water immersion into alkaline medium (designed for algae ponds); $280/t of the $950 is thermal extraction/compression from that solution, so the cost is not directly comparable to humidity-swing-to-gas designs. (6) Conditions are favorable (hot, ~15-17% RH desert air); performance drops with humidity, and night cycles were already slowed to 4 h. (7) 'No material has shown together' is a fair inference from the paper's discussion but is not an explicit statement by the authors and was not independently checked against 2025-26 literature. (8) Authors disclose commercial ties (Carbon Collect, Aircela). Extracted PDF text: (downloaded source text, not kept)

verifs.claim: The only field durability dataset shows the resin at ~10% of initial CO2 capacity after 302 days (~1,380 wet/dry cycles) outdoors, only ~35% recoverable by cleaning, with measured loss of quaternary ammonium groups; this is confounded by biofouling, pH ~10 immersion and UV, but implies ~$1,300/t sorbent cost at $54/kg unless lifetime improves >10x.
verifs.corrected_claim: In Flory et al. (arXiv 2508.04547, preprint), a Purolite A501 anion-exchange resin packet used for 302 days outdoors in an algae raceway pond in Mesa, Arizona (Mar 28 2024 to Feb 17 2025; an estimated 1,379.5 +/- 8.5 wet/dry cycles; 78 of those days in direct contact with cyanobacteria/microalgae cultures) retained ~10% of its initial CO2 delivery capacity, and a peracetic acid / hypochlorite / HCl / NaHCO3 wash restored it only to ~35% of initial capacity. ATR-FTIR and TGA showed a qualitative (not quantified) loss of quaternary ammonium groups after 190 and 302 days. The authors attribute the loss to a mix of biofouling, wet/dry mechanical fracturing, alkaline (pH ~10) exposure, UV and air oxidation, and do not separate these. The paper contains no $54/kg resin price, no ~$1,300/t sorbent-cost figure and no ">10x lifetime" statement; those are downstream derivations, not source findings. The paper also does not claim to be the only field durability dataset.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the full PDF text (main text, Fig. 7 discussion, Table S5, Fig. S21/S23).

CONFIRMED from the primary source:
- 302 days outdoors; Table S5 gives 1379.5 +/- 8.5 cumulative wet/dry cycles (an estimate from logs with low/high bounds for downtime, not a direct count).
- "~10% of its initial capacity" and cleaning "only able to restore ~35% of its initial capacity" (verbatim sense). Note 35% is of INITIAL capacity, i.e. it went from ~10% to ~35%, not "35% of the loss recovered".
- QA loss: FTIR bands at 850/1380/1620 cm-1 decrease and shift; TGA QA degradation step near 170 C is much reduced at 190 and 302 days. Qualitative only; no percent QA loss is reported.
- Confounds named by the authors: wet-dry cycling, pH ~10 alkaline exposure, photosynthetic microorganisms, UV, oxygen.

NOT IN THE SOURCE (errors/overreach in the claim):
- "$54/kg", "~$1,300/t" and ">10x lifetime" appear nowhere in the paper. They are someone's derivation. Rough sanity check using the paper's own delivery rate (~0.17 g CO2 per g sorbent per day, fall 2024, mixed new/used packets, abiotic): 302 days at full performance gives ~51 kg CO2/kg resin, i.e. ~$1,050/t at $54/kg; with a linear fade to 10% it is ~$1,900/t. So $1,300/t is the right order of magnitude but depends on unstated assumptions and an unverified resin price (I could not verify $54/kg; web-search budget was exhausted).
- "The only field durability dataset" is not supported by this paper and could not be independently checked; treat as unverified.

MEASUREMENT CONDITIONS that change how the number should be used:
- Capacity was not a gas-phase 400 ppm isotherm. It is CO2 delivered by a mesh PACKET (air-dried overnight in ambient air, then immersed in 1 L of 10 mM Na2CO3, inferred from pH change over ~1 h). No controlled humidity/temperature reported for the loading step.
- It is packet-level and apparently a single packet per age (no replicates or error bars stated in text), so it conflates resin chemistry with mesh pore clogging and physical bead loss. The paper reports that of the 100 packets installed in spring/summer 2024 (the cohort the 302-day packet belongs to), ~90% were damaged, ~60% had minor bead loss and ~30% had lost more than ~30% of their sorbent. Re-packing used sorbent in new mesh improved delivery (Fig. S21), confirming mesh effects.
- The wash itself uses hypochlorite, which the authors note can strip QA groups, so post-wash capacity is not a clean measure of irreversible loss.
- The 35-day packet (33 days in culture, little UV) already dropped to ~25% and recovered to ~70% with 3-4x slower kinetics, indicating biofouling dominates early loss. This is a direct-immersion-in-algae-culture use case, not a conventional moisture-swing DAC contactor; it is weak evidence for intrinsic resin lifetime in an abiotic DAC system. The authors' own TEA assumes abiotic performance is retained (sorbent on the media recycle stream, UV-stabilized mesh, 3-5 year life) and then projects CO2 cost below $51/t, so they treat the failure as application-specific and fixable, though that 3-5 year life is an assumption, not a measurement.
- Scale: small pilot, 4.2 m2 / 840 L pond, ~100 g CO2/day, 2 g resin per packet, ~300 packets. arXiv preprint; peer-review status not checked.

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04547 (PDF text saved at (downloaded source text, not kept))

items.name: Electrified reversible surface mineralization on MnO2 (Sargent/Farha, Northwestern, Nature Energy Feb 2026)
items.mechanism: Inorganic redox sorbent: MnO2 is electro-reduced to Mn(III) with electron-rich Mn-O- sites that bind CO2 as surface MnOOCO2H (operando Raman); oxidation releases it. One electron per CO2 in principle, near-neutral buffered electrolyte (pH ~7), MEA with gas-diffusion electrode. Concept explicitly imported from carbonic anhydrase's Zn-OH nucleophile. Redox potential (~0.7 V vs RHE) sits inside the water-stability window and positive of superoxide formation, so O2 is not reduced.
items.uptake_and_conditions: House air 435 ppm CO2, 21% O2, inlet RH 20-30%: capacity 0.42 mmol/g MnO2 (0.57 mmol/g in 20 cm2 cell), ~80% peak single-pass capture, pressure drop <150 Pa. Rate maintained at 80% RH where a TEPA amine reference in the same reactor slowed markedly. Only ~4% of Mn atoms are used (surface only; my check: 0.42 of 11.5 mmol/g theoretical = 3.7%). Peak Coulombic efficiency in air only 22% (capture) / 30% (release), up to 33% at -1 V hold.
items.regeneration: Voltage swing -1 V to +0.4 V at 1 mA/cm2, ~1.4 h per cycle. Cell-only electrical energy 3.9 GJ/t (optimised protocol), 4.1 GJ/t when releasing into pure CO2; 6.6 + 4.8 GJ/t before optimisation; 12 GJ/t at 0.5 mA/cm2. Authors state a further 1-2 GJ/t electric would be needed for vacuum pumping and compression, i.e. ~5-6 GJ/t all-in (second-law efficiency ~8-12% against the 0.47 GJ/t floor). Flue-gas case (4% CO2): 1.7 GJ/t at 50 mA/cm2.
items.stability_and_lifetime: >1,000 h cycling in real air with >90% capacity retention (~92% pro-rated), energy stayed <5 GJ/t. That is ~700 cycles; counter electrode and electrolyte had to be replaced at ~210 h. My calculation: at 0.42 mol/kg, 714 cycles gives $379/t sorbent cost at $5/kg; 5,000 cycles needed for ~$54/t.
items.cost: Authors' own TEA (1 Mt/yr, projected laminar contactor): US$90/t capex + US$52/t opex = ~US$142/t. Confound: measured areal productivity in the 5 cm2 cell is only 8.4 kg CO2 per m2 of cell per year (15.2 umol/cycle, 1.4 h) = 119 m2 of MEA per t/yr; a $50/t cell capital charge would then allow only ~$3/m2. The TEA relies on high-loading electrodes (1,230 umol/cycle in 20 cm2) whose cycle time is not stated in the main text.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3. 5 cm2 and 20 cm2 single cells, umol-scale per cycle, 2025-26.
items.bottleneck: Coulombic efficiency 22-33% and ~1 mA/cm2 at 400 ppm, plus 4% active-site utilisation: areal productivity is two to three orders of magnitude below what a membrane-electrode cell needs to pay for itself.

items.name: Hybrid phenazine flow cell with spatially isolated solid electrode (Aziz/Ji, Nature Energy Sept 2025)
items.mechanism: pH swing driven by proton-coupled electron transfer. The O2-sensitive reduced phenazine is confined in a solid cyclic poly(phenazine sulfide) electrode; only the alkaline liquid it generates contacts air, so the redox species never meets O2. Acidification on re-oxidation releases CO2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Direct air capture demonstrated from O2-containing gas at ~400 ppm; Coulombic efficiency 99%. Current density, capacity and cycle count were not retrievable (paywalled full text; abstract only).
items.regeneration: Electrical work 104 kJ/mol CO2 for DAC (= 2.36 GJ/t = 656 kWh/t; second-law efficiency ~20%) and 73 kJ/mol for simulated flue gas. Cell energy only; air contacting, pumping and compression are not included in the abstract figure. Predecessor (Pang et al., Nature Energy 2023, soluble phenazine 1,8-ESP, O2 excluded): 36-55 kJ/mol.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Described as stable with O2-containing feeds; quantitative fade rate and hours not verified by me.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, lab flow cell, 2025.
items.bottleneck: Lowest measured electrochemical DAC energy with O2 present, but it still exceeds the work-equivalent of an ideal heat-driven amine cycle (1.88 GJ/t in OptiLex's reference); areal rate and lifetime unreported in accessible sources.

items.name: Bipolar-membrane electrodialysis (BPM-ED) pH-swing regeneration of alkaline DAC solvent (Mission Zero, Phlair, academic)
items.mechanism: Air is scrubbed by an alkaline (bi)carbonate/hydroxide or amine solvent; a BPM stack dissociates water to make acid and base, CO2 is released on the acid side and the base is returned to the contactor. Fully electric, ambient temperature.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Capture step is conventional hydroxide/carbonate scrubbing. Energy depends strongly on solvent loading: a 1 M KHCO3 (fully loaded) feed needed ~50% less energy than partially loaded KOH (J. Mater. Chem. A 2025). Reaching bicarbonate loading from 400 ppm is slow, so real DAC liquors are mostly carbonate (2 charges per CO2).
items.regeneration: Lab stack data: 630-1,260 kWh/t at ~10-100 mA/cm2 from bicarbonate (Eisaman 2011); lowest validated solvent-regeneration figure cited is ~2,440 kWh/t (387 kJ/mol) at 50 mA/cm2 (Vallejo Castano 2024); 161 kJ/mol (3.65 GJ/t) at 10 mA/cm2 but <60% desorption efficiency from K+ crossover, and 291 kJ/mol (6.6 GJ/t) at 100 mA/cm2 (JMCA 2025). Modelled process: 236 kJ/mol (Sabatino 2020). Thermodynamic floor for a full 14-unit pH swing with 2 charges per CO2 is 0.83 V x 2F = 160 kJ/mol = 3.6 GJ/t (my check: 159.8 kJ/mol). Energy optimum sits at 10-50 mA/cm2.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No long-term validation under real DAC solvent cycling. The 2025 ACS Energy Letters perspective assumes all membranes are replaced 2 times in 5 years at 20 mA/cm2 and 4 times at 50 mA/cm2 (lifetime 1.25-2.5 years).
items.cost: Sabatino 2020 base case US$773/t with BPM at US$750/m2; 819-861 US$/t in the follow-up optimisation; projected ~US$330/t at US$100/m2 membranes and US$50/MWh. My calculation with a 500 EUR/m2 stack: stack capital 10-48 EUR/t but membrane replacement 48-154 EUR/t depending on charges per CO2 and current efficiency.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6-7 as companies: Mission Zero 50 t/yr (Sheffield 2023), 250 t/yr (Norfolk, May 2025), 250 t/yr at Deep Sky Alpha; Phlair demo plants. No independently measured plant energy published.
items.bottleneck: Membrane selectivity for (bi)carbonate and BPM lifetime; replacement cost outweighs stack capital; energy is 2.5-5x the 3.6 GJ/t pH-swing floor at useful current density.

items.name: Mission Zero Technologies pilot design base case versus marketing claim
items.mechanism: Solution-based air contactor, electrochemical (electrodialysis) separation, then depressurised release chamber giving CO2 at ambient temperature.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Ambient air, 60 t/yr pilot designed 2022, 12 h/day operation.
items.regeneration: UK government Phase 1 report (2022), Table 2.01: core DAC load 357.8 kWh/day = 2.18 MWh/t CO2, of which the electrochemical step is 230 kWh/day (64%, = 1.40 MWh/t = 222 kJ/mol); blower only 33 kWh/day (9%). Additional site items add 0.47 MWh/t. Compression and liquefaction excluded. Basis: vendor data for blower and pumps plus lab electrochemical data projected forward, so an engineering estimate, not metered plant data. Company now claims <800 kWh/t (2.7x lower); no measured data supporting that was found.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not disclosed (report is redacted).
items.cost: Report cites the first-generation benchmark as >US$300/t and targets up to 3x lower; no measured cost.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4 to pilot in 2022; 50-250 t/yr units operating 2023-2025.
items.bottleneck: The only primary document with a line-item energy budget gives 2.18-2.65 MWh/t (7.8-9.5 GJ/t electric), not better than thermal DAC on an energy basis.

items.name: Quinone electro-swing adsorption (Hatton group; Verdox)
items.mechanism: Solid polyanthraquinone or poly(vinylanthraquinone)-CNT electrode; reduced quinone binds CO2 as a carbonate adduct, oxidation releases it. Ferrocene-polymer counter electrode. No heat, no pH change.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Voskian and Hatton 2019: 0.6-10% CO2, O2 excluded, faradaic efficiency >90%. Hemmatifar 2022 stackable bipolar cell (8 electrode pairs): 400 ppm CO2 in N2 carrier, explicitly not air, because of quinone oxygen sensitivity.
items.regeneration: 40-90 kJ/mol at 0.6-10% CO2 (2019). 113 kJ/mol (2.57 GJ/t) at 400 ppm in N2, electrical plus pneumatic work, reached after ~7 cycles (first cycle ~900 kJ/mol); current limited to 0.5 mA per step. Verdox claims 1.5 GJ/t and 70% savings (company claim, no published data).
items.stability_and_lifetime: <30% capacity loss after 7,000 cycles without O2 (2019). No published lifetime in air. Verdox claims a material 5,000x more selective for CO2 than O2; my calculation: with O2:CO2 = 499:1 that still diverts ~10% of electrons (faradaic ceiling ~91%), and each O2 reduction can generate destructive superoxide.
items.cost: No measured cost. The 2024 TUM techno-economic study assumed Li-ion-like cell capex of 600-3,500 US$/kW and found no clear cost advantage over TVSA.
items.trl_and_scale: Academic TRL 3-4. Verdox (>US$100M raised) completed a two-month trial on a 1% CO2 aluminium-smelter stream at Hydro Sunndal (announced Nov 2025); first commercial deployment targeted 2029. No Verdox DAC pilot data found.
items.bottleneck: Oxygen: no quinone electro-swing cell has published energy and lifetime from real air; the leading company has moved to 1% CO2 industrial streams.

items.name: Electrolyser-type carbonate/bicarbonate regeneration in a porous solid-electrolyte reactor (Rice / PolyU)
items.mechanism: Three-chamber cell with a porous solid-electrolyte middle layer. HER/HOR (hydrogen looped) or ORR/OER at the electrodes drives Na+ across, regenerating NaOH on one side and releasing >99% pure CO2 in the middle layer. No chemical consumption.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Regeneration-only cell fed NaHCO3/Na2CO3 (Nature Energy 2025). ORR/OER variant captures directly at the cathode: up to 440 mA/cm2 (86.7 kg CO2/day/m2), faradaic efficiency >90% on carbonate basis, >98% removal from simulated flue gas (Nature 2023). Recirculation-mode follow-up ran on ambient air at 30 mA/cm2 with >93% carbon removal and Na+ faradaic efficiency ~85% in a 100 cm2 cell (Nat. Commun. 2025).
items.regeneration: HER/HOR cell: 50 kJ/mol at 1 mA/cm2 and 118 kJ/mol (2.68 GJ/t) at 100 mA/cm2 for bicarbonate feed, regeneration step only; carbonate feed needs roughly twice the charge. Rates up to 1 A/cm2 (~18 mmol/cm2/h). ORR/OER reactor: from ~150 kJ/mol (3.4 GJ/t). Energy for the ambient-air recirculation run was not in the abstract.
items.stability_and_lifetime: >100 h (regeneration cell); >2,000 h on ambient air at 30 mA/cm2 (2025), the longest real-air electrochemical DAC run I found.
items.cost: Not reported. High current density is the cost lever: my calculation gives 3-6 t CO2 per m2 per year at 100 mA/cm2, i.e. a cell capital charge of only ~US$7-22/t for US$300-1,000/m2 cells.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, up to 100 cm2 cells, 2023-2025.
items.bottleneck: Low numbers apply to bicarbonate feed, which an air contactor does not readily deliver at 400 ppm; ORR/OER overpotentials set a ~150 kJ/mol floor; contactor energy and capital are outside the reported figures.

items.name: Hydrogen-recycling electrochemical cells for spent alkaline absorbent (Wetsus/WUR; RepAir; Yan EDCS)
items.mechanism: H2 is oxidised at the anode to acidify spent carbonate and release CO2, and re-evolved at the cathode to regenerate NaOH; hydrogen is looped so net reaction is only the pH swing. RepAir and Yan's shorted-membrane separator apply the same hydroxide/H2 chemistry in a fuel-cell-like membrane device fed directly with air.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Shu 2020: NaOH/Na2CO3 liquor, up to 59% of absorbent capacity regenerated, CO2 purity >95%. Shu 2022: full loop with amine anion-exchange resin on lab air; contactor pressure drop 5 kPa (far too high). Yan 2022: 25 cm2 shorted membrane removed >99% of CO2 from 2,000 sccm air.
items.regeneration: 374 kJ/mol (8.5 GJ/t) at 5 mA/cm2; 520 kJ/mol at 15 mA/cm2; 537 +/- 33 kJ/mol (12.2 GJ/t) at 20 mA/cm2 with real air and resin, about half lost to electrode overpotentials. Theoretical minimum 164 kJ/mol, model 195 kJ/mol. RepAir claims 0.6 MWh/t (2.16 GJ/t = 95 kJ/mol) for DAC: company claim, below the published 164 kJ/mol minimum for the Wetsus configuration, no measured data found.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Five cycles on lab air (Shu 2022); 450 h for Yan's separator (which consumes H2 rather than looping it).
items.cost: Yan: US$112 module for an 80 kW fuel-cell air pretreatment duty (not a DAC cost). RepAir targets <US$100/t by 2030 (claim).
items.trl_and_scale: Academic TRL 3-4; RepAir field prototype announced 2023-24, commercial agreements (Pelican hub, Louisiana), claims only.
items.bottleneck: Measured energy is 2-3x the cell's own theoretical minimum and rises with current density; measured data stop at 20 mA/cm2.

items.name: Oxygen-insensitive aqueous PCET carrier: neutral red with nicotinamide (Seo and Hatton, Nat. Commun. 2023)
items.mechanism: Commercial phenazine dye; reduction takes up protons and raises pH so CO2 is absorbed as (bi)carbonate, oxidation acidifies and releases it. Nicotinamide is a hydrotrope to raise solubility. The reduced leuco form is reported stable to air.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Ambient air (410 ppm CO2, 20% O2): electron utilisation 0.38 mol CO2 per mol e-; 15% CO2: 0.71, declining to 0.5 after 12 h. 45-50 mM solutions, mL scale.
items.regeneration: Headline 65 kJ/mol (air) and 35 kJ/mol (15% CO2) are not measured cell energies: they are computed from the cyclic-voltammetry peak gap (0.26 V) divided by electron utilisation. Batch estimate with the measured peak separation of 0.42 V and utilisation 0.50 was 81 kJ/mol. The authors themselves note that current density must rise and overpotentials fall.
items.stability_and_lifetime: ~45 h of operation with O2 exposure; UV-vis stable after 1 day air bubbling and 1 week sealed.
items.cost: Not reported; dye and nicotinamide are commodity chemicals.
items.bottleneck: Low carrier concentration (50 mM) and an energy number that is an estimate from voltammetry rather than a full-cell measurement.

items.name: Molecular routes to oxygen-stable redox carriers (TCQ + alcohol, BDT-Q, DBQ, phenanthrenequinone, RAMAR acids)
items.mechanism: Shift the carrier's reduction potential positive of O2/superoxide while keeping CO2 affinity: hydrogen-bond-donor additives (ethanol with tetrachloro-benzoquinone, shift up to 350 mV), heterocyclic quinones (benzodithiophene quinone), cyano-substituted quinones (DBQ), micro-environment tuning (phenanthrenequinone), or avoid CO2-binding carriers altogether with Wurster-type redox-tunable acids that regenerate ordinary amines.
items.uptake_and_conditions: BDT-Q: 13% CO2 + 3.5% O2, electron utilisation ~0.8, 32 mA/cm2. TCQ + ethanol: estimated minimum 21 kJ/mol for 10% to 100% CO2. DBQ: computed binding free energy -5.39 kcal/mol, predicted to capture >70% of atmospheric CO2 (prediction, not a device). RAMAR: 10% CO2 + 21% O2. Phenanthrenequinone: conference abstracts (MRS Fall 2025) claim quinone capture from air under O2-rich conditions; no numbers verified.
items.regeneration: BDT-Q: 108 kJ/mol electrochemical work, computed from CV peak gap 0.93 V x utilisation 0.8 (not a cell measurement), at flue-gas concentration.
items.stability_and_lifetime: BDT-Q: 20 cycles, ~100 h. RAMAR: >400 h aerobic in a symmetric flow cell. None reaches 1,000 h in air at 400 ppm.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.bottleneck: The trade-off is thermodynamic: a more positive potential (O2-safe) weakens CO2 binding, which is the wrong direction for 400 ppm. Nearly all data are at 10-15% CO2 and are not evidence for DAC performance.

items.name: Electrochemically mediated amine regeneration (EMAR, copper/ethylenediamine) and descendants
items.mechanism: Cu(II) generated at a copper anode displaces CO2 from a polyamine; Cu is plated out at the cathode to restore amine capacity. Membraneless gas-diffusion-electrode variants and Cu(II)/Cu(I) schemes reported at AIChE 2025.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Developed and tested for flue gas (10-15% CO2). I found no measured EMAR data at 400 ppm.
items.regeneration: Bench: ~100 kJ/mol at 5 mA/cm2 membrane current density (Stern/Hatton 2013); open-circuit thermodynamic requirement 18 kJ/mol at 50 C; process analysis projected <50 kJ/mol captured and compressed. All flue-gas conditions.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Copper dendrite/plating management by periodic polarity reversal; amine and Cu(I) are oxidised by O2, which would be 500x more abundant than CO2 in DAC.
items.cost: Not reported for DAC.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench to small pilot for point sources; not a DAC technology today.
items.bottleneck: Flue-gas results do not transfer: at 400 ppm amine loading per pass is low and O2 exposure per mole CO2 is ~4 orders of magnitude higher.

items.name: Techno-economic cross-check of electrochemical versus thermal DAC (TUM, Energy & Fuels 2024; Sabatino; Leonzio 2025)
items.mechanism: Consistent-framework comparison of absorption with electrochemical regeneration and electro-swing adsorption against calcium looping and TVSA, with cell capex taken by analogy from redox-flow and Li-ion batteries.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Model study. Thermal energy demands were converted to break-even cell voltages: 1.4-5.4 V for absorption routes and 0.7-2.3 V for adsorption routes (1 electron per CO2). Literature cells run at 0.5-1.0 V (absorption/electrochemical) and 1.0-2.0 V (electro-swing).
items.regeneration: Electrochemical regeneration of liquid absorbents is favourable below ~1.8 V. For electro-swing versus TVSA the paper states (13 words) "no clear advantage of the electrochemical steps in DAC adsorption could be deduced".
items.stability_and_lifetime: Economic life 20 years at 7% assumed; cell lifetime not modelled from data.
items.cost: All four routes reach <US$100/t only with electricity around US$10/MWh. Leonzio 2025 ranks electro-swing and PCET cheaper than electrolysis and BPM-ED, but that ranking inherits optimistic lab energies and is a simulation.
items.trl_and_scale: Analysis only.
items.bottleneck: Results are only as good as the assumed cell cost and voltage; none of the inputs for electro-swing or PCET come from air-fed, long-lifetime cells.

items.name: OptiLex executed check: areal productivity and oxygen arithmetic for electrochemical DAC cells
items.mechanism: Faraday's-law calculation using climate/physics.py and climate/sorbent.py (scripts echem_map.py and echem_map2.py in the scratchpad sorbent folder). Tonnes CO2 per m2 of cell per year = j / (F x electrons per CO2) x duty; capital charge at 7%/10 y.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Swing cells (half the time capturing): 1 mA/cm2 and 4 effective electrons per CO2 (25% Coulombic efficiency) gives 0.016 t/m2/yr; 10 mA/cm2 at 1 e- gives 0.65 t/m2/yr. Continuous cells: 100 mA/cm2 at 2 e- gives 6.5 t/m2/yr. Measured MnO2 cell: 0.0084 t/m2/yr.
items.regeneration: 1 electron per CO2 at 1.0 V = 2.19 GJ/t; the 0.47 GJ/t floor corresponds to only 212 mV at 1 e-/CO2. pH swing costs 59 mV per pH unit per charge: 14 units x 2 charges = 160 kJ/mol; 7 units x 1 charge = 40 kJ/mol.
items.stability_and_lifetime: O2:CO2 in air is 499:1. A carrier 5,000x selective for CO2 still loses ~9% of electrons to O2; 500x selective loses half.
items.cost: Cell capital charge: US$300/m2 at 1 mA/cm2 and 25% efficiency = ~US$2,600/t; at 10 mA/cm2 and 1 e-/CO2 = US$66/t; at 100 mA/cm2 and 2 e-/CO2 = US$7/t. Electricity at US$50/MWh: 104 kJ/mol costs US$33/t, 236 kJ/mol costs US$74/t; the reference TVSA's 6.04 GJ/t of heat at US$4/GJ costs US$24/t.
items.trl_and_scale: Calculation.
items.bottleneck: Below ~10 mA/cm2 with near-unity electron use, cell capital rather than energy dominates; energy cost at today's best lab values is already comparable to thermal DAC's heat bill.

bottlenecks: Areal rate. Redox-sorbent cells fed with real air run at ~1 mA/cm2 with 22-33% Coulombic efficiency (MnO2, 2026): measured 8.4 kg CO2 per m2 of cell per year. A US$300/m2 cell needs ~10 mA/cm2 at ~1 electron per CO2 (0.65 t/m2/yr) to get the cell capital charge to ~US$66/t; at 1 mA/cm2 and 25% efficiency it is ~US$2,600/t. Liquid-loop electrolysers already reach 30-440 mA/cm2 but pay in energy.

Energy is not yet below thermal DAC in work terms. Best measured with O2 present at ~400 ppm: 104 kJ/mol = 2.36 GJ/t electricity, cell only (phenazine, 2025); 3.9-4.1 GJ/t cell only plus 1-2 GJ/t vacuum/compression (MnO2, 2026); BPM-ED solvent regeneration 3.65-8.8 GJ/t; H2-recycling 8.5-12.2 GJ/t. OptiLex's ideal amine TVSA reference is 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent (6.04 GJ/t heat). Second-law efficiencies are 5-20% versus 25% for the ideal thermal cycle. The advantage is all-electric, ambient-temperature operation, not lower exergy.

Oxygen. O2 outnumbers CO2 499:1. Quinone electro-swing data at 400 ppm (113 kJ/mol) were taken in N2. Electron utilisation for neutral red falls from 0.71 (15% CO2) to 0.38 in air. A 5,000x CO2:O2 selectivity still caps faradaic efficiency at ~91%, and making carriers O2-safe (more positive potential) weakens CO2 binding exactly where DAC needs it strong.

pH-swing floor. Hydroxide capture at 400 ppm makes carbonate (2 charges per CO2); a full water-dissociation swing costs 0.83 V x 2F = 160 kJ/mol = 3.6 GJ/t before losses, and practical BPM-ED runs 2.5-5x above that at useful current density. Getting to bicarbonate loading (1 charge per CO2) halves this (measured: ~50% less energy with 1 M KHCO3 feed) but CO2 uptake into bicarbonate from 400 ppm is kinetically slow.

Lifetime. Longest real-air runs: >2,000 h at 30 mA/cm2 (PSE reactor, 2025), >1,000 h and ~700 cycles (MnO2, counter electrode replaced at ~210 h), 450 h (H2-fed separator). Quinone cells: 7,000 cycles but without O2. BPM stacks are assumed to need full membrane replacement every 1.25-2.5 years, costing 48-154 EUR/t at 500 EUR/m2, more than the stack capital itself. A commercial cell needs roughly 40,000 h.

Sorbent utilisation and capacity. MnO2 uses ~4% of Mn atoms (0.42 mmol/g); neutral red runs at 50 mM. At 0.42 mol/kg and 714 demonstrated cycles, sorbent cost is ~US$379/t even at US$5/kg; ~5,000 cycles are needed for ~US$54/t.

Evidence gap. I found no independently metered plant-level energy figure for any electrochemical DAC system. Company claims span 0.42-1.5 MWh/t (Verdox 1.5 GJ/t, RepAir 0.6 MWh/t, Mission Zero <0.8 MWh/t, Phlair <1.5 MWh/t); the one primary line-item budget (Mission Zero pilot design, 2022) is 2.18 MWh/t core plus 0.47 MWh/t auxiliaries, excluding compression.
open_problems: Raise active-site utilisation and Coulombic efficiency of inorganic redox sorbents: MnO2 uses 4% of Mn and 22-33% of electrons at 1 mA/cm2 in air. Target: >20% utilisation, >80% efficiency, >=10 mA/cm2. Candidate imports: pseudocapacitor/supercapacitor electrode architectures, high-surface-area birnessite or layered hydroxides, flow-through electrodes. Verifier: Faraday-law areal productivity and cell capital charge (already scripted).

Screen other solid redox couples that sit inside the water-stability window and positive of O2 reduction, whose reduced surface binds CO2 with a free energy near -19 to -25 kJ/mol at 420 ppm. Pourbaix data (Materials Project) plus the Langmuir window in sorbent.py give a cheap numerical filter; the authors screened only MnO2, Co3O4, Fe2O3 and Ni(OH)2. Caveat: DFT surface binding energies are unreliable to ~10-20 kJ/mol, which is as wide as the whole usable window, so any hit needs measurement.

Generalise the spatial-isolation pattern (O2-sensitive species confined to a solid electrode, only an alkalinity-carrying liquid meets air): which solid PCET electrode chemistries maximise charge capacity per m2 and rate, and what is the minimum pH swing that still captures at 420 ppm? Each pH unit avoided saves 5.7 kJ/mol per charge.

Reach bicarbonate loading from 400 ppm fast enough to cut charge per CO2 from 2 to 1: carbonic anhydrase or small-molecule/zinc-hydroxide mimics as hydration catalysts in the contactor of an electrochemical pH-swing loop. Check prior art first (Ucaneo is commercialising an enzyme-inspired electrochemical route).

Membrane problem for pH-swing cells: (bi)carbonate-selective, alkaline-stable anion-exchange layers and BPM junctions with >5-year life at 20-50 mA/cm2, or membrane-free architectures that remove replacement cost entirely.

Hybrid swings: use a small voltage to shift binding strength so that a strong-binding sorbent (dH ~ -80 kJ/mol, 99% loaded at ambient) releases at <60 C instead of ~144 C. The Langmuir verifier can quantify how many mV of redox-tuned binding free energy substitute for how many degrees.

Capital versus intermittency: cells at 1-50 mA/cm2 are capital-heavy and cannot afford low utilisation, yet the all-electric pitch depends on cheap intermittent power. Quantify the break-even electricity price and utilisation for each cell class against the ~US$274/t capital charge already found for thermal DAC.

A reporting standard the engine can enforce: full-system electricity per tonne at 400-430 ppm, 21% O2, stated humidity, including fans, pumps, vacuum and compression, with current density, electrons per CO2 and hours on stream. Almost no paper reports all of these together.

key_claims.claim: As of October 2026 no electrochemical DAC system has a measured energy below thermal DAC in work-equivalent terms under realistic conditions. The best lab values with real air or O2 present are 104 kJ/mol (2.36 GJ/t electricity, cell only; phenazine hybrid flow cell, 2025) and 3.9-4.1 GJ/t cell only, ~5-6 GJ/t with vacuum and compression (MnO2, 1 mA/cm2, >1,000 h, 2026), against 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent for OptiLex's ideal amine TVSA reference and a 0.47 GJ/t floor. Lower published figures were obtained without oxygen (113 kJ/mol in N2), at flue-gas concentration, or estimated from voltammetry rather than measured on a cell (65 kJ/mol).

The binding constraint is areal productivity and lifetime, not energy. Air-fed redox-sorbent cells run at ~1 mA/cm2 with 22-33% Coulombic efficiency (measured 8.4 kg CO2 per m2 per year), and BPM-ED has its energy optimum at 10-50 mA/cm2 with membranes assumed replaced every 1.25-2.5 years; the lowest validated BPM-ED solvent-regeneration energy cited is ~2,440 kWh/t at 50 mA/cm2. A US$300/m2 cell needs about 10 mA/cm2 at ~1 electron per CO2 for a ~US$66/t capital charge.

surprises: Mission Zero's only public line-item energy budget (UK government report, 2022 pilot design) is 2.18 MWh/t for the core process plus 0.47 MWh/t auxiliaries, excluding compression, versus the company's current '<800 kWh/t' claim. The electrochemical step alone was 1.40 MWh/t; the air blower was only 9% of the load. It is a design estimate from lab data, and the company may have improved since, but no measured data supporting the lower figure is public.

Two widely quoted low DAC numbers are weaker than they look: Hatton's 113 kJ/mol 'DAC' bipolar electro-swing cell was fed 400 ppm CO2 in nitrogen, not air; and the 65 kJ/mol neutral-red figure is a 0.26 V voltammetry gap divided by electron utilisation, not a measured cell energy.

The most promising 2026 result drops organic carriers altogether: a commodity oxide (MnO2) with a mechanism borrowed from carbonic anhydrase is insensitive to O2 and humidity and ran >1,000 h in air. It fits the 'conventional core plus one imported mechanism' pattern, but uses only ~4% of its Mn and ~25% of its electrons.

The often-cited 3.6 GJ/t 'floor' for pH-swing capture applies only to full 14-unit water-dissociation swings with two charges per CO2. PCET organics already beat it (104 kJ/mol = 2.36 GJ/t) by swinging a smaller pH range; my check gives 40 kJ/mol for a 7-unit swing at one charge per CO2.

A consistent-framework techno-economic study (TUM, 2024) found no clear advantage for electro-swing adsorption over TVSA and concluded that <US$100/t requires electricity near US$10/MWh for every route, electrochemical or thermal.

Verdox, the best-funded electro-swing company, now reports results on 1% CO2 aluminium-smelter off-gas with first commercial deployment targeted for 2029; I found no published Verdox DAC performance data.

RepAir's claimed 0.6 MWh/t (95 kJ/mol) is below the 164 kJ/mol theoretical minimum published for the academic hydrogen-recycling cell and 4-6x below that cell's measured 374-537 kJ/mol. The architectures differ, so this is not a contradiction, but the claim is unverified.

Energy cost is already not the main gap: at US$50/MWh, 104 kJ/mol is US$33/t, comparable to the reference thermal cycle's heat bill (US$24/t at US$4/GJ). A breakthrough here would have to come from rate and lifetime (cell capital), which is where an idea engine should aim.

verifs.claim: As of October 2026 no electrochemical DAC system has a measured energy below thermal DAC in work-equivalent terms under realistic conditions. The best lab values with real air or O2 present are 104 kJ/mol (2.36 GJ/t electricity, cell only; phenazine hybrid flow cell, 2025) and 3.9-4.1 GJ/t cell only, ~5-6 GJ/t with vacuum and compression (MnO2, 1 mA/cm2, >1,000 h, 2026), against 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent for OptiLex's ideal amine TVSA reference and a 0.47 GJ/t floor. Lower published figures were obtained without oxygen (113 kJ/mol in N2), at flue-gas concentration, or estimated from voltammetry rather than measured on a cell (65 kJ/mol).
verifs.corrected_claim:
As of October 2026 I found no electrochemical DAC system with a measured energy below OptiLex's ideal amine TVSA reference (1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent; floor 0.47 GJ/t) while delivering concentrated CO2 from real air. The best lab values with real air present are:

- Phenazine hybrid flow cell (Nature Energy 2025, 10.1038/s41560-025-01836-3): 104.3 +/- 3.8 kJ/mol (2.37 GJ/t), net cell electricity only, laboratory air, 10 mA/cm2, 4 cm2 cell, about five cycles. It rises to 176 kJ/mol at 60 mA/cm2.
- MnO2 surface mineralization (Nature Energy 2026, 10.1038/s41560-026-01989-9): 3.9-4.1 GJ/t cell only at beginning of life (5 cm2, air at 0.04% CO2 / 21% O2, 20-70% RH, roughly 1 mA/cm2), and 3.25-3.59 GJ/t on a 20 cm2 cell. After 1,000 h the measured cell energy had risen to about 5.0 GJ/t (4.85-5.22). Adding the authors' assumed (not measured) 1 GJ/t for fan plus vacuum and 1 GJ/t for compression gives about 6 GJ/t at beginning of life and about 7 GJ/t after 1,000 h.

Other published figures do not change this:
- 113 kJ/mol (2.57 GJ/t; Hemmatifar et al., ChemSusChem 2022) was measured at 400 ppm CO2 in N2 without oxygen, and is higher than the phenazine value, not lower.
- 65 kJ/mol (1.48 GJ/t; Seo and Hatton, Nat. Commun. 2023) used ambient air with O2, but is an estimated minimum from a voltammetry voltage gap (0.26 V) times flow-cell electron utilization (0.38), not a measured cell energy.
- 1.76 +/- 0.16 GJ/t (Rozzi et al., ChemRxiv preprint 2025-26, 400 ppm) is measured but for only two-fold CO2 enrichment; twenty-fold enrichment took 5.81 GJ/t, or 7.81 GJ/t with condensation and compression.
- Figures in the 60-85 kJ/mol range are for flue-gas concentrations.
verifs.caveats:
**What was checked.** The MnO2 article's main text is paywalled. I verified against its abstract, figure captions, Supplementary Information PDF and source-data spreadsheets, plus the phenazine paper's abstract and SI, and the open text of Seo and Hatton 2023 and Hemmatifar 2022. Web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so the "no system" negative rests on Crossref and Europe PMC queries and is not exhaustive.

**Errors in the original claim**
- **1,000 h energy.** The 3.9-4.1 GJ/t is a beginning-of-life value. Source Data Fig. 4c shows about 4.5 GJ/t at 500 h and about 5.0 GJ/t at 1,000 h.
- **Capacity retention.** End-of-test capacity is about 86% of the initial value (0.356 vs 0.413 mmol/g). The paper's ">90% retention" is a time-averaged figure (SI Fig. 19).
- **Auxiliaries.** "~5-6 GJ/t" understates the total: SI Note 1 assumes 1 GJ/t for fan plus vacuum and 1 GJ/t for compression, neither measured. That gives 5.9-6.1 GJ/t at beginning of life.
- **113 kJ/mol.** It is not a "lower" figure than 104 kJ/mol.
- **Missing category.** The list of lower figures omits low-enrichment results (Rozzi preprint, 1.76 GJ/t at 2x enrichment), which is the one measured number below 1.88.

**Context that changes how the claim is used**
- **Current density.** "1 mA/cm2" for MnO2 comes only from an SI table footnote ("DAC conditions (1mA/cm2, 30% coulombic efficiency)"). The device runs a voltage protocol (-1 V to 0.4 V), and my back-calculation gives roughly 0.4-1 mA/cm2.
- **Scale.** The MnO2 cell separates about 16 micromol CO2 per 1.4 h cycle at 5 cm2 and about 115 micromol at 20 cm2. The phenazine result is five cycles in a 4 cm2 cell with 15 h air-capture steps.
- **Phenazine accounting.** The 104 kJ/mol is net electrical work with discharge energy credited. It excludes pumping, the 1 L/min air sparging and vacuum.
- **Unequal comparison.** The 1.88 GJ/t reference is an ideal Langmuir cycle with Carnot-weighted heat (output of climate/sorbent.py), not a measured plant. Real solid-sorbent DAC is higher: the MnO2 SI lists a Climeworks target of 7.2 GJ/t. The electrochemical numbers are measured but cell-only. Against real thermal plants with real heat-pump COPs, the phenazine cell value is roughly comparable, not clearly worse.
- **Floor.** 0.47 GJ/t is the repo's minimum separation work for 420 ppm, 75% capture, 99% purity (0.465).

verifs.claim: The binding constraint is areal productivity and lifetime, not energy. Air-fed redox-sorbent cells run at ~1 mA/cm2 with 22-33% Coulombic efficiency (measured 8.4 kg CO2 per m2 per year), and BPM-ED has its energy optimum at 10-50 mA/cm2 with membranes assumed replaced every 1.25-2.5 years; the lowest validated BPM-ED solvent-regeneration energy cited is ~2,440 kWh/t at 50 mA/cm2. A US$300/m2 cell needs about 10 mA/cm2 at ~1 electron per CO2 for a ~US$66/t capital charge. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12442064/
verifs.corrected_claim: Jovanov et al., ACS Energy Lett. 2025, 10, 4686-4702 (PMC12442064; a Perspective, not new experiments) supports only the BPM-ED part of this claim. (1) Supported: minimum energy consumption in lab- and pilot-scale BPM-ED DAC systems falls at 10-50 mA/cm2 (the paper calls 20 mA/cm2 the optimum for the current state of the art). (2) Supported as a modelling ASSUMPTION, not a measured lifetime: its cost model replaces all membranes 2x per 5 years at 20 mA/cm2 (every 2.5 y) and 4x per 5 years at 50 mA/cm2 (every 1.25 y). (3) Needs correction: the review does print "~2440 kWh/tonne CO2 at 50 mA/cm2" for Vallejo Castaño et al. 2024, but the primary paper (Chem. Eng. J. 488, 150870) reports its lowest energy, 8.8 GJ/t (= 2,444 kWh/t), at 250 A/m2 = 25 mA/cm2, measured on synthetic partially carbonated KOH solutions mimicking flue-gas-contacted solvent (carbon loading 0.6, 0.5-2 M K+), i.e. post-combustion solvent regeneration, not air capture. It is also not the lowest BPM-ED figure the review cites: its own Table 1 lists Eisaman et al. 2011/2012 at 630-1,260 and 630-1,890 kWh/t (lab scale, ~10-100 mA/cm2). (4) Not in this source: the redox-sorbent figures (~1 mA/cm2, 22-33% Coulombic efficiency, 8.4 kg CO2/m2/yr). The review says only that redox-mediated systems have "very low operational current densities". The nearest match is a paper it cites, Seo & Hatton, Nat. Commun. 2023 (neutral red): electron utilization (mol CO2 per mol e-, not Coulombic efficiency) of 0.21 average / 0.33 peak in an air-bubbled batch H-cell at 50 mA, and 0.38 in a continuous flow cell on 410 ppm air at 30 mA; it gives no area-normalised current density or kg/m2/yr figure. (5) Not in this source: the US$300/m2 and ~US$66/t figures. The review assumes an ED stack cost of 500 EUR/m2 falling 50 EUR/m2 every 5 years, a 6%/20-year annuity, 8,000 h/yr and 70-90% permselectivity. At 10 mA/cm2 and 1 e- per CO2 at 100% current efficiency, productivity is ~1.31 t CO2/m2/yr (8,000 h) to ~1.44 t (8,760 h), so US$66/t on US$300/m2 implies an unstated ~29-32% annual capital charge (roughly a 3.2-3.5-year stack life); under the review's own 6%/20-year annuity the charge would be ~US$18-20/t before membrane replacement. (6) "Not energy" is the claimant's inference: the review says the largest cost share "may arise" from membrane replacement, but also flags energy as unresolved (2,440 kWh/t exceeds the ~1,500 kWh/t competitiveness benchmark; modelled CapEx:OpEx is 1:1 at 20 mA/cm2 with electricity at 200 EUR/MWh).
verifs.caveats: Access: the PMC page returned a reCAPTCHA, so I read the same article's full text through the Europe PMC API (fullTextXML for PMC12442064). Only the abstract of Vallejo Castaño 2024 was reachable (via OpenAlex; ScienceDirect returned 403), so the 25 mA/cm2 correction rests on that abstract's "250 A/m2 exhibited the lowest energy consumption (8.8 GJ/ton CO2)". The web-search budget for this session was exhausted, so I could not locate the origin of the 1 mA/cm2 / 22-33% / 8.4 kg/m2/yr redox figures; they are unverified, not refuted. They also look internally inconsistent unless a duty cycle or other loss is assumed: 1 mA/cm2 run continuously at 22-33% efficiency and 1 e-/CO2 gives ~32-47 kg CO2/m2/yr, and 8.4 kg/m2/yr corresponds to ~6% effective utilisation. Measured vs modelled: the review's cost curves (LCOC, replacement frequency, stack cost) and its cell voltages (1.3 V at 20 mA/cm2, 1.81 V at 50 mA/cm2) are modelled or assumed; the Eisaman and Vallejo Castaño energies are lab-scale stack measurements on prepared solutions, not integrated air-capture systems, and the review itself notes a lack of long-term validation under realistic DAC cycling. Conflict of interest: the lead and corresponding author is at Ucaneo Biotech, a BPM-ED DAC company, and the paper argues for membrane-driven systems over redox-mediated ones, so its qualitative dismissal of redox systems should not be read as neutral. The directional point that low current density drives membrane area and replacement cost is consistent with the review; the specific numbers attached to redox cells and the US$66/t capital charge should not be attributed to it.

title: Liquid solvents, hydroxide loops and crystallization routes

items.name: KOH absorption + Ca(OH)2 causticization + 900 C oxy-fired calciner (Carbon Engineering design; 1PointFive Stratos)
items.mechanism: Air contacts ~1.0 M OH- / 0.5 M CO3 2- / 2.0 M K+ liquor in cooling-tower-type packing; carbonate is precipitated as CaCO3 pellets with Ca(OH)2; pellets are calcined at 900 C to release CO2; CaO is steam-slaked back to Ca(OH)2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Keith et al. 2018 (Joule), design for 0.98 Mt/yr at 20 C, 64% RH, 400 ppm: capture fraction 74.5% per pass at 1.4 m/s air velocity, 7 m packing depth, 9.7 Pa/m; mass-transfer coefficient KL 1.3 mm/s (pilot + lab data). The 1 t/day Squamish pilot (operating since 2015) reached only 42% capture fraction with its shallower packing. My calculation from KL: 17-31 kg CO2 per m2 wetted area per year, i.e. ~58 million m2 of wetted packing for 1 Mt/yr.
items.regeneration: Design values (Aspen simulation, NOT plant measurements): 8.81 GJ natural gas per t CO2, or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh electricity, CO2 delivered at 15 MPa; 5.25 GJ + 77 kWh at 0.1 MPa. Calciner 5.25 GJ/t vs reaction minimum 4.05 GJ/t (78% thermal efficiency); fans 61 kWh/t, contactor pumping 21 kWh/t, compression 132 kWh/t. Computed here: calcination heat at 900 C carries 3.0 GJ/t of exergy against the 0.47 GJ/t floor, so the chemistry caps second-law efficiency near 15% before any loss; whole-plant work-equivalent 2.6-5.3 GJ/t (14-20%).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Inorganic liquor does not degrade; liquid surface self-renews. Pilot: 98% CaCO3-to-CaO conversion, 90% Ca retention in pellet reactor, calciner run 90 h near-continuous after re-carbonation fouling was controlled; 1% of circulating Ca purged per cycle (make-up cost stated $0.22/t). KOH drift measured <0.6 mg/m3 at contactor outlet. Water loss 4.7 t H2O per t CO2 at design climate. An et al. 2022 (simulation): energy 11.1 -> 8.3 GJ/t as capture rises 40 -> 85%; 75% capture only reachable above 17 C and 90% RH.
items.cost: Keith 2018 levelized $94-232/t (2016 dollars, design estimate, gas at $3.5/GJ, 90% utilisation). An 2022 (simulation, climate-dependent): $240-409/t. OptiLex earlier run: Stratos-like capital charge ~$274/t at 95% utilisation. Phase-in reality: no audited cost exists.
items.trl_and_scale: Pilot 1 t/day measured (unit operations only, not an integrated closed loop: some low-risk units were omitted). Stratos (500,000 t/yr design, construction since May 2023, originally slated for end-2024) had NOT started commercial operation as of August 2026; Occidental now says end-2026 after a 'non-process component' problem in Phase 1 commissioning. So there is no public measured energy or capture data from Stratos.
items.bottleneck: Binding is far too strong for the job: CaCO3 decomposition needs 178 kJ/mol (4.05 GJ/t) at 900 C, about 9x the 20.5 kJ/mol separation floor, and it requires combustion or high-temperature electric heat plus an air-separation unit. Capital and commissioning risk dominate: ~20 months of slippage and zero operating data.

items.name: Electrochemical pH-swing regeneration of hydroxide/carbonate DAC liquor (BPMED, H2-looping cells, two-stage H2-loop + MnO2 proton sponge)
items.mechanism: Keep the KOH/NaOH air contactor but replace the calcium loop and calciner: an electrochemical cell supplies H+ to the carbonate liquor (releasing CO2) and regenerates OH- on the other side. Variants: bipolar-membrane electrodialysis; H2 oxidation/evolution loop; staged pH downshift.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Feed is synthetic post-contactor liquor, not a liquor loaded in an air contactor. PNAS 2026 (Northwestern): 0.32 M KOH + 1.34 M K2CO3, pH 13.5; that composition needs 2.24 H+ per CO2 (my arithmetic). Shu 2020: NaOH/Na2CO3, regenerated up to 59% of absorbent capacity.
items.regeneration: Measured, lab cells: Shu et al. 2020 H2-recycling cell 374 kJ/mol (8.5 GJ/t electric) at 50 A/m2 (5 mA/cm2), CO2 >95% pure; 520 kJ/mol at 150 A/m2. PNAS 2026 two-stage: ~4.5 GJ/t total = 2.4 (H2 loop, pH 13.5 -> 9, 25 mA/cm2) + 2.1 (MnO2 stage, 30 mA/cm2, 125 h, ~80% charge efficiency); the same paper puts BPMED-type single-stage swings at >=10 GJ/t and notes a single H2-loop cell emits CO2 mixed with H2, costing a further 3-4 GJ/t to separate. Sabatino 2020 KOH + BPMED: 24 MJ/kg (simulation). Computed floor: 0.83 V x 2 H+ = 160 kJ/mol = 3.6 GJ/t for carbonate at dpH 14; 80 kJ/mol = 1.8 GJ/t for bicarbonate.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Longest reported run in these sources: 125 h (MnO2 stage). MnO2 is stable only in the bicarbonate regime, not at high pH. Bipolar-membrane durability at high current density and physical scale is an acknowledged open issue (junction adhesion, polymer breakdown). No multi-thousand-hour data.
items.cost: No measured cost. Current densities of 5-30 mA/cm2 imply very large membrane/electrode area per tonne; this, not electricity alone, is the likely cost driver.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, cm2-scale cells, hours to ~125 h.
items.bottleneck: Proton stoichiometry times Nernst penalty: a carbonate liquor needs >=2 H+ per CO2 across ~14 pH units. Best measured total (4.5 GJ/t electric) is still ~10% second-law efficiency and was obtained at 25-30 mA/cm2; energy rises steeply with current density.

items.name: Amino-acid salt absorption + bis-iminoguanidine (BIG) carbonate crystallization (ORNL; licensed to Holocene, acquired by Occidental April 2025)
items.mechanism: Aqueous potassium sarcosinate or glycinate absorbs CO2 from air; a sparingly soluble guanidine (MGBIG, GBIG, m-BBIG) pulls carbonate out of solution as a hydrated crystalline salt at room temperature, regenerating the amino acid without heating the liquid; the filtered crystals are heated to 60-120 C to release CO2 and water.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Cyclic capacity 0.12-0.20 mol CO2 per mol amino acid for sarcosine/m-BBIG over three cycles (lab); glycylglycine/GBIG 0.16 mol/mol. Holocene/ORNL bench: MGBIG carbonate crystal yield 25-45% from 1 M K-sarcosinate, strongly dependent on stirring. Loading experiments in the CRADA report used 13% CO2, not air.
items.regeneration: m-BBIG: 360 kJ/mol = 8.2 GJ/t (CO2 + water release + sensible heat). MGBIG: ~7.0 GJ/t by DSC/TGA; ORNL 2024 gives 7.0-10.2 kJ per g CO2 and attributes a significant portion to water leaving the crystal (MGBIG carbonate dihydrate). Direct 100 C steam regenerated GBIG carbonate 4.5x faster than 130 C conductive heating (30 vs 135 min for 10 g) with ~99% CO2 recovery; CO2 release in liquid water starts near 78 C. On an exergy basis 7-10 GJ/t of 120 C heat is 1.7-2.5 GJ/t work-equivalent (computed).
items.stability_and_lifetime: No cycle-life data beyond a few cycles. Holocene DOE final report (Nov 2025): washed BIG carbonate was stable at 120 C in air; unwashed crystals carrying residual amino-acid liquor decomposed when heated in air (HPLC products, discolouration) but not under nitrogen. The project was terminated before the sorbent-stability report, the 1 kg synthesis (2 batches of ~165 g made), the vacuum/steam desorption reports and the final techno-economic analysis were delivered. Sarcosine itself: <=2% loss after 500 h under oxygen (MEA >90%), but 21% loss after 700 h at 120 C.
items.cost: Company claim only: Google contract at $100/t for 100,000 t by the early 2030s (a price, not a measured cost). ORNL TEA claims steam stripping halves capture cost versus conductive heating (model).
items.trl_and_scale: Bench to small pilot (Holocene pilot launched Knoxville, May 2024); no public pilot performance data. Now inside Occidental R&D.
items.bottleneck: The crystals carry water: 7.0-10.2 GJ/t is more heat than the calciner's 5.25 GJ/t, just at lower temperature. Needle-shaped crystals hold liquor in the filter cake, adding evaporation load and bringing oxidisable amino acid into the hot step. Sorbent cost and lifetime are unmeasured.

items.name: Passive Ca(OH)2 / CaO looping on trays with electric kiln (Heirloom-type)
items.mechanism: Hydrated lime powder is spread in thin layers and carbonates in ambient air over days; CaCO3 is calcined near 900 C in an electric kiln; CaO is re-hydrated and re-spread. No fans or liquid loop.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Company statement: carbonation in about 3 days. Independent lab data (Dostie, Rausis and Power, Trent University, 2024): CaO deposits 0.5-1.5 cm thick at 85-95% RH for 24 days gave 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr; CaO passivates at constant humidity, but a humidity swing (e.g. 40% -> 95% RH) reached >85% carbonation, and Ca(OH)2 reached >90% CaCO3 at 100-500 ppm CO2; a flow-through bed was CO2-supply limited. Heriot-Watt 2025: thin layers (<10 mm, re-spread every 5-10 days) gave >2 t CO2/ha/day (73 kg/m2/yr). Abanades-group mortars: conversion >0.6 needs RH above 50%, preferably 80-100%. Nature Communications 2025: an interfacial water film thinner than 8.5 nm completed Ca(OH)2 carbonation within 1 h under ambient conditions (rate plateaus near 2 kPa CO2); in air, near-complete carbonation required nine film renewals.
items.regeneration: No measured plant energy published. Computed here without heat recovery: 178 (reaction) + ~96 (sensible to 900 C) + 33 kJ/mol (re-dehydrating the 15% unconverted hydroxide) = ~308 kJ/mol = 7.0 GJ/t = ~1,940 kWh/t at 85% conversion; 9.1 GJ/t at 60% conversion. Heirloom's own perspective says hydration returns roughly 30% of calcination energy.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Limestone is cheap and tolerant: at $0.15/kg and only 10 cycles before purge, sorbent cost is ~$22/t (computed), versus $218/t for a $20/kg solid amine at 2,000 cycles. Sintering and loss of reactivity over calcination cycles are known for Ca looping but unquantified here for ambient carbonation.
items.cost: Not published. Inventory is small: ~12 kg CaO per t CO2/yr at a 3-day cycle (computed). Tray area is large: 855-8,300 ha of exposed layer per Mt/yr at the measured 12-117 kg/m2/yr.
items.trl_and_scale: Tracy, California facility: up to 1,000 t/yr nameplate, launched November 2023; Louisiana ~17,000 t/yr planned for 2026. Heirloom's 2024 Frontiers article contains no measured energy, kinetics or cost data.
items.bottleneck: Same 900 C calcination thermodynamics as the KOH route (>=4.05 GJ/t before sensible heat), plus slow, humidity-dependent, passivation-prone carbonation that sets tray area and materials handling.

items.name: Aqueous amino-acid salt (potassium sarcosinate) with direct or catalytic low-temperature regeneration
