items.mechanism: Non-volatile amino-acid salt solution replaces KOH in a cross-flow contactor; CO2 bound as carbamate/bicarbonate is stripped thermally at 80-140 C, optionally over a TiO2 catalyst to stay below 100 C.
items.uptake_and_conditions: ORNL 2025 high-flux cross-flow contactor, 3 M K-sarcosinate, air >1 m/s, inlet ~410-500 ppm (indoor air): capture per pass 42.1% at 35 C, 33.9% at 20 C, 24.3% at 0 C, 20.3% at -5 C; pressure drop 52.5 Pa (35 C) to 69.2 Pa (-5 C). 1 M solution fell below 10% capture after 10 h as it saturated. Equilibrium loading 0.63 mol/mol at 13% CO2 (not air). Computed fan work from these figures: 76 kWh/t at 35 C, 108 at 20 C, 209 at -5 C.
items.regeneration: ORNL calorimetry (2023): desorption enthalpy 3.68 GJ/t plus sensible heat 1.5 GJ/t for 3 M K-sarcosinate (stripping-steam losses not included); CO2 release above 80 C. ORNL technology note claims TiO2 lowers regeneration from 120-140 C to below 100 C with up to 50% column energy saving (lab claim, no cycle data).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Oxidative stability is good (<=2% loss after 500 h with oxygen vs >90% for MEA) but thermal stability is the weak point: 21% amine loss after 700 h at 120 C, 34% at 150 C (first-order half-life ~2,060 h at 120 C, computed). Water evaporation is severe: 6.5 L of 20 L lost in 10 h (1 M); ~20% of volume in 8 h (3 M). Viscosity of 3 M K-sarcosinate rises from 2.3 mPa.s at 40 C to 10.8 at -10 C; ethylene-glycol antifreeze added <$5/t in ORNL's model.
items.cost: Model-only; not independently measured.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench contactor (20 L solvent), TRL 3-4.
items.bottleneck: Per-pass capture of 20-42% roughly doubles the air (and fan work) per tonne versus KOH's 74.5%, performance halves from 35 C to -5 C, and the solvent loses water quickly in dry air.

items.name: Redox-mediated organic pH-swing cells (phenazine DSPZ, anthraquinone AQDS)
items.mechanism: A dissolved proton-coupled redox molecule is reduced to generate hydroxide (capture) and oxidised to consume it (release), so the pH swing happens in one electrolyte without water splitting.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Jin et al. 2022 (Harvard): measured only with CO2/N2 mixtures at 0.1-0.5 bar CO2, 20-150 mA/cm2. Air (0.4 mbar) performance is an extrapolation, not a measurement.
items.regeneration: 61.3 kJ/mol measured for 0.1 bar inlet -> 1 bar outlet at 20 mA/cm2 (a flue-gas-like condition; not transferable to air as-is). Extrapolated for 0.4 mbar: 121-237 kJ/mol (2.7-5.4 GJ/t electric) at 20 mA/cm2. RSC Advances 2026 AQDS dual-electrolyser with hydrogen pump, built to keep the mediator away from oxygen: 257 kJ/mol (5.8 GJ/t) actual.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Reduced DSPZ is chemically oxidised by atmospheric or dissolved O2; capacity fades quickly when cycled under air; an electrochemical rebalancing step restores composition. Air is 21% O2, so the side reaction competes directly with 0.04% CO2.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, small flow cells.
items.bottleneck: Oxygen: the molecule that makes the energy low is destroyed by the 500-fold excess of O2 over CO2 in air; isolating it (dual electrolysers) brought the measured energy back up to 257 kJ/mol.

items.name: Open cooling-tower air contactor for aqueous sorbents: climate, water and kinetics limits (applies to every liquid route)
items.mechanism: Cross-flow structured packing wetted by the capture liquid; CO2 uptake is limited by liquid-side reaction/diffusion; water evaporates or condenses according to the liquid's water activity versus ambient humidity.
items.uptake_and_conditions: KL 1.3 mm/s at 20 C for ~1 M OH- (pilot + lab). Zn(II) carbonic-anhydrase mimics raised capture rate up to 2x and mass transfer 40-60% in 1 M K2CO3 at ambient CO2 (University of Kentucky, 2026, bench); carbonic anhydrase itself gave 6-20x in K2CO3 at 25 C in older flue-gas-oriented work (not DAC conditions).
items.regeneration: Not applicable (front end). Fan + pumping in Keith design: 82 kWh/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Water loss 4.7 t per t CO2 at 20 C/64% RH for ~2 M K+ liquor = 11.5 mol H2O per mol CO2, ~12,900 m3/day for a 1 Mt/yr plant (computed). An et al. 2022 (simulation): 75% capture only above 17 C and 90% RH; energy 8.3-11.1 GJ/t and cost $240-409/t across climates. Freezing and viscosity limit cold sites.
items.cost: Contactor cost scales with ~58 million m2 wetted area per Mt/yr at KL 1.3 mm/s (computed); a 2x faster liquid halves it.
items.trl_and_scale: Pilot-proven hardware (cooling-tower components).
items.bottleneck: Flux of only 17-31 kg CO2/m2/yr and 4.7 t water lost per tonne in a temperate climate; Stratos sits in arid West Texas.

items.name: Membrane-free electrochemical acid/base generation for ambient-temperature limestone-to-Ca(OH)2 or Mg(OH)2 (calciner replacement)
items.mechanism: H2 oxidation and evolution electrodes separated by a simple porous separator make acid and base from salt water; acid dissolves CaCO3 or silicate (releasing CO2 or extracting Mg), base precipitates the hydroxide, which then captures CO2 from air.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Nature Communications 2025: cell outputs extracted Mg(OH)2 from olivine and serpentine, which removed CO2 from ambient air as Mg carbonates (demonstration, rates not extracted here).
items.regeneration: Acid/base energy 0.060-0.066 kWh per mol at 140 mA/cm2 productive current density (0.87 M outputs); best prior BPMED 0.073-0.145 kWh/mol at ~30 mA/cm2; 2.30 MWh per t Mg(OH)2 from olivine. Computed: used as a closed CaCO3 loop (2 H+ per CO2) this is 432-475 kJ/mol = 9.8-10.8 GJ/t electric, versus 5.25 GJ/t heat for the calciner; with a bicarbonate feed (1 H+) 4.9-5.4 GJ/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 35 h run at 100 mA/cm2 with Mg and Si impurities; voltage drifted 1-2 mV/h and was recovered by periodic polarity reversal. Proton crossover costs 27% of charge at 50 mA/cm2 and 60% at 500 mA/cm2 in NaCl.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, lab cell.
items.bottleneck: Two protons per CO2 at ~1 V each: about twice the calciner's energy in electricity unless crossover and voltage fall substantially; best use is open-loop with silicate feedstock rather than a closed DAC loop.

items.name: Solid-electrolyte reactor: O2/H2O redox with in-cell carbonate formation and release (Rice University and follow-ups)
items.mechanism: Oxygen reduction at the cathode makes a strongly alkaline interface that absorbs CO2 as carbonate; carbonate crosses an anion membrane into a porous solid-electrolyte layer where protons from water oxidation release pure CO2. No circulating chemical.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Zhu et al. 2023 (Nature): headline numbers are for simulated flue gas: up to 440 mA/cm2 (86.7 kg CO2/day/m2), >90% Faradaic efficiency on carbonate, >98% removal. Follow-up (Nature Communications 2025, recirculation mode): direct air capture at 30 mA/cm2 with >93% removal, >2,000 h operation, ~85% Faradaic efficiency for Na+ transport; energy for the air case is not given in the abstract.
items.regeneration: Energy 'starting from about 150 kJ/mol' (3.4 GJ/t electric) at low current density on flue-gas-strength feed; this figure should not be read as an air-capture result. The O2 reduction/evolution couple carries large overpotentials at practical current density.
items.stability_and_lifetime: >2,000 h reported in the 2025 follow-up (lab cell).
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4; 100 cm2 cell reported for flue gas.
items.bottleneck: At 400 ppm the cathode interface is CO2-starved, so current density drops ~15x (440 -> 30 mA/cm2), multiplying cell area per tonne; ORR/OER voltage losses set the energy.

items.name: Commercial electrochemical liquid DAC (Mission Zero Technologies; Phlair)
items.mechanism: Liquid air contactor plus heat-free electrochemical release: Mission Zero uses an electrodialysis-type separation and a depressurised release chamber; Phlair uses a hydrogen-looping electrolyser to make acid and base.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Not published in measured form.
items.regeneration: Mission Zero's 2022 UK government Phase 1 report: pilot design estimate 2.18 MWh/t (7.85 GJ/t electric), built from vendor data and lab electrochemical experiments projected forward, at 12 h/day operation; ancillaries add 0.47 MWh/t. The company separately claims <800 kWh/t at scale (claim). Phlair's stated target is <1.5 MWh/t (5.4 GJ/t); no measured figure published.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No public membrane-lifetime or solvent-loss data.
items.cost: Phlair/Frontier offtake: $30.6 million for 47,000 t over 2027-2030 = ~$651/t (computed contract price). Mission Zero has stated first-generation DAC exceeds $300/t and targets a 3x reduction (claim).
items.trl_and_scale: Outdoor pilots (tens to hundreds of t/yr); Phlair's first commercial plant planned in Alberta.
items.bottleneck: Gap between claim (0.8-1.5 MWh/t) and the only documented design number (2.18 MWh/t); the academic best for the same step is 4.5 GJ/t = 1.25 MWh/t at 25-30 mA/cm2.

items.name: Water-lean / CO2-binding organic liquids for DAC (PNNL CO2BOLs: BEPBEGDA, BEEDIDA)
items.mechanism: Low-water amine solvents that bind CO2 as neutral carbamic acid, giving lower regeneration enthalpy and temperature than aqueous carbamate chemistry; molecules were dimerised to raise molecular weight and cut vapour pressure for open-air use.
items.uptake_and_conditions: PNNL-36148 (Feb 2024): BEPBEGDA took up 13.2 wt% (97 mol%) under PURE CO2; in a flow-through test with ambient air at 25 C both new solvents captured slightly less than 0.1 M NaOH; humidity slightly helped. BEEMPA became non-flowable at 7 wt% loading.
items.regeneration: Parent CO2BOLs: regeneration enthalpy 70-75 kJ/mol at ~75-80 C (flue-gas work). No DAC regeneration measurement, no contactor test, no techno-economics yet (listed as future work).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Parent solvent 2-EEMPA was ruled out for DAC by PNNL because evaporative losses 'would become significant'. New solvents' vapour pressure at 80 C is described as an order of magnitude below ~3 Torr. Computed ceiling for open-air contact: a $10/t make-up budget at $5/kg allows only ~2 kg/t, i.e. an exhaust vapour pressure of ~0.02 Pa (1.4e-4 Torr), roughly three orders of magnitude lower than that benchmark (which is quoted at 80 C, so the ambient gap is smaller but unmeasured).
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, gram-scale property measurements.
items.bottleneck: Volatility and viscosity: 1.8 million m3 of air per tonne strips any liquid with measurable vapour pressure, and the molecular-weight increases that fix volatility raise viscosity and cut mass transfer.

items.name: Conventional aqueous amine (30% MEA) absorber-stripper applied to air
items.mechanism: Standard post-combustion amine scrubbing with packed absorber and ~120 C reboiler, run on ambient air.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Kiani, Jiang and Feron 2020 (CSIRO, rate-based Aspen model): 50% capture chosen; absorber pressure drop 0.73 kPa.
items.regeneration: Reboiler duty 10.7 GJ/t plus 1.45 MWh/t electricity (blower 0.70, liquid recirculation 0.50, wash 0.24 MWh/t).
items.stability_and_lifetime: MEA evaporation 53.4 kg per t CO2 without mitigation (equivalent to ~0.8 Pa in the exhaust, computed); a water-wash column cut this to 0.28 kg/t but raised capital ~60%. MEA oxidises rapidly (>90% lost after 500 h with oxygen in the comparison cited by ORNL).
items.cost: Baseline $1,691/t; with a non-volatile absorbent and cheap cooling-tower-style contactor $676/t (model).
items.trl_and_scale: Simulation only for DAC.
items.bottleneck: Volatility and oxidation at air volumes; this is why liquid DAC moved to hydroxides and amino-acid salts. Useful as the kill criterion for any new organic solvent idea.

items.name: Direct ocean capture and seawater electrolysis (Captura; Equatic)
items.mechanism: Use the ocean as the air contactor. Captura acidifies seawater with bipolar-membrane electrodialysis, strips CO2 through hollow-fibre membrane contactors and returns alkalinity-restored water. Equatic electrolyses seawater to precipitate carbonates/hydroxides and co-produce hydrogen.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Seawater holds ~2.2 mol/m3 dissolved inorganic carbon, so 10,300-17,200 m3 of seawater must be processed per t CO2 at 100-60% extraction (computed): 5-9x the mass of air a DAC plant handles.
items.regeneration: Captura states ~1,800 kWh/t (6.5 GJ/t electric), ~60% of it electrodialysis (company figure, 2024). Equatic states ~2.5 MWh/t with hydrogen co-product (company deck, April 2026). A 2026 review lists BPMED ocean capture at 300-500 kJ/mol and electrochemical routes overall at 118-730 kJ/mol.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Membrane fouling, chlorine evolution and electrode corrosion in seawater are the cited issues; Captura claims proprietary membranes cut contactor pressure drop from ~2 bar to <0.5 bar.
items.cost: Literature cited by Captura: best case $436/t co-located with desalination, $1,839/t standalone, the gap being seawater intake, pumping and pre-treatment. Company targets $100-200/t (claim).
items.trl_and_scale: Captura 100 t/yr pilot demonstrated end-to-end (since Nov 2023), 1,000 t/yr unit planned late 2024. Equatic: two 100 kg/day pilots operated >1 year; ~4,000 t/yr Singapore plant commissioning July 2026.
items.bottleneck: Water handling: if pumping is not shared with another facility, 0.5-2 kWh/m3 would add 5-20+ MWh/t (computed), which is why economics depend on co-location or passive flow.

bottlenecks: Over-strong binding in the hydroxide/calcium loop: CaCO3 calcination needs 178 kJ/mol (4.05 GJ/t) at 900 C against a 20.5 kJ/mol (0.47 GJ/t) separation floor. The heat's exergy alone is 3.0 GJ/t, capping second-law efficiency near 15%; the published design needs 5.25 GJ/t in the calciner and 8.81 GJ/t of gas overall (Keith 2018, design values).

No plant-scale measurement exists for liquid DAC. Stratos (500,000 t/yr) began construction May 2023, was slated for end-2024, and as of August 2026 is promised for end-2026. All energy figures for the KOH route remain 2018 simulation values validated on a 1 t/day pilot whose units were not run as a closed loop.

Electrochemical regeneration is bounded by protons x pH gap: a carbonate liquor needs ~2 H+ per CO2 (2.24 for 0.32 M KOH + 1.34 M K2CO3) at up to 0.83 V each, a 3.6 GJ/t floor for single-stage swings. Best measured: 4.5 GJ/t electric at 25-30 mA/cm2 over 125 h; BPMED-type single stage >=10 GJ/t; H2-loop cells emit CO2 mixed with H2 (3-4 GJ/t more to purify).

Low current density: measured cells run at 5-30 mA/cm2 (Shu 2020: 374 kJ/mol at 5 mA/cm2, 520 kJ/mol at 15 mA/cm2), so cell area and membrane lifetime, not just electricity, set cost. No lifetime data beyond ~125-2,000 h lab runs.

Co-released water in 'low-temperature' crystallization: guanidine carbonate regeneration costs 7.0-10.2 GJ/t (308-449 kJ/mol), more heat than the calciner, because hydrate and filter-cake water evaporate with the CO2; implied 4-6 mol water per mol CO2 (computed).

Gas-liquid kinetics at 400 ppm: KL 1.3 mm/s gives 17-31 kg CO2 per m2 wetted area per year, ~58 million m2 per Mt/yr. Amino-acid salts capture only 20-42% per pass at >1 m/s and lose half their performance between 35 C and -5 C.
Water balance of open contactors: 4.7 t water lost per t CO2 at 20 C/64% RH for KOH; potassium sarcosinate solutions lost 20-33% of their volume in 8-10 h of testing.

Volatility ceiling for any organic liquid in open air contact: ~1.8 million m3 air per tonne means make-up under $10/t (at $5/kg) requires exhaust vapour pressure below ~0.02 Pa; MEA loses 53.4 kg/t unmitigated.

Oxygen and heat degrade the organic options: reduced phenazine mediators are oxidised by air; unwashed guanidine carbonate with residual amino acid decomposes at 120 C in air; sarcosine loses 21% in 700 h at 120 C. No liquid organic DAC system has published cycle-life data beyond a few cycles.

Passive Ca(OH)2 carbonation: 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr measured, humidity-dependent and passivation-prone (>85-90% conversion needs a humidity swing or true hydroxide feed), implying 855-8,300 ha of tray area per Mt/yr, and it still pays the 900 C calcination bill (~7 GJ/t computed without heat recovery).
open_problems: Design a CO2-binding crystal that releases CO2 without releasing water (anhydrous guanidinium carbonate/bicarbonate phases, or regeneration in liquid water near 78 C where ORNL saw CO2 release begin). Computed target: ~115 kJ/mol (2.6 GJ/t) with zero water released versus 308-449 kJ/mol today. Checkable by lattice-water count, DSC and the sorbent.py heat balance.

Shift capture liquor from carbonate to bicarbonate without losing uptake rate, so release needs 1 H+ per CO2 across a smaller pH gap (floor 0.8-1.8 GJ/t instead of 3.6). Conventional core (K2CO3 contactor) plus one import: CO2-hydration catalysts (Zn carbonic-anhydrase mimics gave up to 2x rate in 1 M K2CO3). Needs a rate-vs-pH calculation at 420 ppm to see whether catalysis can offset the lost OH- driving force.

Staged pH downshift with pure-CO2 output at >=100 mA/cm2: generalise the Northwestern two-stage result (2.4 + 2.1 GJ/t at 25-30 mA/cm2). A Nernst-plus-ohmic verifier (protons per CO2, dpH per stage, area-specific resistance) can rank stage counts and chemistries before any experiment.

Crystal-habit engineering for filterability: Holocene found high-aspect-ratio needles hold liquor in the cake, which adds evaporation heat and carries oxidisable amino acid into the hot step. Import from pharmaceutical crystallization (habit modifiers, seeding, temperature cycling) is a classic recombination and is measurable by cake moisture.

Water-neutral contactor liquids: tune water activity (salt concentration, hygroscopic co-solutes) to the site's humidity so the 4.7 t/t water loss goes to zero or reverses, without wrecking viscosity and KL. Calculable from water-activity data and psychrometrics.

Zero-volatility, oxidation-proof capture liquids with low viscosity (amino-acid salts, zwitterions, ionic liquids): screen against the 0.02 Pa vapour-pressure ceiling and a viscosity cap (~10 mPa.s at -10 C, where 3 M K-sarcosinate sits).

Passivation-free ambient Ca(OH)2 carbonation: exploit humidity swings and nanometre water films (complete carbonation in 1 h under ambient conditions in the lab; nine film renewals in air) to cut the 3-day cycle and tray area; test whether the gain survives at 400 ppm and over calcination cycles.

Lower-temperature or electrified release from CaCO3 that beats 5.25 GJ/t: acid/base electrochemistry currently costs 9.8-10.8 GJ/t electric for a closed loop; identify whether any route (reduced crossover, staged pH, partial thermal assist) can get under ~4 GJ/t, or rule it out by calculation.

Oxygen-tolerant proton carriers for redox pH swing: inorganic proton sponges such as MnO2 work only near bicarbonate pH; find carriers stable at pH >12 in air, or architectures that keep organics out of contact with O2 at less than the 257 kJ/mol achieved so far.

Cold and arid siting: capture halves from 35 C to -5 C for amino acids and 75% capture with KOH needs >17 C and 90% RH; ideas that decouple uptake from climate (enclosed humidified contactors, heat-integrated contactors) need a fan-plus-water cost check.

Independent measurement gap: no public cycle-life, sorbent-loss or integrated energy data for the guanidine route (project terminated before delivering them) or for Stratos. A low-cost lab partner study of 100+ cycle stability would be new information regardless of outcome.

key_claims.claim: The only detailed energy numbers for the KOH/calcium-loop DAC route are still the 2018 design values (8.81 GJ gas per t CO2, or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh, at 15 MPa; calciner at 900 C, 74.5% capture, KL 1.3 mm/s), derived from Aspen simulation plus a 1 t/day pilot. Stratos had produced no public operating data by August 2026 (start-up now promised for end-2026). Because calcination alone needs 4.05 GJ/t at 900 C, this route cannot fall far below ~5 GJ/t of high-grade heat whatever the engineering.

Replacing the calciner with electrochemistry has now been measured at ~4.5 GJ/t electric (2.4 GJ/t hydrogen-loop stage taking pH 13.5 to 9, plus 2.1 GJ/t MnO2 stage; 25-30 mA/cm2; 125 h; synthetic post-capture KOH/K2CO3 liquor), against >=10 GJ/t for single-stage bipolar-membrane swings. This is the best measured liquid-route regeneration figure found, but it is a lab cell at low current density, about 10% second-law efficiency, with no lifetime or cost data.

surprises: There is no 'Stratos measured data'. As of the latest reports found (E&E News, 7 August 2026) the plant had not started; Occidental cites a non-process component fault found in Phase 1 commissioning and now targets end-2026. Source: https://www.eenews.net/articles/worlds-largest-carbon-removal-plant-to-open-at-the-end-of-2026-2/

The 'low-temperature' guanidine crystallization route needs MORE heat per tonne (7.0-10.2 GJ/t) than the 900 C calciner (5.25 GJ/t), because water leaves with the CO2. Its advantage is heat grade (1.7-2.5 GJ/t work-equivalent at 120 C, computed), not quantity. ORNL's own paper says: "A breakthrough in achieving low-energy regeneration would involve releasing only CO2 molecules while retaining H2O molecules bound with the BIG compound."

Holocene's DOE-funded project was terminated before delivering the sorbent-stability assessment, the 1 kg guanidine synthesis, vacuum and steam desorption reports and the final techno-economic analysis (final report November 2025, https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/3015786). The widely cited $100/t figure is a contract price to Google, not a measured cost; Occidental bought the company in April 2025.

Hydrogen-looping cells, the basis of several start-ups' 'heat-free' claims, release CO2 mixed with H2 when run in one stage; the 2026 PNAS paper puts the clean-up at 3-4 GJ/t, which is why it moved to two stages.

PNNL describes its new water-lean DAC solvents as having low vapour pressure because it is an order of magnitude below ~3 Torr at 80 C; my air-volume calculation puts the economic ceiling near 1.4e-4 Torr at the contactor, so 'low' by solvent standards may still be far too high (ambient-temperature vapour pressures were not reported in the text I read).

Amino-acid salts fix oxidation but not heat: sarcosine lost <=2% in 500 h under oxygen (MEA >90%) yet 21% in 700 h at 120 C, where MEA lost nothing measurable. Any thermal-regeneration idea for amino acids must stay below ~100 C.

Direct ocean capture must move 10,300-17,200 m3 of seawater per tonne of CO2 (computed from 2.2 mol/m3 dissolved carbon): 5-9 times the mass of air a DAC plant handles for the same tonne. Its published best-case costs differ four-fold ($436 vs $1,839/t) depending only on whether pumping is shared with a desalination plant.

Cheap sorbent changes the lifetime arithmetic completely: lime at $0.15/kg costs ~$22/t CO2 even if purged after 10 cycles, the same as a $20/kg solid amine lasting 20,000 cycles. The calcium routes lose on energy and area, not on sorbent durability.

Scope and method notes: the WebSearch quota for this session ran out partway through, so later sourcing used direct fetches plus the OSTI and Europe PMC APIs; Sabatino et al. 2021 (Joule) and Occidental's stated Stratos cost could not be opened and are not relied on. Kiani 2020 and An 2022 numbers were read via page summaries rather than full text. Calculation scripts: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/liquid_loops.py and liquid_loops2.py.

verifs.claim: The only detailed energy numbers for the KOH/calcium-loop DAC route are still the 2018 design values (8.81 GJ gas per t CO2, or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh, at 15 MPa; calciner at 900 C, 74.5% capture, KL 1.3 mm/s), derived from Aspen simulation plus a 1 t/day pilot. Stratos had produced no public operating data by August 2026 (start-up now promised for end-2026). Because calcination alone needs 4.05 GJ/t at 900 C, this route cannot fall far below ~5 GJ/t of high-grade heat whatever the engineering.
verifs.corrected_claim: The reference energy numbers for the KOH/calcium-loop DAC route are still the 2018 Keith et al. design values, and they are simulated, not measured: 8.81 GJ natural gas per t CO2 captured from air (all-gas variant A), or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh electricity (variant C), both delivering CO2 at 15 MPa. The design basis is a calciner at 900 C, a modelled 74.5% capture fraction (7 m packing, 1.4 m/s air, 400 ppm) and KL = 1.3 mm/s at 20 C. These come from an Aspen Plus simulation whose unit models were informed by vendor data and a nominal 1 t-CO2/day pilot at Squamish; the pilot's coupled contactor/pellet-reactor loop ran at 0.6 t/day, its contactor measured only 42% capture (3 m packing), and its calciner ran in batch mode. No measured energy balance from a commercial plant exists: Stratos had not started up or published operating data by August 2026 (after a May 2026 "non-process component" delay, Occidental said start-up would be end-2026). The calcination reaction itself needs a thermodynamic minimum of 4.05 GJ/t-CO2 (3.18 GJ/t-CaO); the paper's calciner design needs 5.25 GJ/t-CO2 (4.07 GJ/t-CaO, about 78% thermal efficiency). So the calciner heat demand of this route is bounded below at about 4.05 GJ/t and realistically sits around 4.5-5.25 GJ/t of ~900 C heat; that floor is an inference from the paper, not a statement in it.
verifs.caveats:
Verified against the full text of Keith et al., Joule 2018 (archived copy of the cell.com page, 2021 snapshot). The quoted figures (8.81 GJ; 5.25 GJ + 366 kWh; 15 MPa; 900 C; 74.5%; 1.3 mm/s; 4.05 GJ/t-CO2; Aspen Plus; "1 t-CO2/day pilot plant operated since 2015") all appear in the paper. The corrections are about what they mean.

1. **4.05 vs 5.25 GJ/t.** Table 1 lists the calciner's "Energy consumption" as 4.05 GJ/t-CO2 "determined by Aspen Plus simulation". The body text says the minimum reaction energy is 3.18 GJ/t-CaO (which equals 4.05 GJ/t-CO2) and the design requires 4.07 GJ/t-CaO, "equivalent to 5.25 GJ/t-CO2". So 4.05 is the thermodynamic floor and 5.25 the design demand; the paper is internally inconsistent in its labelling.
2. **"Cannot fall far below ~5 GJ/t" is loose.** The paper cites limestone shaft kilns at 89% efficiency, which would imply about 4.55 GJ/t. The hard floor is 4.05 GJ/t per t CO2 passing through the calciner.
3. **The floor applies only to the calcium loop.** The heat need not come from gas (an electric calciner would do), and part of it is recovered at lower grade (slaking heat at about 300 C, steam for power). Regenerating KOH electrochemically is a different route and is not bound by it.
4. **Basis of the 8.81 GJ figure.** It is per t CO2 captured from air. The plant also captures 0.48 t of gas-combustion CO2 per t (0.98 Mt/yr atmospheric, 1.46 Mt/yr delivered). Variant D needs 5.25 GJ + 77 kWh but delivers at 0.1 MPa with oxygen supplied free.
5. **Measured vs simulated.** The 74.5% capture fraction is a model output "validated by pilot data", not a measurement. The pilot had no CO2 compression or gas clean-up and used a stirred-tank slaker rather than the steam slaker, so no integrated energy balance was measured. Humidity and climate sensitivity are not in the headline numbers.
6. **"Only detailed energy numbers" is overstated.** Other detailed model-based estimates exist, for example NETL's 2022 "Direct Air Capture Case Studies: Solvent System". I confirmed that report exists from a search snippet only and did not read it; these are also simulations, so "no measured commercial-scale data" still holds.
7. **Stratos status is not in the Joule source.** It rests on news listings: E&E News (7 May 2026 delay; 6-7 Aug 2026 "end of 2026"), gasworld (12 May 2026) and Energy Intelligence (7 Aug 2026). The E&E article summary mentions no operating data. A search-result snippet from late September 2026 described the plant as still delayed with no confirmed date, so the end-2026 date is a promise. I did not check whether Stratos as built matches the 2018 design.

The web search budget was exhausted, so the status checks used direct page fetches and search-result pages rather than a full search.

verifs.claim: Replacing the calciner with electrochemistry has now been measured at ~4.5 GJ/t electric (2.4 GJ/t hydrogen-loop stage taking pH 13.5 to 9, plus 2.1 GJ/t MnO2 stage; 25-30 mA/cm2; 125 h; synthetic post-capture KOH/K2CO3 liquor), against >=10 GJ/t for single-stage bipolar-membrane swings. This is the best measured liquid-route regeneration figure found, but it is a lab cell at low current density, about 10% second-law efficiency, with no lifetime or cost data.
verifs.corrected_claim: Jung, ..., Sargent (Northwestern), PNAS 123(9), published 27 Feb 2026, "Electrified release of pure CO2 from postcapture liquid: A two-stage system lowers the total energy cost", report a measured ~4.5 GJ/tCO2 electric for releasing pure CO2 from a simulated post-DAC liquor (0.32 M KOH + 1.34 M K2CO3; no air-contacted liquid was used). The figure is the SUM of two separately run lab stages, not an integrated continuous process: (1) a hydrogen-loop cell at 25 mA/cm2 that took pH ~13.5 to ~9 over a single continuous 16 h run (cell voltage rising 0.4 to 0.75 V, ~80% charge efficiency, 95% of carbonate converted to bicarbonate) = 2.4 GJ/t; (2) an MnO2 "proton sponge" insertion/deinsertion stage at 30 mA/cm2 on 4 cm2 electrodes (~+/-0.4 V, ~80% CO2 charge efficiency) = 2.1 GJ/t when fed the pH ~8.9 stage-1 outlet. The 125 h stability figure belongs to the MnO2 stage only, apparently on pure KHCO3 feed, where energy ranged 1.9-2.5 GJ/t; the hydrogen-loop stage has only 16 h. The >=10 GJ/t comparator for pH-swing methods such as bipolar-membrane electrodialysis is a literature value cited by the authors (they note ~22 GJ/t is often seen in practice), not measured in this work. The paper does not state a second-law efficiency: its own route-specific thermodynamic floors are 2.4 GJ/t (two-stage) and 1.6 GJ/t (infinite-stage), so the cell is at roughly 53% of its route limit; "about 10%" is only obtained by dividing the ~0.45 GJ/t ideal air-separation minimum by 4.5, which compares a regeneration-only number to a full capture-plus-release minimum. No techno-economics, no lifetime/degradation data; authors explicitly say capital costs of two cells remain to be evaluated.
verifs.caveats: Source access: PNAS page returned 403; verified via Crossref abstract (verbatim) and the open-access Europe PMC full text (PMC12956883) read through a summarizing fetch tool, so body-text details (16 h, 125 h on pure KHCO3, 4 cm2, 1.9-2.5 GJ/t range, catalysts) are one step removed from the raw text and the exact feed used in the 125 h run should be rechecked before quoting. Web search budget was exhausted, so "best measured liquid-route regeneration figure found" could not be independently tested and remains the claimant's judgment, not a finding of the paper. Use-changing context: (a) 4.5 GJ/t is regeneration electricity only; it excludes air-contactor fans, pumping, H2 recirculation, CO2 compression, and is electricity rather than heat, so it is not like-for-like with the 6-8 GJ/t (mostly thermal) calciner baseline the paper cites. (b) Stages were batch-run separately and summed; 4 cm2 cells at 25-30 mA/cm2 imply very large electrode area per tonne. (c) Stage 1 uses platinum-group catalysts (PtRu anode, Pt/C cathode) with Nafion 212 and Piperion AEM; authors note charge-efficiency losses from ion crossover and MnO2 kinetic limits, and MnO2 is stable only in the bicarbonate regime, not strong alkali. (d) No cycle count is given for the 125 h run. (e) Simulated liquor only, so contaminant effects from real air contact are untested.

title: Mineral and oxide looping, passive carbonation

items.name: Ca(OH)2 lime looping on stacked trays (Heirloom)
items.mechanism: CaCO3 is calcined at ~900 C in an electric kiln to CaO + pure CO2; CaO is slaked to Ca(OH)2, spread in thin layers on trays, and passively carbonated by ambient air; the CaCO3 returns to the kiln.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Company claim (blog, Mar 2022, no conditions given): 85% carbonation extent in 2.5 days, improved 10x from ~4 weeks. Company's 2021 Stripe application: peak 2 weeks, average ~4 weeks, target 12.5 days; capacity ~0.59 g CO2/g CaO per cycle (0.53 at 90% calcination). At 85% conversion Ca(OH)2 carries 11.5 mol CO2/kg (0.505 kg/kg) per cycle, but only 0.17 kg CO2/kg/day at a 3-day cycle versus ~1.1 kg/kg/day for a fast-cycling amine (my calculation). OptiLex diffusion model says 85% in 3 days at 420 ppm requires loose layers of only ~4 mm (~1.9 kg/m2).
items.regeneration: Company figure (2021 application, not plant-measured): calcination heat 5.9 GJ/t CO2 excluding heat integration, plus ~0.5 GJ/t for condensing and compression = ~6.4 GJ/t. My check with the verifier: reaction 4.07 + sensible 2.6 + residual Ca(OH)2 dehydration 0.4 = 7.1 GJ/t with no heat recovery, 5.8 GJ/t with 50% sensible-heat recovery. All-electric at 7.1 GJ/t is 6.5% second-law efficiency and $59/$99/$159 per t at $30/$50/$80 per MWh.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No public multi-cycle data. 2021 application: sorbent replaced 'pessimistically, every 10 cycles'; optimistically hundreds; deactivation expected from sintering in the kiln. No integrated cycling had been completed at that time.
items.cost: 2021 application: ~$20,000/t at prototype scale, ~$8,500/t projected at 1 t/day. Secondary reporting of company estimates (unverified by me): $600-1,000/t currently, industry $200-300/t by early 2030s, $100/t long-term target. Make-up limestone itself is cheap: ~$8-10/t CO2 at 8-10 cycles (my calculation at $30/t limestone), but adds 12-15% kiln duty and 0.27-0.33 t spent solids per t CO2.
items.trl_and_scale: Tracy, California plant: up to 1,000 t CO2/yr (opened Nov 2023). Louisiana (Shreveport) first phase announced at ~17,000 t/yr for 2026, $475M investment; I could not confirm its status as of Oct 2026. Series B $150M (Dec 2024); Japanese investors added Dec 2025.
items.bottleneck: Thermodynamic over-binding (calcination dG 131 kJ/mol = 6.4x the separation floor) and diffusion-limited CO2 supply (~120 kg CO2/m2/yr of exposed bed at a 3-day cycle, i.e. ~8,400 m2 of tray per 1,000 t/yr).

items.name: Measured CO2-supply limit for passive CaO/Ca(OH)2 beds (Trent University; Heriot-Watt)
items.mechanism: Flow-through and flux experiments on thin CaO and Ca(OH)2 powder deposits in humid ambient air; carbonation proceeds as a diffusion-limited front, with CaO additionally passivated if hydration and carbonation overlap.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Dostie, Rausis, Power (Goldschmidt 2024 abstract; J. Cleaner Prod. 2025): CaO deposits 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 cm thick at 85-95% RH for 24 days removed 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr. All Ca(OH)2 runs at 100-500 ppm CO2 reached >90% CaCO3; CaO was limited by passivation unless a humidity swing (e.g. 40% to 95% RH) separated hydration from carbonation (>85%). In a 21-day flow-through test (0.5 cm, 100 g CaO, 0.1-20 L/h humid air) outlet CO2 never recovered to lab level. Hawrot and Renforth (Sci. Total Environ. 2025): layers 2.5-50 mm at ambient; layers <10 mm reapplied every 5-10 days gave the best areal rate, >2 t CO2/ha/day (= 73 kg/m2/yr). My parameter-free Fick shrinking-front model gives 119 kg/m2/yr for a 3-day cycle, 205 for 1 day, 55 for 14 days.
items.regeneration: Not studied (carbonation only).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Single carbonation; no cycling.
items.cost: Not given. Implied exposed bed area 5-18 km2 per Mt CO2/yr for 1-14 day cycles (my calculation).
items.trl_and_scale: Bench (grams to 100 g), 2024-2025.
items.bottleneck: CO2 transport at 420 ppm (17.2 mmol/m3), not surface chemistry; average flux falls as 1/sqrt(cycle time). Stagnant-air gas film alone caps flux at ~50-120 kg/m2/yr for k_g 2-5 mm/s.

items.name: Independent Ca(OH)2 carbonation kinetics and humidity threshold (Criado and Abanades, CSIC)
items.mechanism: Porous Ca(OH)2 mortars/plates carbonated in room air; carbonation front follows z = k*sqrt(t) (Fickian gas diffusion through the carbonated layer).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2022: samples 4-15 mm thick, porosity 0.2-0.8, at 500 +/- 25 ppm CO2, 52 +/- 3% RH, 19 C. Maximum conversion after 500 h: 0.6 for low-grade Ca(OH)2 (18.2 m2/g), 0.85-0.90 for high-surface-area grade (39.3 m2/g). At RH >95% low-grade also reaches ~0.9. RH >80% gives fast rates; below 50% RH rates are extremely slow; at 0% RH conversion stays <0.05. Follow-up (Criado et al., Chem. Eng. J. 2026) maps maximum conversion over 500-120,000 ppm, 10-95% RH, 30-80 C for standard and high-surface-area Ca(OH)2 (abstract not retrievable; numbers not verified).
items.regeneration: Not tested; oxy-fired or electric calcination assumed in companion design work.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Single carbonation only.
items.cost: Not given in this paper.
items.bottleneck: Humidity (needs RH >50%, ideally >80%) and sorbent surface area set the attainable conversion; diffusion sets the time. Humidifying dry air is prohibitive: ~37 t water per t CO2 to lift 20% to 80% RH (my calculation), so siting must be humid.

items.name: Fan-assisted Ca(OH)2 contactor with oxy-fuel flash calciner (8 Rivers Calcite / Origen)
items.mechanism: Hydrated lime exposed to fan-driven air carbonates in under a day; CaCO3 goes to an oxy-fuel flash calciner (~900 C) that delivers pure CO2; CaO is slaked and reused.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Company claim (Stripe application, spring 2022): 85% of maximum carbonation in <24 h in ambient air, lab scale (grams of CO2 per test), said to be corroborated by a US national lab's TGA tests; 0.663 g CO2/g Ca(OH)2 quoted per cycle at 85% (note: stoichiometry gives 0.505; the company figure appears to be per g CaO basis). Pilot site chosen for ~80% average humidity; low humidity listed as risk 1.
items.regeneration: Company example: 4.9 GJ per t CaO, which is 7.35 GJ per t atmospheric CO2 at 85% carbonation (my conversion; 15.8x the floor). 7-21 cycles per week.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Sorbent 'conservatively assumed to be replaced every 8-10 cycles' to limit reactivity loss.
items.cost: Company model: ~$1,000/t at pilot scale (83% opex, labour dominated; electricity $125/MWh, gas $10.5/MMBtu); <$300/t at 100,000 t/yr; <$200/t at megaton scale; <$100/t projected later.
items.trl_and_scale: Planned pilot 1,711 t CO2/yr gross using a 3,000 t/yr oxy-fuel kiln (2022). Origen reported a pre-FEED for zero-emission lime in March 2026; current DAC scale not confirmed.
items.bottleneck: Same calcination energy as all lime looping; short sorbent life (8-10 cycles) adds 12-15% kiln duty; humidity dependence.

items.name: Measured ambient carbonation of MgO (Trent University; Oak Ridge)
items.mechanism: MgO hydrates to brucite and slowly forms hydrated Mg carbonates (dypingite); a thin reacted layer armours the surface.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Rausis, Stubbs, Power, Paulo (Goldschmidt 2022 abstract): 10 cm MgO powder deposit (76 kg/m2), tilled daily, wet-dry cycles, 5 months, lab air. CO2 flux 3.9 (saturated), 12.5 (optimal: porosity 44-61%, water 7-17 wt%) and 2.2 (dry) kg CO2/m2/yr. Linear extrapolation: only 3-18% of MgO reacts in 1 year; 90% would take 5-27 years; 80,000-455,000 km2 per Gt CO2/yr. Carbon isotopes showed CO2 supply was rate-limiting despite daily mixing. ORNL (Environ. Sci. Technol. 2023): reacted layer on MgO crystals exposed for 27 years is only ~1.5 micrometres thick on average.
items.regeneration: Not tested. Product is hydrated carbonate, so calcination must also drive off water: ~4.1 GJ/t CO2 for hydromagnesite versus 2.3 GJ/t for anhydrous MgCO3 (my calculation from formation enthalpies, +/- a few percent), which removes most of magnesium's energy advantage over calcium (4.07 GJ/t).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Passivation worsens with time; the authors note linear extrapolation is optimistic.
items.cost: Not given; land need is 13-75x the 6,100 km2/Gt in the original design.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench (one 10 cm deposit), 2022-2023.
items.bottleneck: Surface passivation plus CO2 supply: measured flux is 15-87x below what the MgO-looping cost study assumed.

items.name: MgO looping design study (McQueen, Kelemen, Dipple, Renforth, Wilcox 2020)
items.mechanism: Magnesite calcined at 600-1200 C to MgO; MgO spread 0.1 m deep on land for a year to carbonate; recollected and recalcined.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Assumed, not measured: 90% carbonation in one year for 20 micrometre particles in 0.1 m layers, extrapolated from an aqueous brucite carbonation rate of ~3e-8 mol/m2/s. Implies 192 kg CO2/m2/yr (my calculation from 21,500 t MgO on 11 ha).
items.regeneration: Oxy-fired calcination 5.89-7.97 GJ/t CO2 (natural gas) plus ~0.3 GJ/t electricity for air separation and condenser.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Assumed 5-10% environmental loss per cycle; capacity loss 5-7% after 10 cycles.
items.cost: $46-159/t CO2 net removed (grid or solar electricity, no post-processing).
items.trl_and_scale: Paper design only; 0.61 Mha and 2.9 Gt magnesite (~29% of reserves) for 1 Gt/yr.
items.bottleneck: The central kinetic assumption is contradicted by later measurement (3-18%/yr). The low cost should be treated as unsupported until depassivation is demonstrated.

items.name: KOH contactor with calcium-looping regeneration (Carbon Engineering design, Keith et al. 2018)
items.mechanism: Air CO2 absorbed in aqueous KOH; carbonate transferred to CaCO3 pellets by causticisation; pellets calcined at ~900 C in an oxy-fired calciner; CaO slaked and recycled. The mineral loop is the regeneration step, not the air contactor.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Liquid contactor with fans (61 kWh/t fan energy from pilot pressure-drop data). Avoids the solid-bed diffusion limit by using a wetted packing.
items.regeneration: Design values: 8.81 GJ natural gas per t CO2, or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh electricity, CO2 delivered at 15 MPa. Calciner needs 5.25 GJ/t CO2 against 3.18 GJ/t CaO reaction heat; APS 2011 had estimated 8.1 GJ/t. Slaking heat recovers 77 kWh/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Pellet/calciner loop based on commercial lime and pulp-mill equipment; not a sorbent-lifetime-limited design.
items.cost: Levelised $94-232/t CO2 (2018 design study; gas $3.5/GJ, 90% utilisation). OptiLex's earlier run found a Stratos-like capital charge of ~$274/t, so the paper's range has not been realised.
items.trl_and_scale: Engineering design from a ~1 t/day pilot for a 1 Mt/yr plant (2018). Commercial scale-up is the Stratos plant (not re-verified here).
items.bottleneck: Same CaCO3 calcination penalty: 8.81 GJ/t is 18.9x the floor (5.3% second-law if counted as work); capital dominates.

items.name: Thermal Ca/Mg exchange to make reactive single-use minerals (Chen and Kanan, Nature 2025)
items.mechanism: CaCO3 or CaSO4 is heated with Mg-rich silicates (olivine, serpentine, augite) to form Ca2SiO4 and MgO, both far more reactive to air than the input silicate; the products are used once (for example spread on soil), not looped.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured: in ambient air under wet conditions Ca2SiO4 converts to CaCO3 and silicic acid, and MgO partly to Mg carbonate, 'within weeks'; under 1 atm CO2 at room temperature, within hours; the untreated Mg silicate shows no reaction over 6 months. University summary: about 1 t of material removes ~1 t CO2 net of kiln fuel emissions.
items.regeneration: None (single use). Kiln ~1,400 C. Authors' energy analysis (not measured): less than 1 MWh per t CO2 removed (3.6 GJ/t = 7.7x the floor).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable; permanence as carbonate or bicarbonate.
items.cost: Not published.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab kiln producing ~15 kg material per week (2025). Feedstock: >400 Mt/yr suitable mine tailings; silicate reserves >100,000 Gt.
items.bottleneck: Field kinetics are unmeasured: 'weeks' is for wet lab samples, and MgO passivation (see measured MgO item) applies to half the alkalinity. Kiln CO2 from the limestone must be captured or netted off. Verification of removal in soil is hard.

items.name: Passive carbonation of large stacked Ca(OH)2 plates (Abanades, Criado, Fernandez 2020)
items.mechanism: Sintered porous Ca(OH)2 plates are stacked with air gaps and left to carbonate by natural air movement for months, then recalcined in an oxy-fired calciner. No fans, very large contactor volume.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Design basis: plates 2 x 2 m, 3 cm thick, porosity 0.5, fully carbonated in about 6 months at ambient CO2. My independent Fick model with no fitted parameters gives a 15.0 mm front after 6 months, matching the half-thickness.
items.regeneration: Oxy-calcination of the carbonated plates; energy not extracted here.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Plates recycled through calcination; mechanical integrity over cycles untested.
items.cost: $140-340/t CO2 (authors' estimate; depends on fuel, land, plate manufacture and transport, contingencies).
items.trl_and_scale: Concept with lab kinetics, 2020.
items.bottleneck: Six-month cycles give only ~17 kg CO2/m2/yr of plate face (my calculation) and tie up ~33 kg sorbent-years per kg CO2/yr; contactor volume is 10-100x conventional DAC.

items.name: Potassium and sodium carbonate on porous supports
items.mechanism: M2CO3 + CO2 + H2O forms 2 MHCO3 in humid air; mild heating (80-300 C depending on support) reverses it. Water is a reactant, so humidity helps rather than hurts in principle.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Jansuda et al. (ACS Omega 2026): K2CO3/Al2O3 took up only 5 mg CO2/g (0.11 mmol/g, 39% carbonate utilisation) at ~450 ppm, 60-65% RH, 26 C, versus ~40 mg/g for an amine-modified zeolite in the same rig. Veselovskaya et al. (K2CO3/gamma-Al2O3, ambient air): stable 4.0-4.9 wt% (0.9-1.1 mmol/g) but with regeneration at 250-300 C (search snippet, not verified). Rodriguez-Mosqueda (Twente thesis 2023): ~6 wt% K2CO3 on activated-carbon honeycomb, full regeneration at 150 C; energy dominated by how desorption is done; higher salt loading needs stronger supports.
items.regeneration: My verifier calculation: reaction heat 3.18 GJ/t (includes 1 mol water vapour per mol CO2); bicarbonate decomposes near 127 C (Na) or 146 C (K) at 1 bar gases. A 150 C swing costs 9.8 GJ/t at 6 wt% loading, 5.2 at 20 wt%, 4.2 at 40 wt% (optimistic Langmuir bound). Minimum work of the regeneration reaction is only 1.7-2.0x the floor versus 6.4x for CaCO3.
items.stability_and_lifetime: K2CO3/Al2O3: at least 90% capacity after 10 cycles at 80 C regeneration (Jansuda 2026). Alumina forms a stable K-Al carbonate phase that forces high regeneration temperature (literature, not verified here). No long-cycle data found.
items.cost: Salts cost under ~$2/kg (general knowledge, not verified); no DAC cost data found.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench; greenhouse CO2-enrichment concept studies.
items.bottleneck: Low active loading and slow gas-solid kinetics: measured 0.11 mmol/g under realistic humid conditions; sensible heat dominates below ~20 wt% loading; salt deliquescence and pore blocking at high humidity.

items.name: Hydroxide-loaded carbon 'charged sorbents' (Li et al., Nature 2024)
items.mechanism: Hydroxide ions are electrochemically inserted into activated-carbon pores; they capture CO2 as (bi)carbonate and release it at 90-100 C; the conductive carbon allows direct Joule heating.
items.uptake_and_conditions: ~0.2 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2 in dry air, 30 C; drops to ~0.14 mmol/g at 11% RH and 0.08 mmol/g at 38% RH. Saturates in ~10-15 minutes. Adsorption heat falls from -137 to -33 kJ/mol with coverage.
items.regeneration: 90-100 C; Joule heating reaches ~90 C in ~1 minute. Authors' minimum energy estimate 6.5-11.4 GJ/t CO2 depending on humidity.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 150 adsorption-desorption cycles with minimal loss; 10% capacity lost after 14 months storage; stable after 12 h in dry air at 100 C.
items.cost: Not given.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench (activated carbon cloth), 2024.
items.bottleneck: Capacity is ~5x below the 1 mol/kg amine reference and falls 60% at just 38% RH; energy is no better than amines.

items.name: Hydrotalcites / layered double hydroxides (LDH)
items.mechanism: Mg-Al layered hydroxides and their calcined mixed oxides are basic solids used for CO2 sorption at 200-400 C and high CO2 pressure. For air capture they mainly serve as supports for amines, where surface hydroxyls stabilise the amine.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Zhao et al. (Advanced Science 2025): PEI-loaded LDH reached 3.92 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2, 21% O2, 3% H2O, 25 C (180 min adsorption). The bare LDH's own 400 ppm capacity is not reported; I found no measured DAC data for unmodified hydrotalcite (absence of evidence after a limited search).
items.regeneration: 120 C for 15 min (amine chemistry, not mineral looping).
items.stability_and_lifetime: 90.8% capacity after only 20 cycles; retains 1.06 mmol/g after 3 h at 120 C in simulated air, better than the calcined mixed-oxide support.
items.cost: Not given.
items.bottleneck: As a mineral sorbent hydrotalcite binds too weakly at 400 ppm and 25 C; as an amine support it inherits amine lifetime limits, and 20 cycles says little about the 2,000-20,000 cycles that set cost.

items.name: Alkaline industrial wastes: theoretical potential (Renforth 2019)
items.mechanism: Ca- and Mg-bearing slags, dusts, ashes and tailings react with CO2 to form carbonates or dissolved bicarbonate; no kiln, single use.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Carbonation potential (kg CO2 per t, from composition, not rates): blast-furnace slag 413, basic-oxygen slag 402, electric-arc slag 368, cement kiln dust 330, lime 777, hard-coal ash 36, lignite ash 146, red mud 47, ultrabasic tailings 40-250, demolition waste 77-110. Measured ambient uptake cited: 90-230 kg/t for blast-furnace slag. The paper states that much more research is needed on ambient-condition capture.
items.regeneration: None.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Permanent mineral storage.
items.cost: Described as potentially low because feedstocks are wastes; not quantified.
items.trl_and_scale: 7 Gt/yr of alkaline materials produced today; potential 2.9-8.5 Gt CO2/yr by 2100 (8-23% of 2024 fossil CO2), a scenario estimate.
items.bottleneck: The potential is stoichiometric; realised passive rates are orders of magnitude lower (see legacy slag item), and hard-coal fly ash holds only 36 kg/t.

items.name: Legacy steel-slag heap: field-measured passive carbonation (Pullin et al. 2019)
items.mechanism: Cores drilled through a >30 Mt slag heap (Consett, UK; deposited 1840-1980) and analysed for carbon to measure how much CO2 was actually taken up passively.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Only 3.6% of the carbon-capture potential used after ~140 years; mean total carbon 0.42%; alteration rinds 0-5 mm; ~80% of material >4 mm and >50% >10 mm; pore-gas CO2 at depth ~85 ppm versus 403 ppm at surface. Earlier leachate-based estimate: 1,176-1,428 t CO2 over ~150 years, about 8-10 kg CO2 per t slag (roughly 60 g/t/yr) against a ~400 kg/t potential.
items.regeneration: None.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Stable carbonate.
items.cost: Not given.
items.trl_and_scale: Full-scale field site, measured 2017.
items.bottleneck: Particle size and gas/water access. Authors recommend shallow piles without topsoil cover. Fine grinding and thin spreading would be needed, with energy and land costs not yet quantified.

items.name: Ultramafic mine tailings (brucite-bearing) as passive air-capture media
items.mechanism: Brucite and serpentine in nickel and diamond tailings react with atmospheric CO2 to form hydrated Mg carbonates in the tailings surface.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Harrison et al. (Environ. Sci. Technol. 2013): accelerated brucite carbonation at Mount Keith could offset ~22-57% of the mine's annual emissions; rate rises linearly with CO2 partial pressure (tests used elevated CO2, so not a 420 ppm rate). From memory, not re-verified: field-measured passive uptake at Mount Keith is ~39,800 t CO2/yr, about 11% of mine emissions (Wilson et al. 2014).
items.regeneration: None (single use).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Hydrated Mg carbonates; stable under dry storage.
items.cost: Not found.
items.trl_and_scale: Field observation at mine scale; commercial pilots by tailings-carbonation startups not verified here.
items.bottleneck: Reactive brucite is only a few weight percent of tailings and uptake is CO2-supply limited, so the scale is tied to mine output (tens of kt per mine, not Mt).

bottlenecks: CO2 supply by gas diffusion at 420 ppm (17.2 mmol/m3) caps passive solid-bed flux: measured 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr for CaO beds 0.5-1.5 cm at 85-95% RH (Dostie 2024/2025) and 73 kg/m2/yr for lime layers <10 mm (Hawrot and Renforth 2025). OptiLex Fick model with no fitted parameters: 205, 119 and 55 kg/m2/yr for 1-, 3- and 14-day cycles, reacting only 2.2, 3.9 and 8.3 mm of loose powder. That means 5-18 km2 of exposed bed per Mt CO2/yr, and ~8,400 m2 of tray for a 1,000 t/yr plant. Flux scales as 1/sqrt(cycle time), so faster cycles trade area for solids handling.

Thermodynamic over-binding in calcium chemistry: Ca(OH)2 captures CO2 with an effective free energy of about -76 kJ/mol at 50% RH when only -19.2 is needed; undoing it (CaCO3 calcination) has dG 131 kJ/mol = 2.98 GJ/t = 6.4x the 0.47 GJ/t floor, so even a perfect lime loop cannot exceed ~16% second-law efficiency. Reaction heat alone is 4.07 GJ/t at ~900 C; realistic kiln duty is 5.25 GJ/t (Keith 2018 design), 5.9-6.4 GJ/t (Heirloom 2021 figure), 7.1-7.4 GJ/t without heat recovery (my calculation; 8 Rivers figure). All-electric at 7.1 GJ/t costs $59-159/t for power at $30-80/MWh. No sorbent tweak inside Ca chemistry removes this.

Humidity: Ca(OH)2 carbonation is extremely slow below 50% RH, fast above 80%, and <5% conversion in dry air (Criado and Abanades 2022). CaO passivates if hydration and carbonation overlap. Raising air from 20% to 80% RH would take ~37 t water per t CO2 (my calculation), so plants are restricted to humid sites or lose productivity.

MgO passivation: measured 3-18% carbonation per year (2.2-12.5 kg CO2/m2/yr; 5-27 years to 90%) versus the 90% per year assumed in the $46-159/t design, a 15-87x shortfall; a 27-year-old MgO surface carries only ~1.5 micrometres of reacted layer. Hydrated carbonate products raise calcination heat to ~4.1 GJ/t, erasing magnesium's energy advantage.

Sorbent life in looping is unproven: companies assume replacement every 8-10 cycles (8 Rivers) or 'pessimistically, every 10 cycles' (Heirloom 2021) because of kiln sintering. At 8-10 cycles that adds 12-15% kiln duty and CO2 to store, and 0.27-0.33 t spent solids per t CO2; limestone make-up itself is only ~$8-10/t. No public data beyond ~10 integrated ambient cycles.

Low sorbent productivity drives capital and handling: Ca(OH)2 at a 3-day cycle yields 0.17 kg CO2 per kg per day versus ~1.1 for an amine cycling 24 times a day, so ~6 t of lime must be moved through a 900 C kiln per tonne-per-day of capacity every 3 days. Stated costs remain $600-1,000/t (company estimates via secondary reporting) against a $100/t target.

Supported alkali carbonates have the right thermodynamics but poor measured performance: 5 mg CO2/g (0.11 mmol/g) for K2CO3/Al2O3 at ~450 ppm and 60-65% RH; at 6 wt% salt loading a 150 C swing costs ~9.8 GJ/t because sensible heat dominates; 40 wt% would give ~4.2 GJ/t but needs supports that survive deliquescence.

Alkaline wastes: stoichiometric potential is large (2.9-8.5 Gt/yr by 2100) but passive realisation is tiny: 3.6% of potential after ~140 years in a 30 Mt slag heap, with pore-gas CO2 depleted to ~85 ppm. Particle size (>50% above 10 mm) and gas/water access are the limits; hard-coal fly ash holds only 36 kg CO2/t.
open_problems: Beat the diffusion limit without fans or robots: design a lime form (fibres, foams, thin coatings on a moving belt or falling curtain) that exposes less than 2 mm reaction depth with high area per volume. Target more than 300 kg CO2/m2/yr of footprint-equivalent area; check each idea against the sqrt(t) front model and the gas-film ceiling (k_g x 17.2 mmol/m3) in the scratchpad script.

Use a humidity swing instead of constant high humidity: Dostie et al. reached >85% conversion of CaO by moving from 40% to 95% RH, separating hydration from carbonation. Can a daily cycle (dry day, humid night) or waste low-grade steam from the slaker do this for free, and what is the measured rate at 420 ppm?

Right-sized binding: sodium and potassium bicarbonate chemistry sits at -24 to -30 kJ/mol effective free energy (needed: -19.2) and regenerates at 127-146 C with only 1.7-2.0x the minimum work, yet measured DAC capacity is ~0.1 mmol/g. Find a support and salt architecture that holds at least 40 wt% salt, stays porous when the salt deliquesces, and reaches at least 1 mmol/g at 420 ppm and 50-80% RH over hundreds of cycles. One imported mechanism to test: carbonic-anhydrase-like or amine promoters for the slow CO2 hydration step.

Low-temperature regeneration of CaCO3 by one imported mechanism (electrochemical acid/base swing instead of a 900 C kiln). Screening number to beat: 2 electrons per CO2 at 2.0 V is 8.8 GJ/t electricity, worse than a kiln, so the idea only works below ~1.2 V or with a hydrogen credit. This needs an executed energy balance before any novelty claim.

Kiln heat integration for lime loops: slaking releases 64 kJ/mol (1.5 GJ/t) and hot CaO and CO2 carry ~2.6 GJ/t sensible heat. How much of the gap between 7.1 and 4.07 GJ/t can real solids heat exchangers close, and can cheap intermittent electricity with thermal storage run the kiln?

Measure sorbent life: nobody has published capacity versus cycle number for an integrated ambient carbonation / calcination / hydration loop beyond ~10 cycles. Hydration each cycle may reactivate sintered CaO; a 100-cycle bench test at 420 ppm would settle whether make-up is 1% or 15% of kiln duty.

MgO depassivation: test whether attrition, wet-dry cycling, seeding or ligand additives can lift the measured 3-18% per year toward the 90% the low-cost design needs, and whether the carbonate product can be steered to low-water phases so calcination stays near 2.3 rather than 4.1 GJ/t. Brucite-to-magnesite binding (-23 kJ/mol effective) is almost ideal thermodynamically, so kinetics is the whole problem.

Single-use reactive minerals (Chen and Kanan route, ground slag, tailings): measure thin-layer uptake at 420 ppm and field humidity over months, per m2 and per tonne, including the MgO half of the alkalinity. Compare energy per tonne against lime looping once grinding and kiln CO2 capture are included.

Cheap computational screen (no lab): extend the scratchpad model to rank every binary oxide, hydroxide and carbonate couple by effective capture free energy at ambient humidity, regeneration free energy and temperature, and material cost, to find couples between the over-binding Ca system and the weak Mg system (mixed Ca-Mg, Li, Sr, Ba, Zn hydroxy-carbonates, double salts), then check prior art before claiming any as new.

key_claims.claim: Passive carbonation of lime at ambient CO2 is limited by CO2 supply, not sorbent chemistry: CaO deposits 0.5-1.5 cm thick at 85-95% RH removed only 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr over 24 days, while Ca(OH)2 itself reached >90% conversion at 100-500 ppm. An independent Fick model reproduces the upper value (119 kg/m2/yr at a 3-day cycle), so lime-based DAC needs roughly 5-18 km2 of exposed bed per Mt/yr and better lime materials alone cannot change that.

The only sub-$100/t mineral-looping estimate (MgO looping, $46-159/t) rests on an assumed 90% carbonation per year that measurement contradicts: a tilled 10 cm MgO deposit under wet-dry cycling took up 2.2-12.5 kg CO2/m2/yr, meaning 3-18% reacted per year, 5-27 years to 90%, and 80,000-455,000 km2 per Gt/yr.

surprises: A textbook diffusion model with no fitted parameters matched three independent results: Abanades's '3 cm plate in about 6 months' (model: 15.0 mm front at 6 months), Dostie's measured upper flux (117 versus 119 kg/m2/yr), and Heirloom's '85% in 2.5 days' (implies ~4 mm loose layers). The kinetics of lime DAC are therefore predictable, and the company speed claims are physically plausible but imply very thin beds and large tray area.

Calcium is the wrong strength, not just an expensive regeneration: it over-binds by ~57 kJ/mol. The alkali bicarbonate couples are the only mineral chemistry in this map inside the useful window (effective -24 to -30 kJ/mol; regeneration minimum work 1.7-2.0x the floor versus 6.4x for CaCO3). The gap between that thermodynamic promise and the measured 0.11 mmol/g is a materials-engineering problem, which is where sorbent research has real headroom in this dimension.

Brucite to magnesite is almost thermodynamically ideal at ambient humidity (about -23 kJ/mol, equilibrium CO2 ~90 ppm), yet MgO is the slowest material measured; and because the real product is a hydrated carbonate, calcination heat rises to ~4.1 GJ/t, the same as limestone. Magnesium's two supposed advantages both disappear in practice.

CO2 starvation appears at every scale: carbon isotopes showed supply limitation in a daily-tilled 10 cm MgO bed, a 0.5 cm CaO bed never let inlet-level CO2 through in 21 days, and gas inside a 140-year-old slag heap sits at ~85 ppm.

Heirloom's own 2021 filing gave a 2-4 week cycle, sorbent replacement 'pessimistically, every 10 cycles', and ~$20,000/t at prototype scale; it also listed MgO alongside CaO. The later move to Ca(OH)2 and 2.5-3 day cycles is consistent with the measured MgO slowness, though the filing does not state that as the reason.

Single-use lime is not carbon-negative (making it releases the CO2 it later absorbs), so only wastes and silicate-derived materials qualify as kiln-free sorbents, and for those the field evidence (3.6% of potential in 140 years) is far below the headline 2.9-8.5 Gt/yr potential.

Evidence gaps to note: no plant-measured energy or cycle-life number for any lime-loop DAC plant is public; the Heirloom Louisiana status, the Abanades 2020 cost range, the Veselovskaya K2CO3 figures and the Mount Keith field number could not be re-verified because the session's web-search budget ran out. Calculation scripts: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/mineral_looping.py and mineral_looping_addendum.py.

verifs.claim: Passive carbonation of lime at ambient CO2 is limited by CO2 supply, not sorbent chemistry: CaO deposits 0.5-1.5 cm thick at 85-95% RH removed only 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr over 24 days, while Ca(OH)2 itself reached >90% conversion at 100-500 ppm. An independent Fick model reproduces the upper value (119 kg/m2/yr at a 3-day cycle), so lime-based DAC needs roughly 5-18 km2 of exposed bed per Mt/yr and better lime materials alone cannot change that.
verifs.corrected_claim: Lab-scale measurements (Dostie, Rausis & Power, Trent University; Goldschmidt 2024 conference abstract, 100 g scale) indicate that passive carbonation of lime powder at ambient CO2 is strongly constrained by CO2 supply and diffusion into the bed, in addition to a material limit (CaO passivation at constant high humidity, which a 40%->95% RH swing overcomes to >85% carbonation). CaO deposits 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 cm thick at 85-95% RH for 24 days gave CO2 removal rates of 12-117 kg CO2/m2/yr (annualised from a 24-day test); the peer-reviewed follow-up (J. Cleaner Production 2025, doi 10.1016/j.jclepro.2025.146635) reports an AVERAGE of 32 kg CO2/m2/yr and 64 +/- 2 wt% CaCO3 for deposits >=0.5 cm under the same conditions, and states carbonation is "readily limited by CO2 supply". In flow-through tests at 100, 200, 300 and 400-500 ppm, all Ca(OH)2 runs reached >90% CaCO3 while CaO was again passivation-limited. The measured range implies about 8.5-83 km2 of exposed bed surface per Mt CO2/yr (about 31 km2 at the peer-reviewed 32 kg/m2/yr average). The 5-18 km2 per Mt/yr figure is NOT from the source: it comes from our own shrinking-front Fick model of a Ca(OH)2 layer at 420 ppm for 1-14 day cycles (205 -> 55 kg/m2/yr; 119 at 3 days) with assumed bed parameters. That model does not reproduce the measurement like-for-like: at the experiment's 24-day duration it gives about 42 kg/m2/yr, which is near the peer-reviewed 32 average, not the 117 upper value. The statement that better lime materials cannot change the area requirement is our inference, not a finding of the source.
verifs.caveats:
VERIFIED against the primary PDF (read directly): 0.5/1.0/1.5 cm CaO deposits, 85-95% RH, 24 days, 12 to 117 kg CO2/m2/yr; Ca(OH)2 >90% CaCO3 at 100, 200, 300, 400-500 ppm; all measured, not simulated. Errors and overreach in the claim:
1) "Not sorbent chemistry" overstates. The abstract hedges ("suggesting larger scale deployments of CaO may be CO2 supply limited") and explicitly reports a material limit: passivation capped CaO carbonation at constant high RH. The supply-limitation evidence in the abstract is a flow-through test at very low flow (0.1-20 L/h over 100 g, 0.5 cm, 21 days) where effluent CO2 never recovered to lab level. The 2025 journal paper is firmer ("readily limited by CO2 supply even under high flow rates, e.g. 25 mmol CO2/h over 100 g CaO"; "CO2 diffusion limitations for CaO deposits >=0.5 cm"), so the direction of the claim holds, but cite that paper, not the abstract, for it.
2) Fick-model "reproduction" is a mismatched comparison. Model source: scratchpad sorbent/mineral_looping.py section 4 (re-run: 119 kg/m2/yr for loose hydrated lime, 500 kg/m3, porosity 0.78, tortuosity 1.3, 85% conversion, 420 ppm, 3-day cycle). It models Ca(OH)2, not CaO; uses a 3-day cycle versus the 24-day experiment; flux scales as t^-0.5 so the 24-day model value is ~42; and bed parameters are assumed (calibrated to one Abanades 2020 data point). The 119 vs 117 match is coincidental (the same script also gets 119 from an unrelated gas-film ceiling at k_g = 5 mm/s). It is independent of the Dostie data but is not validation of the upper value.
3) 5-18 km2 per Mt/yr is model-derived (1-day 4.9 km2, 14-day 18.2 km2), not derived from the measured 12-117 (which gives 8.5-83 km2). Presenting it as following from the source is wrong.
4) "Exposed bed area" is not land footprint: tray systems (Heirloom-type) stack bed area vertically, and thin layers, short cycles or forced airflow raise flux (the same model gives 205 kg/m2/yr at a 1-day cycle; gas-film ceiling ~477 at k_g = 20 mm/s). Bed structure (porosity, layer thickness, particle size) is itself a materials/engineering lever, so "better lime materials alone cannot change that" is not supported by the source; what the source supports is that faster intrinsic chemistry will not help once diffusion/supply limits dominate.
5) Evidence grade and conditions: conference abstract, not peer reviewed; lab scale (100 g); rates annualised from a 24-day test; temperature not stated; CO2 concentration for the flux/thickness tests not stated in the abstract (journal paper gives ambient lab 397-490 ppm); the abstract does not say which thickness gave 12 vs 117 or whether rates are per-thickness averages or peaks. The journal paper reports Ca(OH)2 carbonation rates of 2.1 wt% CaCO3/h at 100 ppm vs 5.2 wt%/h at ambient, consistent with fast intrinsic Ca(OH)2 chemistry. Journal full text was not accessible (ScienceDirect 403); its abstract was reconstructed verbatim from OpenAlex. WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no broader search for contradicting measurements was possible.
Sources: https://goldschmidtabstracts.info/2024/23207.pdf (doi 10.46427/gold2024.23207); https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2025.146635; model at climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/mineral_looping.py

verifs.claim: The only sub-$100/t mineral-looping estimate (MgO looping, $46-159/t) rests on an assumed 90% carbonation per year that measurement contradicts: a tilled 10 cm MgO deposit under wet-dry cycling took up 2.2-12.5 kg CO2/m2/yr, meaning 3-18% reacted per year, 5-27 years to 90%, and 80,000-455,000 km2 per Gt/yr.
verifs.corrected_claim: The McQueen et al. 2020 (Nat. Commun. 11, 3299) MgO-looping estimate of ~$46-159 per tCO2 net removed (only the low end is sub-$100; compression/storage excluded) rests on an assumed, not measured, 90% carbonation in one year for 20 um caustic MgO spread 0.1 m thick and stirred daily (land need ~6,100 km2 per Gt/yr). A 5-month laboratory-controlled test (Rausis et al., Goldschmidt 2022 conference abstract; Trent University) of a 10 cm (76 kg/m2) MgO powder deposit, tilled daily under wetting-drying cycles, measured CO2 fluxes of 2.2 (dry), 3.9 (saturated) and 12.5 (optimal moisture/porosity) kg CO2/m2/yr. Linearly extrapolated, that is only 3-18% of the MgO reacted per year, 5-27 years to 90% carbonation, and 80,000-455,000 km2 per Gt CO2/yr - and the authors say the linear extrapolation likely underestimates the time, because rates slow as reactant depletes. Whether this is "the only" sub-$100/t mineral-looping estimate was not verified.
verifs.caveats:
All numbers on the measurement side match the primary source verbatim (10 cm deposit, daily tilling, wet-dry cycles, 2.2-12.5 kg CO2/m2/yr, 3-18%/yr, 5-27 yr, 80,000-455,000 km2/Gt). The McQueen side was checked against the full text (Europe PMC, PMC7335196): "$46-159 tCO2-1 net removed", "conservative assumption that 20 um particles of caustic magnesia achieve 90% carbonation in a year", 0.1 m layer, stirred daily, ~6,100 km2 per Gt. Corrections and context that change how the claim should be used:

1. "The only sub-$100/t mineral-looping estimate" is an unverified superlative. The web search budget for this session was exhausted, so no survey of other mineral-looping cost estimates (e.g. CaO/Ca(OH)2 looping, Kelemen et al. 2020) was possible. Treat that clause as unsupported. Also, only the lower part of the $46-159 range is below $100.

2. Evidence grade: the cited source is a one-page conference abstract, not peer-reviewed. A peer-reviewed version exists (Rausis, Stubbs, Power, Paulo, "Rates of atmospheric CO2 capture using magnesium oxide powder", Int. J. Greenhouse Gas Control 119, 103701, 2022, doi 10.1016/j.ijggc.2022.103701 - existence confirmed via Crossref) but was paywalled (403), so its final numbers were not checked and may differ from the abstract.

3. Measured vs extrapolated: the fluxes are measured (CO2 flux plus total inorganic carbon, lab-controlled, 5 months). The 3-18%/yr, 5-27 yr and km2 figures are linear extrapolations from 5 months, not 1-year measurements. The authors state the extrapolation is optimistic, so 5-27 yr is a lower bound on time, which strengthens the claim's direction.

4. The 2.2-12.5 range is not a noise band: it is three moisture regimes (dry 2.2, saturated 3.9, optimal 12.5 at 7-17 wt% water and 44-61% porosity). A managed field process would aim for the optimal end (about 18%/yr, about 5 yr, about 80,000 km2/Gt), still roughly 13x McQueen's land figure; the worst case is roughly 75x.

5. Conditions not given in the abstract: CO2 concentration (presumably ambient lab air), temperature, relative humidity, and MgO particle size/surface area. It is therefore not confirmed that the material matched McQueen's assumed 20 um caustic MgO; "contradicts" is fair in direction but not a like-for-like test of the exact assumed material.

6. Mechanism: carbon isotopes showed CO2 supply into the bed was rate-limiting despite daily mixing, and the product was dypingite (0.8 mol CO2 per mol Mg), not magnesite (1:1) as McQueen's stoichiometry assumes. Because the limit is areal CO2 supply, a thinner layer would raise the percent reacted per year but would not reduce the 80,000-455,000 km2 per Gt land requirement. The failure mechanism (diffusion-limited CO2 supply, passivation) is physical and still applies; an independent 2023 Environ. Sci. Technol. study (Weber et al., doi 10.1021/acs.est.3c04690) reports MgO surface passivation limiting the reacted layer to ~1.5 um after 27 years on single crystals.

7. The authors' own conclusion is that rates "will need to be accelerated" for MgO looping to compete with existing DAC - not that the approach is impossible. The abstract gives no revised cost figure; any re-costed $/t is an inference, not a sourced number.

title: Zeolites, carbons, physisorbents and cold or dry operation

items.name: Zeolite 13X (Na-X) at ambient temperature: works dry, fails humid
items.mechanism: Physisorption of CO2 on Na+ cation sites in faujasite cages; water binds the same sites far more strongly and displaces CO2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Dry: 0.34-0.36 mmol/g at 400 ppm CO2, 25 C (gravimetric DVS on ~20 mg and packed-bed breakthrough on 230 mg, Zeochem binderless pellets, 2025). Humid: CO2 uptake 'negligible ... close to 0' at both 30% and 60% RH, same 400 ppm / 25 C, while H2O uptake is ~15 and ~17 mmol/g. About 80% of the water capacity is already reached below 1% RH. CO2 outlet rolls up to nearly 2x inlet when the water front arrives. Independent values: 0.4 mmol/g at 500 ppm, 298 K dry, Qst 39 kJ/mol, 18.8 mmol/g H2O at 95% RH (Sci. Adv. 2019); 0.30 mmol/g at 20 C, 420 ppm, pre-dried real air (iScience 2022).
items.regeneration: Activation at 300 C in these tests; 200 C plus vacuum used in DAC cycle studies. OptiLex verifier (my calculation): with 0.30 mol/kg and a 200 C swing, sensible heat alone is 12.5 GJ/t CO2.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Framework is robust; >15 years life cited for 13X in dry air pre-purification service (cited in Wilson 2022, not DAC-measured). No multi-thousand-cycle humid DAC data found.
items.cost: Commodity industrial zeolite. Verifier: at an assumed $3/kg, 0.30 mol/kg and 15 years at 4 cycles/day, replacement cost is about $10/t CO2 (vs $218/t for the amine reference at 2,000 cycles).
items.trl_and_scale: Sorbent is produced at industrial scale; DAC use is lab scale (mg to g) in the measured data.
items.bottleneck: CO2/H2O selectivity: capacity falls from ~0.35 mmol/g to ~0 at >=30% RH; air at 20 C / 50% RH carries 27 mol H2O per mol CO2.

items.name: Cold-climate Na-X / Li-X TVSA with desiccant pre-drying (Wilson 2022, TerraFixing)
items.mechanism: Same physisorption, but run on naturally cold, dry air: capacity rises as temperature falls and there is little water to remove. 5-step temperature-vacuum swing with a desiccant guard bed regenerated by sensible heat from the zeolite bed.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Na-X at 420 ppm, real Ottawa air dried over a desiccant, 9.5 g pellet bed, breakthrough: 0.30, 0.65, 1.1, 1.9, 2.5 mmol/g at 20, 0, -20, -40, -58 C. Li-X: 0.31, 0.47, 0.77, 1.3, 1.9 mmol/g at 20, 1, -20, -40, -58 C. Isosteric heat 44-49 kJ/mol (Na-X), 49-54 kJ/mol (Li-X). Capture fraction for Na-X improves from 71.6% (58 C) to 91.5% (-58 C).
items.regeneration: 200 C with vacuum. Reported energy 1.1-1.23 MWh/t CO2 (about 4.0-4.4 GJ/t) at -37 to -58 C; this is calculated from breakthrough data plus an energy model, not metered on a plant. Sensible heat falls from 3.1 MWh/t at 20 C to 0.56 MWh/t at -58 C. Desiccant regeneration needs no extra heat at -19 C and below, but dominates at 0 C and 20 C in humid air. Verifier cross-check (my calculation): sensible heat 12.5 GJ/t at 20 C and 2.2 GJ/t at -58 C, consistent with the paper.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No cycling data in the paper; relies on the >15-year industrial life of Na-X in dry air pre-purification.
items.cost: Company claim (TerraFixing website): 'pathway to carbon removal below $100 per tonne' and '2-4x more energy efficient'. No published pilot cost or energy data found.
items.trl_and_scale: Bench (9.5 g bed) in the paper; company describes modular units for the far north, no pilot results published as of Oct 2026.
items.bottleneck: Geography and exergy. Capacity >=1.1 mmol/g needs air at -20 C or colder. In work-equivalent terms the 200 C heat is not better than the amine reference: verifier gives 1.7-2.4 GJ/t for heat alone at -58 to -20 C vs 1.88 GJ/t total for the reference amine cycle. Author is the company founder (interest to flag).

items.name: Water load and pre-drying penalty versus climate (OptiLex verifier calculation)
items.mechanism: A dry-air physisorbent process must remove essentially all water from every cubic metre of air before the CO2 bed. Calculated from saturation vapour pressure, 420 ppm CO2 and 75% capture.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Mol H2O to remove per mol CO2 captured: 93 (30 C, 70% RH), 37 (20 C, 50% RH), 13 (0 C, 70% RH), 2.3 (-20 C, 70% RH), 0.3 (-40 C, 70% RH). The source slides give 31,284 ppm water at 25 C dew point and 1,239 ppm at -20 C versus ~400 ppm CO2.
items.regeneration: Brute-force desiccant regeneration at 50 kJ/mol H2O with no heat recovery: 41.5 GJ/t CO2 at 20 C / 50% RH, 15 GJ/t at 0 C, 2.6 GJ/t at -20 C, 0.3 GJ/t at -40 C. Thermodynamic floor for the drying step (about RT per mol water): 2.0 GJ/t at 20 C / 50% RH, which is about 4x the 0.47 GJ/t CO2 separation floor; 0.11 GJ/t at -20 C. Taking up all the water adiabatically warms the air by about 20 K at 20 C / 50% RH and 1.2 K at -20 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable (calculation).
items.cost: Each 100 Pa of extra pressure drop for a dryer or heat exchanger costs 0.29 GJ/t (82 kWh/t) of fan electricity. Heating or cooling the whole air stream costs 2.1 GJ per kelvin per tonne CO2 before recuperation.
items.trl_and_scale: Calculation only. Scripts: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/cold_dry.py and air_side.py.
items.bottleneck: In temperate air the dominant separation is water, not CO2. Dry physisorbent DAC only closes its energy balance below roughly -10 to -20 C, or with a near-heatless water-management scheme that does not yet exist at DAC scale.

items.name: Sub-ambient (-20 C) 13X TSA with water co-production (Song et al. 2022, Georgia Tech)
items.mechanism: Commercial zeolites (13X, 5A, 4A) used at -20 C where humidity is low; water is taken up on a desiccant layer and recovered as a co-product.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Verified only from the group's DOE review slides and the bibliographic record: 13X TSA at -20 C, 400 ppm CO2, with 'stable performance of 13X during cyclic TSA experiments' in a fixed bed. Exact capacities in the paper could not be retrieved (publisher blocked); Wilson 2022 independently measured 1.1 mmol/g for Na-X at -20 C.
items.regeneration: Desorption at 200 C in 99.99% CO2. Predicted thermal energy 4.36 GJ/t CO2 for TSA (model prediction on the slide). Verifier cross-check: 5.2 GJ/t at 1.1 mol/kg with no heat recovery.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Cyclic stability shown; cycle count not retrieved.
items.cost: None reported in the retrieved material.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3 (stated project goal), lab fixed bed.
items.bottleneck: The same group wrote in 2025 that sub-ambient (~253 K) physisorbent DAC is 'hindered by the need for a water-removal process, location-specific constraints, and insufficient working capacity'.

items.name: Near-cryogenic DAC (160-220 K) with 13X or CALF-20, coupled to LNG regasification (Kim et al., EES 2025)
items.mechanism: Cool air to about 195 K using waste cold from LNG terminals so that weak physisorbents fill almost completely; desorb with a small enthalpy.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 4.5-5.5 mmol/g for zeolite 13X and CALF-20 from breakthrough tests at 195 K (abstract does not state humidity; at 195 K the feed must already be dry). Candidates were chosen by molecular simulation first, then measured.
items.regeneration: 'Low desorption enthalpy' (no number in abstract). Levelized cost 'down to 68.2 USD per tonne CO2', a threefold reduction, from techno-economic modelling, not a plant.
