items.stability_and_lifetime: 'Robust long-term stability' claimed in abstract; cycle count not retrieved.
items.cost: $68.2/t is a model result. Verifier arithmetic (my calculation): cooling the air by 93 K is 196 GJ/t CO2 before recuperation; 98% recuperation leaves 3.9 GJ/t of cold, about 4.7 t LNG regasified per t CO2. Frost load at 15 C / 60% RH is about 13 t ice per t CO2.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab plus TEA. Authors estimate 103-142 Mt CO2/yr globally by 2050. My check: that implies 3-7 t LNG per t CO2 and equals only 5-13% of the CO2 released when that LNG is burned.
items.bottleneck: Hard cap near 0.1 Gt/yr set by LNG cold supply; needs >=98% air-to-air heat recuperation and complete upstream dehydration; ties removal to fossil gas infrastructure.

items.name: Cold operation with weak chemisorption: TEPA-impregnated MIL-101(Cr) regenerated at 25 C (Rim et al., JACS Au 2022)
items.mechanism: At -20 C a 30 wt% amine loading binds CO2 by weak chemisorption, so warming to room temperature releases it. Included because it shows cold changes the answer for amines as well as zeolites.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 400 ppm CO2, -20 C: 1.12 mmol/g. Working capacity 0.73 mmol/g dry over 15 cycles (-20 C to 25 C). At 70% RH and -20 C (870 ppm H2O) working capacity 0.82 mmol/g over 5 cycles: humidity raises capacity. 35 mg fixed bed. 3D-printed MIL-101/PEI monolith: 0.95 mmol/g, adsorb -20 C, desorb 60 C. For contrast, 50% TEPA loading drops from 1.37 mmol/g at 20 C to 0.38 at -20 C.
items.regeneration: 25 C (temperature swing of 45 K) in inert purge; no product-purity or vacuum energy measured. Verifier (idealised single site): a 13X-like site loaded at -20 C and desorbed at 25 C / 100 Pa gives about 2.0 GJ/t heat and 1.1 GJ/t work-equivalent, so small swings are thermodynamically attractive.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 5-15 cycles only. Slide notes polymeric amines stiffen at low temperature, slowing kinetics. No oxidation data at these conditions.
items.cost: MIL-101(Cr) is a chromium MOF; cost and scale-up not addressed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, mg-scale powders, fibres and monoliths.
items.bottleneck: Cycle count (5-15 vs >10,000 needed), slow kinetics (2 h adsorption steps), and recovery of concentrated CO2 at 25 C not shown.

items.name: Mordenite (MOR) zeolites: highest dry zeolite uptake at 400 ppm near ambient (Fu, Park, Davis, PNAS 2022)
items.mechanism: Na+ in the 8-ring side pocket (O33 site) confines CO2; pore-size confinement raises affinity at trace pressure without chemisorption.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Up to 1.15 mmol/g (volumetric) and 1.05 mmol/g (gravimetric) from 400 ppm CO2 at 30 C, dry. About 2.0 mmol/g at sub-ambient temperature. N2 and O2 have negligible effect.
items.regeneration: Described as low heat of adsorption and fast kinetics; no regeneration temperature in the abstract.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not reported in the abstract.
items.cost: Synthetic mordenite is an industrial zeolite family; no cost given.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab powder.
items.bottleneck: Humidity is not addressed in the abstract; a follow-up (Fu and Davis, Cell Rep. Phys. Sci. 2023, 'water management') exists but I could not retrieve its numbers.

items.name: Cation-exchanged small-pore zeolites: Zn-CHA, K-CHA, K-MER, Ba-GIS
items.mechanism: Divalent or large monovalent cations placed at specific ring sites (for example Zn2+ on paired Al sites in CHA 6-rings) create strong, localised CO2 sites; small pores and weaker water binding may ease regeneration.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Zn-CHA: about 0.51 mmol/g (Si/Al ~7, 17x the H-form) and 0.67 mmol/g (Si/Al ~2) at ~400 ppm CO2, dry (Angew. 2022). K-CHA: 0.7 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 298 K, dry (as tabulated in a 2025 review). K-MER vs 13X under ~400 ppm CO2 with 2,095 ppm H2O and 100 C regeneration: K-MER keeps 73% of its dry uptake over 5 cycles, 13X keeps 47% (Chem. Eng. J. 2025). Ba-GIS (J. Mater. Chem. A 2026): claimed strong binding and fast mass transfer; numbers not retrievable.
items.regeneration: 100 C for the K-MER cycling test; Zn-CHA described as low desorption energy without a number.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 5 cycles at most.
items.cost: Not reported.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab powders.
items.bottleneck: The 'humid' K-MER test is only about 7% RH at 25 C (2,095 ppm H2O), so it is nearly dry; the authors also note K-MER's CO2 selectivity advantage disappears at atmospheric concentration. No data at 50-70% RH.

items.name: Fluorinated ultramicroporous MOF physisorbents (NbOFFIVE-1-Ni, SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta, WO2F4-pillared)
items.mechanism: Narrow square channels lined with fluorine atoms give strong electrostatic CO2 pockets; alkyl groups or polarizable pillars reduce water affinity.
items.uptake_and_conditions: NbOFFIVE-1-Ni: ~1.3 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 298 K, dry; but 10.1 mmol/g water at 95% RH. SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta: 0.4 mmol/g at 500 ppm, 298 K; only 1.6 mmol/g water at 95% RH; CO2/H2O IAST selectivity 16.2 at 500 ppm / 74% RH; humid breakthrough shown only at 1,000-10,000 ppm, not 400 ppm. [Ni(WO2F4)(pyrazine)2]: 0.934 mmol/g dry and 0.685 mmol/g at 75% RH, both at 400 ppm (73% retained; temperature and cycles not in abstract).
items.regeneration: NbOFFIVE-1-Ni: full desorption at 328 K (55 C) under vacuum, 54 kJ/mol. SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta: Qst 52 kJ/mol, regenerated at 348 K in pure-CO2 cycling and 403 K after breakthrough runs.
items.stability_and_lifetime: SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta: 100 cycles in 1 bar CO2 (not DAC conditions) and 6 dry/humid cycles at 1,000-10,000 ppm; it changes phase at 95% RH but recovers on heating. Earlier work found competition and reaction with moisture 'significantly reduced' DAC performance of SIFSIX-3-Ni and other physisorbents.
items.cost: Not reported; nickel, pyrazine-type linkers and fluorinated pillars are far costlier than zeolites.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab powders.
items.bottleneck: The SIFSIX-18 authors state DAC needs CO2/H2O selectivity >=100, which 'disqualifies all known physisorbent materials'; best measured is 16 (at 500 ppm). The WO2F4 result is the strongest humid 400 ppm number but lacks cycle data.

items.name: Binding-entropy window for physisorbents (OptiLex verifier calculation)
items.mechanism: The verifier's narrow window around -70 kJ/mol assumes an amine-like adsorption entropy of -165 J/mol/K. Confined physisorption sites lose less entropy, which moves the usable enthalpy window.
items.uptake_and_conditions: NbOFFIVE-1-Ni (1.3 of ~2.2 mmol/g filled at 400 ppm, 298 K, Qst 54 kJ/mol) implies dS of about -113 J/mol/K. With dS = -117, half-filling at 420 ppm needs dH = -54 kJ/mol at 25 C, -50 at 0 C, -46 at -20 C and -42 at -40 C. Na-X's measured 44-49 kJ/mol therefore matches the -20 C optimum, not the 25 C one.
items.regeneration: The trade-off reverses for regeneration: at equal 65% ambient filling, a -45 kJ/mol site needs 143 C to unload to 20% at 1 kPa CO2 (81 C at 100 Pa), versus 92 C for -70 kJ/mol. Heat per tonne is higher for the weaker site (5.5 vs 4.1 GJ/t, dry, q_max 2 mol/kg) because working capacity per degree is lower. Weaker binding trades reaction heat for a larger swing or deeper vacuum.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable (calculation).
items.cost: Not applicable.
items.trl_and_scale: Calculation; script entropy_window.py in the same scratch folder. Caveat: single-site Langmuir overstates cold gains. Wilson's Na-X data rise 8x from 20 C to -58 C (apparent slope 14 kJ/mol) where a single -45 kJ/mol site would predict near-saturation.
items.bottleneck: There is no free lunch from 'low heat of adsorption': the gain must come from low water co-adsorption, low sensible heat and long life, not from enthalpy alone.

items.name: Carbons: negligible as bare physisorbents at 400 ppm, useful as supports
items.mechanism: Dispersion-only binding (about 25-35 kJ/mol) is too weak at 42 Pa CO2; carbons contribute as cheap, conductive, hydrophobic supports for carbonate or amine sites.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Verifier estimate for bare microporous carbon at 420 ppm, 25 C: 0.002-0.10 mol/kg for dH -25 to -35 kJ/mol (assumed dS -85 J/mol/K, 5 mol/kg pore capacity). Measured supported systems: K2CO3 on activated-carbon fibre felt 0.478 mmol/g in 4 h from ambient air (400-450 ppm, 19% RH); raising dew point from 0 to 12 C cut performance by 40% (ChemSusChem 2025). Aminosilane-grafted 3D-printed carbon monolith 0.25 mmol/g at 0.04 kPa (2026).
items.regeneration: K2CO3 felt: 125 C in air, 0.5 h. Aminosilane carbon: 75 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 10 cycles for the K2CO3 felt.
items.cost: Described as cheap and easy to make; no figure.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab.
items.bottleneck: No measured bare-carbon DAC capacity worth using at ambient temperature. The verifier suggests a -30 kJ/mol carbon would hold about 3 mol/kg at 195 K, so carbons only become candidates in near-cryogenic schemes.

items.name: Zeolite DAC companies: Removr (Norway) and TerraFixing (Canada)
items.mechanism: Removr: passive drying unit removes most water, air is cooled in heat exchangers, then passes over zeolite; electricity only. TerraFixing: cold-climate zeolite TVSA from the Wilson work.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No sorbent performance data published by either company.
items.regeneration: Removr states no external heat, water or fossil fuel is needed; no kWh/t figure published on the pages retrieved.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Claims of long zeolite lifespan; no DAC cycling data.
items.cost: TerraFixing claims a path below $100/t and 2-4x better energy efficiency. Removr publishes no cost.
items.trl_and_scale: Removr: 'Genesis' pilot at SINTEF Oslo, 56 million NOK, first demonstration expected autumn 2025; roadmap lists 50,000 t/yr for 2028-2030 and 1 Mt/yr for 2030. An earlier 300 t/yr pilot at Technology Centre Mongstad from 2024 is reported in trade press, which I could not open. TerraFixing: no pilot results found.
items.bottleneck: No independently measured energy, capture rate or uptime from any zeolite DAC pilot was found; the drying step is the undisclosed part.

items.name: Hybrid water plus CO2 capture (water co-production)
items.mechanism: Use the water that must be removed anyway as a product, or use a moisture-driven sorbent so water handling replaces heat.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Verifier: water passing through the contactor per tonne CO2 captured (75% capture) is 38 t at 30 C / 70% RH, 15 t at 20 C / 50% RH, 6 t at 20 C / 20% RH, 0.9 t at -20 C / 70% RH. Avnos (moisture-responsive hybrid DAC, not a zeolite) states its Project Cedar will capture 3,000 t CO2/yr and produce more than 6,000 t water/yr, about 2 t water per t CO2.
items.regeneration: Avnos says it uses low-grade waste heat; no energy figure published.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not published.
items.cost: Not published. My arithmetic: 6-15 t water per t CO2 at an assumed $2/t water is $12-30 per t CO2, small against a ~$274/t capital charge, so water revenue matters only where water is scarce and expensive.
items.trl_and_scale: Avnos: demonstration unit operating with the US Office of Naval Research; Project Cedar construction 'due to complete by the end of 2026'; over $100 million raised.
items.bottleneck: Collecting liquid water needs condensation heat rejection (44 kJ/mol); the co-product value is low in most markets; no measured plant data.

bottlenecks: Water selectivity of cheap physisorbents: zeolite 13X falls from 0.34-0.36 mmol/g (dry, 400 ppm, 25 C) to about zero at 30% and 60% RH while holding 15-17 mmol/g water; temperate air (20 C, 50% RH) carries 27 mol water per mol CO2.

Air-side heat: the processed air is about 2,090 t per tonne CO2 (75% capture), so every kelvin of heating or cooling costs 2.1 GJ/t before recuperation, and removing all the water adiabatically warms the air by about 20 K at 20 C / 50% RH. Brute-force desiccant regeneration is 41.5 GJ/t at 20 C / 50% RH versus 2.6 GJ/t at -20 C (verifier calculation).
Thermodynamic floor of the drying step is about 2.0 GJ/t at 20 C / 50% RH, roughly 4x the 0.47 GJ/t CO2 separation floor; it falls to 0.11 GJ/t at -20 C.
Low ambient capacity drives sensible heat: Na-X at 0.30 mol/kg (20 C) with a 200 C swing needs 12.5 GJ/t of sensible heat alone; at -58 C (2.5 mol/kg) it is 2.2 GJ/t.

Geography: Na-X needs -20 C or colder for >=1.1 mmol/g. Seasonal operation hurts capital recovery: a $274/t capital charge at 95% utilisation becomes about $650/t at 40% utilisation. LNG cold caps near-cryogenic DAC at roughly 0.1 Gt/yr.

Humid-tolerant physisorbents are far from the target: best CO2/H2O selectivity reported is 16 (SIFSIX-18-Ni-beta at 500 ppm) against a stated need of >=100; best humid 400 ppm retention is 73% at 75% RH (WO2F4-pillared MOF) with no cycle data.
Evidence depth: studies in this area report 5-15 cycles (100 at most, in pure CO2) against the >10,000 cycles a plant needs, and no zeolite DAC pilot has published measured energy.
Pressure drop: each extra 100 Pa for dryers or heat exchangers adds 0.29 GJ/t (82 kWh/t) of fan electricity.
open_problems: Kinetic-window or self-guarding beds: in 13X at 30% RH the CO2 front broke through at about the same time as in dry gas (~100 min) and the water front at ~200 min. Can a short-cycle layered or rotary bed, borrowed from air-separation pre-purification units, harvest CO2 before water arrives and regenerate the wet inlet zone with the dry CO2-lean exhaust? Checkable with a two-component breakthrough model.

Near-heatless water management: the whole dry exhaust stream is available as purge. Is there a heat-coupled desiccant wheel or enthalpy-exchanger design (import from building ventilation) that keeps the drying penalty under 1 GJ/t and 200 Pa at 10-20 C? The bound to beat is 2.1 GJ per kelvin per tonne.

Cheap, non-fluorinated sites that bind CO2 but not water at 400 ppm: small-pore zeolite pockets (MOR side pocket, MER, GIS, CHA with Zn, K or Ba) screened with binary CO2/H2O adsorption calculations and then measured at 50-70% RH, not 7% RH.

Low-temperature regeneration of cold-loaded 13X: the verifier's idealised single-site model gives 0.85 mol/kg working capacity and about 3 GJ/t when adsorbing at -20 C and desorbing at 60 C / 1 kPa, yet practice uses 200 C. Is the gap due to strong-site heterogeneity or to slipped water? Needs measured isotherms from -20 to 60 C.

Humidity-enhanced weak chemisorption at cold with room-temperature release (0.82 mmol/g at -20 C, 70% RH, regenerated at 25 C): does it survive thousands of cycles, and can concentrated CO2 actually be recovered with a 45 K swing plus vacuum?

Cold sources other than LNG for near-cryogenic capture (polar winter air, liquid-air or liquid-hydrogen regasification), and whether cheap hydrophobic carbons can replace zeolites at 195 K (verifier suggests about 3 mol/kg for a -30 kJ/mol carbon).

A replacement for the verifier's single-site Langmuir when judging physisorbents: Na-X capacity rises 8x from 20 C to -58 C where a single -45 kJ/mol site predicts near-saturation; a two-site or Toth model fitted to the Wilson data would stop the engine overrating cold operation.

Honest valuation of co-produced water: 6-15 t per tonne CO2 in temperate air is worth roughly $12-30/t CO2 at $2/t water; identify the specific arid, high-water-price sites where it changes the economics.

key_claims.claim: Humidity removes essentially all CO2 capacity from zeolite 13X at ambient temperature: 0.34-0.36 mmol/g dry at 400 ppm and 25 C falls to negligible (about zero) at both 30% and 60% RH, with 15-17 mmol/g water taken up instead (lab breakthrough, 230 mg, 2025).

Cold, dry air reverses the picture for the same cheap zeolite: Na-X holds 0.30, 1.1 and 2.5 mmol/g at 20, -20 and -58 C from 420 ppm pre-dried real air (9.5 g bed), giving a modelled, not plant-measured, energy of 1.1-1.23 MWh/t CO2 with 200 C regeneration.

surprises: Water, not CO2, is the main separation in dry-sorbent DAC: the thermodynamic floor for drying temperate air (about 2.0 GJ/t at 20 C / 50% RH) is roughly 4x the CO2 separation floor of 0.47 GJ/t (verifier calculation).

The air stream is so large that changing its temperature by 1 K costs 2.1 GJ per tonne CO2. Any scheme that cools or warms the air (cold DAC, desiccant heat release, near-cryogenic capture) lives or dies on recuperation above about 95-98%.

Given a physisorption entropy near -115 J/mol/K, the ideal binding enthalpy for half-filling at 420 ppm is about -46 kJ/mol at -20 C, which is exactly Na-X's measured 44-49 kJ/mol. 13X is the thermodynamically right sorbent for -20 C air and the wrong one for 25 C air.

The 'lowest reported DAC energy' of 1.1 MWh/t for cold Na-X is a first-law number for 200 C heat. In work-equivalent terms (1.7-2.4 GJ/t for the heat alone) it is about the same as the reference amine cycle (1.88 GJ/t).
LNG-coupled near-cryogenic DAC, even at the authors' 103-142 Mt/yr estimate for 2050, would remove only about 5-13% of the CO2 emitted by burning the LNG that supplies the cold.
Humidity helped rather than hurt an amine-loaded MOF at -20 C (0.73 dry vs 0.82 mmol/g at 70% RH) and it regenerated at 25 C, so cold climates may favour weak chemisorbents as much as zeolites.

Two published 'humid' results are less than they look: the K-MER zeolite test used 2,095 ppm water (about 7% RH), and a 2026 paper reporting 0.27 mmol/g for plain 13X at 60-65% RH conflicts with the near-zero equilibrium value, most likely because it was read before water displaced the CO2.

A lower heat of adsorption does not by itself cut regeneration energy: at equal ambient filling, a -45 kJ/mol site needs 143 C to release at 1 kPa versus 92 C for a -70 kJ/mol site (verifier calculation).
Statistic that is not DAC evidence: a 2026 clay-derived LTA zeolite reports 5.0 mmol/g with selectivity quoted at 5% CO2, which is a flue-gas condition and says nothing about 400 ppm.

Access limits on this run: the web-search budget for the session was already exhausted and publisher bot checks blocked the full text of Kim 2025, Song 2022 and Fu and Davis 2023, so those are verified only from abstracts, a repository record or DOE slides; I did not attempt to get past the checks.

verifs.claim: Humidity removes essentially all CO2 capacity from zeolite 13X at ambient temperature: 0.34-0.36 mmol/g dry at 400 ppm and 25 C falls to negligible (about zero) at both 30% and 60% RH, with 15-17 mmol/g water taken up instead (lab breakthrough, 230 mg, 2025).
verifs.corrected_claim: At equilibrium (bed fully saturated with water), humidity removes essentially all CO2 capacity from zeolite 13X at 25 C and 400 ppm CO2 in N2. Dry uptake is 0.36 mmol/g (single-step gravimetric DVS, about 20 mg sample) and 0.34 mmol/g "average" across the single-component DVS runs; the dry packed-bed breakthrough run (230 mg, 50 sccm) is reported only as "in good agreement" with those, with no number given in the text. In the humid breakthrough runs the integrated equilibrium CO2 uptake falls to "negligible levels close to 0 and within the margin of error of the instrument" at both 30% and 60% RH, while water uptake is about 15 mmol/g (30% RH) and about 17 mmol/g (60% RH). Measured, not simulated; Surface Measurement Systems Case Study 621, document dated 21 March 2025.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the primary PDF (full text plus Figure 5). All the numbers in the claim are in the source; two details of attribution and scope need fixing.

**What the source supports**
- 0.36 mmol/g: 1.57% mass gain at 400 ppm CO2 in 200 sccm dry N2, 25 C.
- 0.34 mmol/g: stated as the "average capacity" from the single-component results.
- Humid result: CO2 uptake "negligible levels close to 0" at 30% and 60% RH; water about 15 and 17 mmol/g respectively.
- 230 mg bed, 4 mm ID column, crushed binderless Zeochem 13X pellets, 50 sccm, activated in situ at 300 C under N2.

**Corrections**
1. **The dry 0.34-0.36 figures are not breakthrough values.** They come from gravimetric DVS on about 20 mg. The 230 mg breakthrough run gives no dry number in the text, only "good agreement" (the value sits in the Figure 6 bar chart).
2. **"Removes all capacity" holds only at equilibrium.** Figure 5 shows that in the humid runs CO2 still breaks through at about 100 minutes, the same as dry, and is then displaced by the slower water front (roll-up to about 2x inlet at 30% RH and about 3.7x at 60% RH; water breaks through at roughly 230 and 130 minutes). A short cycle stopped before the water front would retain transient CO2 capacity. The source does not quantify this.

**Context that limits its use**
- Vendor application note from an instrument maker, not peer-reviewed. No error bars, no replicates, no cycling data: single adsorption runs on freshly activated material.
- Gas is CO2 in N2, not air (no O2).
- "About zero" means below the instrument's detection margin, not a measured zero.
- The source itself says DVS equilibrium "has not been reached below 1000 ppm", so the dry 0.34-0.36 mmol/g may understate true equilibrium capacity.
- Only 0%, 30% and 60% RH were tested in co-adsorption. The single-component water isotherm reaches about 80% of capacity below 1% RH, so the equilibrium loss probably sets in at far lower humidity than 30%; that is an inference, not a measured co-adsorption point.
- Date: document stamp and PDF creation date are 21 March 2025; the file was modified April 2026 and the URL path is 2026/05. "2025" is right for the work.

verifs.claim: Cold, dry air reverses the picture for the same cheap zeolite: Na-X holds 0.30, 1.1 and 2.5 mmol/g at 20, -20 and -58 C from 420 ppm pre-dried real air (9.5 g bed), giving a modelled, not plant-measured, energy of 1.1-1.23 MWh/t CO2 with 200 C regeneration.
verifs.corrected_claim: Optional tightening, not a correction of the numbers: "Na-X pellets (9.5 g, 1.09 cm x 14.5 cm column) took up 0.30, 1.1 and 2.5 mmol/g CO2 at 20, -20 and -58 C in single breakthrough runs on desiccant-dried outdoor Ottawa air (390-461 ppm CO2, nominally 420 ppm) chilled in a lab temperature bath; a modelled 5-step TVSA cycle with 200 C evacuation gives a total (thermal + mechanical, incl. compression to 15 MPa) energy quoted as 1.1 MWh/t in the abstract and 1.23 MWh/t in the results. The full cycle was never run experimentally."
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the full text of PMC9720019 via the Europe PMC XML mirror (the PMC page itself was behind a CAPTCHA, which I did not attempt to pass): Wilson, S.M.W., "The potential of direct air capture using adsorbents in cold climates", iScience 2022. All numbers in the claim match the paper (Na-X: 0.30 / 0.65 / 1.1 / 1.9 / 2.5 mmol/g at 20 / 0 / -20 / -40 / -58 C; 9.5 g pellets; 200 C evacuation step; energy modelled). I read the text through a summarising fetch tool, not the raw XML, and could not run independent web searches (session search budget exhausted), so figure-level detail is unverified.

Context that changes how the claim should be used:
1. "420 ppm" is nominal. The feed was real outdoor Ottawa air measured at 390-461 ppm CO2, dried over a layered silica gel + 3A desiccant bed. No dew point is given.
2. The cold was simulated. Air was conditioned with a lab temperature-controlled bath; this is not a field test in a cold climate.
3. The capacities are single-pass breakthrough (saturation) capacities on a ~10 g bed. Between runs the column was degassed at 250 C under N2 purge, not by the 200 C vacuum step in the model. No multi-cycle or durability data is reported, and cyclic working capacity would be lower than these values.
4. "1.1-1.23 MWh/t" is not a sensitivity range. The abstract says 1.1 and the results text says 1.23 (apparently Na-X at about -37 C and low relative humidity, per the Figure 7 context); the paper does not reconcile the two. Treat 1.23 as the documented figure.
5. The energy total sums thermal and mechanical energy in one MWh figure (sorbent sensible heat, desorption, desiccant regeneration, fans at 213 Pa design pressure drop, vacuum, compression to 15 MPa) at 95% CO2 purity. It is sensitive to humidity: desiccant regeneration dominates at higher humidity and temperature, so the headline number holds only for cold, low-humidity sites. The sensible-heat component alone falls from 3.1 to 0.56 MWh/t for Na-X between 20 and -58 C.
6. The model extrapolates pellet-column data to large monolithic contactors; that scale-up is assumed, not demonstrated.
7. Single-author paper from TerraFixing Inc., a company commercialising cold-climate zeolite DAC, so the "lowest reported DAC energy" framing comes from an interested party and is not independently replicated in this source.
8. The paper also reports Li-X (0.31 to 1.9 mmol/g over the same range); Na-X is the better performer.

items.name: Parasitic thermal mass of contactor and housing: kg-scale steam-assisted TVSA pilot (Schellevis & Brilman, U Twente, 2024)
items.mechanism: Fixed-bed supported-amine sorbent, steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing; four parallel beds. Heat goes mostly into warming sorbent, inert material and housing, not into breaking the CO2 bond.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured over several weeks on ambient air: 1.3 kg CO2/day = 0.27 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day. Song et al. 2025 cite this pilot as showing sensible heat of housing (40%) and heat-transfer media (21%) dominating.
items.regeneration: Measured 14.5 MJ/kg CO2 base case; authors' projected optimum 5.1 MJ/kg (not demonstrated). OptiLex calc: each extra kg of inert structure per kg sorbent adds ~1.5 GJ/t at 1.04 mol/kg and a 75 K swing; a 6.9 wt% washcoat monolith would need ~26 GJ/t without heat recovery.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Reproducible over a multi-week campaign; no long-term degradation data.
items.cost: Not costed. At 14.5 GJ/t and COP 1 electric heat, energy alone is ~$200/t at $50/MWh.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4-5, kg-scale pilot (about 5 kg sorbent), 2023-24.
items.bottleneck: Measured heat is 2.4x the OptiLex ideal-cycle 6.04 GJ/t and ~30x the 0.47 GJ/t floor; heat-only second-law efficiency ~16%.

items.name: Water co-adsorption penalty (measured swing ratios and modelled climate effect)
items.mechanism: Amine sorbents take up several times more water than CO2 from humid air; that water is evaporated every cycle (about 44 kJ/mol, i.e. 1.0 GJ/t CO2 per mol H2O per mol CO2). Moderate humidity also raises CO2 capacity 30-50%.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured: PEI/silica hollow fibres cycled ~8x more water than CO2 (6 mmol/g vs 0.72 mmol/g; 400 ppm, 22 C, 45% RH; 10 cycles, 2026). Amine-alumina: ~3.2 mmol/g H2O vs ~0.55 mmol/g CO2 at ~50% RH, 25 C (ETH, 2025). TEAs assume far less: NETL Rev.1 1:1, OptiLex reference 2:1.
items.regeneration: Campbell 2026: water desorption needed ~5x the energy of CO2 desorption. Cai et al. 2024 (gPROMS model, amine resin TVSA): total energy >16,000 kWh/t humid-hot vs 3,000 kWh/t dry-cold, mostly water desorption. OptiLex calc: 8:1 gives 12.0 GJ/t vs 6.0 at 2:1.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not a degradation issue per se, but TDA/GE saw bench performance fall after ~300 cycles from steam condensation.
items.cost: NETL Rev.1: raising water in the desorbed stream from 75 to 90 wt% raises cost 28% ($1,028 to $1,313/t net). Location choice leaves ~25% productivity spread even after cycle optimisation (Cai 2024, modelled).
items.trl_and_scale: Lab modules (grams) for measurements; continental-US simulation for climate effect.
items.bottleneck: Largest gap between TEA assumptions and measurement: 1-2 mol/mol assumed vs 6-8 mol/mol measured swing at ~50% RH.

items.name: NETL sorbent DAC techno-economic case study, Revision 1 (2025): how much each lever moves cost
items.mechanism: Independent TEA of a generic monolith sorbent plant (100,000 t/yr net, direct-steam TVSA, May-2023 dollars). Base: 0.8 mol/kg, 1 h adsorption, 2 GJ/t CO2 desorption energy, 1:1 water, $9.27/kg sorbent, 1-year life, 895 Pa, 60% capture.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Base cost $1,028/t net (gas-fired case 1-NG); electric-boiler case ~$616-931/t over +/-50% capex. Capital is ~54% (NG) or ~41% (electric) of cost.
items.regeneration: CO2 desorption energy 2 to 0.3 GJ/t: -1% cost (to 12 GJ/t: +53%). Vacuum 0.4 to 0.2 bar: +1%. TSA vs TVSA configuration: minor.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Sorbent life 1 to 2 years: -2%; to 0.25 years: +10%. Sorbent price to $148/kg: +58%.
items.cost: Working capacity 0.8 to 2 mol/kg: -7% (to 0.2: +70%). Capture fraction 0.6 to 0.8: -7%. Pressure drop 895 to 200 Pa: -8% (to 3,200 Pa: +36%). Cycle 60 to 20 min: -4%. Capex -50%: -30%. Capacity factor 85% to 30%: +150%. All sorbent levers together: $630/t (-38%); plus cheap gas and financing: ~$430/t.
items.trl_and_scale: AACE Class 5 estimate (+/-50% capex); neither first- nor Nth-of-a-kind. Authors call several base assumptions optimistic.
items.bottleneck: No single sorbent or contactor lever moves cost more than ~10% downward; capital, capacity factor and financing dominate. Downside risks (low capacity, high water, high pressure drop) are much larger than upside gains.

items.name: Climeworks + Svante structured laminate beds: one-year field test (DOE DE-FE0031952, California, 2022-23)
items.mechanism: Amine sorbent formed into thin laminate sheets with printed spacers (parallel channels), run in Climeworks' vacuum-temperature swing with low-grade steam. Aim: fast mass transfer at packed-bed-like thermal mass.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 30 kg/day field unit, real air. Gen2 targets met in cyclic operation: fast-cycling capacity 0.5-0.7 mol/kg laminate, uptake rate 0.05-0.07 mol/kg/min, pressure drop 800-1,000 Pa (Gen3 targets: 0.8-1 mol/kg, 0.08-0.1 mol/kg/min, 400-700 Pa). OptiLex calc: ~0.95 kg CO2/kg/day at 30+10 min cycles.
items.regeneration: Steam-assisted vacuum-temperature swing; energy not disclosed. Company claim (June 2024): Gen 3 structured sorbent doubles capture per module and halves energy versus packed beds.
items.stability_and_lifetime: >3,000 cycles (Gen2) and >5,000 cycles (Gen3), accelerated. Target <10% capacity loss per year reachable but weather-dependent; FTIR showed oxidation, stronger at the air-inlet side.
items.cost: Not disclosed. Company target $250-350/t captured by 2030 (claim).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5 reached (2023); Gen 3 at full module scale in Switzerland from June 2024 (company statement).
items.bottleneck: Measured uptake is ~10-20x below the gas-film limit for a 100 um coating in 1 mm channels (OptiLex calc), so sorbent-layer transport controls; 800-1,000 Pa costs ~3.3 GJ_e/t of fan work at 60% capture.

items.name: Climeworks Mammoth actual output versus nameplate (2025-26)
items.mechanism: Commercial solid-amine TVSA plant in Iceland on geothermal heat and power; modular collector containers.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Reported net removal 675 t in H1 2026 versus 119 t in H1 2025, against a nameplate of up to 36,000 t/yr. Annualised, that is about 4% of nameplate.
items.regeneration: Energy use not disclosed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Improvement attributed to new sorbent and mechanical upgrades; operating cost per tonne reported down >50% in a year. Next-generation technology testing planned at Mammoth from early 2027.
items.cost: Not disclosed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8-9 plant, but not operating near design output.
items.bottleneck: Confounds: the plant was reportedly not fully built out, the figure is net (after own emissions and losses), and causes are not broken down. It shows an integration and reliability gap, not a sorbent-physics limit.

items.name: Rotary-wheel steam-assisted TSA prototype (Wu et al., Adv. Sci. 2026)
items.mechanism: PEI/silica coated glass-fibre honeycomb in a continuously rotating wheel (imported from desiccant wheels); sectors pass through air then direct steam. No vacuum, short cycles.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured: 42 kg sorbent, 0.8 m rotor; inlet 450-600 ppm CO2 (above outdoor air), 60-85% RH; 36-52 min cycles; 50-85% capture; productivity 0.235-0.352 kg CO2/kg/day, which the authors call the highest reported; 22.03 kg CO2 in 64 h; pressure drop <=220 Pa.
items.regeneration: Measured thermal energy >22 MJ/kg (pipe losses, steam leakage between sectors, unrecovered condenser heat). Simulated: 7.4-9.6 MJ/kg with heat recovery; 2.5-3.1 MJ/kg with heat recovery plus a better sorbent.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Capture fraction drifted 59% to 53% and purity 94% to 88% over 8 days; no long cycling.
items.cost: Not costed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4-5 prototype (about 2.7 t/yr equivalent), tested Sept-Oct 2024.
items.bottleneck: Factor ~3-9 between measured and simulated energy; sealing and latent-heat recovery are unproven. Elevated inlet CO2 flatters productivity.

items.name: Sorbent-coated heat-exchanger contactor (TDA Research + GE, DOE DE-FE0032261, final report 2025-26)
items.mechanism: Amine sorbent coated on fins of a commercial tube-in-plate heat exchanger; hot/cold water in tubes gives fast indirect heating and cooling under vacuum (rapid TSA, 5 min adsorb / 5 min regenerate).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured at 500 ppm CO2, 40-50% RH, 20 C: 32 g CO2/kg sorbent/h (~0.77 kg/kg/day) at sub-bench scale; volumetric productivity 0.89 kg CO2/m3/h (target 0.2); air-side pressure drop <150 Pa sub-bench, <2 kPa bench. Capacity ~50% higher at 70-80% RH.
items.regeneration: 90-100 C water, ~1 psia vacuum. Key finding: heat to warm the metal exchanger far exceeded sorbent regeneration energy, so an electric boiler was judged infeasible and the design relies on industrial waste heat.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Sub-bench: >6,500 cycles, ~2.2% capacity fade per 1,000 cycles. Bench: degradation after ~300 cycles attributed to steam condensation.
items.cost: Their TEA: $251/t (2019 $, excl. transport and storage) with waste heat; $153/t with $30/MWh power, $15/kg sorbent, 5 mbar pressure drop, 90% capacity factor.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4-5; bench module 10-50 g CO2/h; full-scale 100,000 t/yr design on paper.
items.bottleneck: Metal thermal mass. Fast kinetics and durability were achieved, but only by adding inert mass that dominates the heat bill. Tested at 500 ppm, not 420.

items.name: Hollow-fibre sorbents with hot water in the bore (Georgia Tech, IECR 2026)
items.mechanism: PEI/silica in polysulfone hollow fibres with an impermeable lumen barrier; hot (86 C) and cold water flow through the fibre bore so the fibre is both sorbent and heat exchanger (rapid TSA).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured, 400 ppm CO2, 22 C, 45% RH: swing capacity 0.81 falling to 0.72 mmol/g fibre over 10 cycles; productivity 1.01 falling to 0.90 mmol/g/h (~0.95 kg CO2/kg fibre/day); optimum 33 min adsorption + 13 min desorption + 2 min cooling; CO2 recovery 68%.
items.regeneration: Low-grade heat (86 C water). About 7 kJ was put into the module, well above the CO2 plus water desorption enthalpy, because the module casing outweighed the fibres. Water swing ~8x CO2.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only 10 cycles; ~10% early loss attributed to PEI repacking.
items.cost: Not costed. Earlier ARPA-E target for the related wind-driven fibre project: 1.5 kg/kg/day, <4 GJ_e/t, $100/t (targets, not results).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, gram-scale module.
items.bottleneck: Same two penalties in miniature: water (5x CO2 desorption energy) and casing thermal mass. Needs module-scale energy accounting and >1,000 cycles.

items.name: Direct electrical (Joule) heating of conductive sorbent structures
items.mechanism: Current through a conductive support (carbon fibre, silver-nanowire coating, graphene foam/aerogel) heats the sorbent from inside, removing steam generators and condensers and cutting heating time to about a minute.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Lee et al. 2025 (amine-zeolite fibres, silver coating, 13-fibre module): 110 C in 80 s at 3 V; humid (52% RH, 400 ppm) working capacity ~0.35 mmol/g coated fibre; silver roughly halved capacity per mass. Song et al. 2025 (PEI/graphite-oxide foam, 70% RH): 1.54 mmol/g; 120 C in 60 s; desorption 2.5x faster than TVSA.
items.regeneration: Lee 2025: 6.1 GJ_e/t Joule energy, of which 4.1 GJ/t is contactor sensible heat. Song 2025: TVSA needed ~2-3x more energy. Shen et al. 2026 (graphene aerogel): 3.4 GJ/t heat duty on a 20 mg-scale sample. Earlier carbon-fibre system (Lee 2023): ~80% purity.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Lee 2025: 88% retention over 10 humid cycles. Song 2025: ~0.02 mmol/g lost per cycle for 25 cycles, purity 83% to 77% over 36 cycles (PEI loss, air leak). Shen 2026: 3.7% loss by cycle 100, stable to 500.
items.cost: Georgia Tech projection $150-200/t (press claim, 2023). Shen 2026 TEA: variable cost $48-62/t (modelled).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3; milligram to gram scale. No kg-scale wall-plug energy measurement found.
items.bottleneck: Heat is electricity at COP 1, so 6 GJ_e/t costs ~$85/t at $50/MWh versus ~$28/t for the same heat from a COP-3 heat pump (OptiLex calc). Conductive supports add mass and cost.

items.name: Mass-transfer limits: monolith versus packed bed at 400 ppm (ETH Zurich, 2024-25) and the gas-film ceiling
items.mechanism: At 400 ppm the CO2 flux to the wall is tiny, so film, pore and amine-layer resistances all matter. Monolith washcoats shorten diffusion paths but carry little active material.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured (dry air, 22-24 C): mass-transfer coefficients fall two orders of magnitude from 5.6% CO2 to 400 ppm; the monolith was faster and gave higher productivity and lower fan energy than 3 mm pellets at 400 ppm but no advantage at 5.6%. The monolith carried only 6.9 wt% active alumina. Separate kinetics study: diffusion in the amine layer slows as loading rises.
items.regeneration: Modelled: monolith cooling 950 s vs 450 s for packed bed; monoliths need >80% sorbent loading to compete on sorbent use.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed.
items.cost: OptiLex calc (laminar channel, perfect-sink wall): film-limited pressure drop is only ~14 Pa at 2.5 m/s and 60% capture, ~85 Pa at 5 m/s and 75%; fan work ~0.3 GJ_e/t per 100 Pa. Adsorption time is set by air supply: 60 kg sorbent per m2 face at 2 m/s needs ~29 min.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab columns (tens to hundreds of grams) plus validated models.
items.bottleneck: Trade-off triangle: thin coatings give speed but low sorbent density and high inert mass; thick walls give density but slow kinetics. No design yet has all three.

items.name: Heat pumps and heat recovery
items.mechanism: Deliver ~90-100 C regeneration heat with a high-temperature heat pump instead of resistance or boiler heat; recover sensible heat between beds and latent heat from condensing product steam.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No measured DAC-plus-heat-pump pilot data found. Terlouw et al. 2024 assume COP 2.9. Hunter-Sellars et al. 2026 use Climeworks-sourced 11.9 GJ/t steam plus 2.0 GJ_e/t for fans, vacuum and compression, with an 86 C heat pump, learning to 7.0 GJ/t.
items.regeneration: Wu 2026 simulation: heat recovery cuts thermal energy 21-57%. OptiLex calc: Carnot COP for a 15 to 100 C lift is 4.4; at COP 3 the ideal 6.0 GJ/t cycle needs 560 kWh/t and a realistic 12.5 GJ/t cycle 1,150 kWh/t. Recovering 50% of sensible heat with an inert ratio of 3 saves 3.4 GJ/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable.
items.cost: Terlouw 2024 (Europe, today): 450-1,500+ EUR/t with grid power and heat pump; capex is the largest contributor. Hunter-Sellars 2026: $2,850/t average on today's US grid (net-removed), $250/t long-term with wind/PV and learning (range $210-980).
items.trl_and_scale: Heat pumps at 90-100 C are commercial; integration with cyclic DAC beds is modelled only.
items.bottleneck: A heat pump roughly divides the energy bill by 3 but adds capex to a process already capital-dominated, and does nothing for productivity. Cyclic, intermittent heat demand suits heat pumps poorly without storage.

items.name: Passive (wind-driven) contactors
items.mechanism: Let ambient wind move air across the sorbent, removing fans. Examples: Georgia Tech/Global Thermostat 3D-printed fibre contactor (ARPA-E), Carbon Collect MechanicalTree, ASU moisture-swing belt of anion-exchange resin packets.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured (ASU, outdoor, Arizona, May 2024, 24 C, 17% RH): 782 g CO2 delivered in 7 days (~100 g/day) into an alkaline pond; loading rate tracks wind speed. ARPA-E fibre project targets only: 1.5 kg/kg/day, wind-speed ratio 0.15, >95% purity. Carbon Collect ~90 kg/day per tree is a company claim.
items.regeneration: ASU: moisture swing into solution; practical-scenario electricity 490 kWh/t net (conveyor), no heat for capture step.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Resin replacement every 5 years assumed; water uptake of the sorbent is a main cost driver.
items.cost: ASU TEA from measured rates: $950/t net today ($670 capture into solution + $280 extraction and compression); aspirational $160/t; best case $66/t. OptiLex calc: fans at 100 Pa are only 0.29 GJ_e/t (~$4/t at $50/MWh); even 300 Pa is ~$15/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4 (100 g/day outdoor).
items.bottleneck: Passive contact removes a small cost (fan energy) while lowering air flux and capacity factor, which drive the dominant capital term. It pays only if contactor capex per tonne is far lower.

items.name: Microwave and induction regeneration
items.mechanism: Volumetric heating that couples to water, polar groups or susceptors in the sorbent rather than the vessel, aiming to skip heating inert mass and shorten desorption.
items.uptake_and_conditions: ORNL 2023 (crystalline bis-iminoguanidine carbonate, lab): CO2 release at 120 C, up to 17x faster than a 160 C oven. Amornsin et al. 2025 (10 g zeolite 13X, ambient air, domestic microwave): 300 W for 10 min, 95% regeneration.
items.regeneration: ORNL: 40% less electrical energy than conductive heating. Zeolite study: 0.06 kWh vs 0.62 kWh per run at the wall plug (350 C zeolite regeneration, not amine conditions). No induction-heated DAC measurement found.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Zeolite: 9% capacity loss by cycle 3. No long cycling.
items.cost: Not costed.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3, gram scale.
items.bottleneck: All comparisons are against inefficient ovens at gram scale, with no per-tonne energy at kg scale in humid air. Microwaves heat co-adsorbed water preferentially, which may worsen the water penalty. Electricity at COP 1.

items.name: 3D-printed triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) contactors (Shao et al., Adv. Sci. 2026)
items.mechanism: Gyroid/diamond metal lattices coated with PEI on mixed metal oxide; curved channels induce secondary flows that thin the boundary layer versus straight square channels.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Measured, dry 400 ppm CO2 in N2, 25 C, 0.066-0.131 m/s (very low velocity): breakthrough delayed 49-54%; 80% desorption in 16.8-20.8 min vs 29.5 min. Modelled at 300 mm scale: 145.8 vs 92.4 kg CO2/m3/day (+58%).
items.regeneration: 120 C with dry N2 purge (not a product-grade cycle). Modelled 11.9 vs 24.7 GJ/t, no heat recovery.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not reported.
items.cost: Not costed; laser-printed AlSi10Mg is expensive and heavy.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, centimetre-scale coupons.
items.bottleneck: Dry gas, velocities ~20x below practical, metal thermal mass, higher pressure drop than straight channels. Humid, realistic-velocity tests are missing.

bottlenecks: Parasitic thermal mass. Sensible heat per tonne scales with (kg heated per kg sorbent) / (working capacity actually used). OptiLex calc: +1.5 GJ/t per extra kg of inert per kg sorbent (1.04 mol/kg, 75 K swing, no recovery). Measured consequences: 14.5 MJ/kg at a kg-scale pilot (2024), >22 MJ/kg at a 42 kg rotary prototype (2026), 4.1 of 6.1 GJ/t in an electrified fibre module (2025), and TDA/GE finding exchanger metal heat exceeded sorbent regeneration energy.

Water co-desorption. 1.0 GJ/t per mol H2O per mol CO2. Measured swing ratios are ~6-8 mol/mol at 45-50% RH (2025-26 lab data) versus 1-2 assumed in TEAs and in the OptiLex reference cycle; modelled energy spans 3,000 to >16,000 kWh/t between dry-cold and humid-hot sites; NETL: +28% cost for a wetter product stream.

Capital per tonne, set by productivity and utilisation. Capital is 41-54% of NETL's levelized cost; capacity factor 85% to 30% raises cost 150%. Measured integrated-system productivity is 0.24-0.35 kg CO2/kg/day versus 0.76 (NETL Rev.1) to 2.5 (Hunter-Sellars 2026) assumed in TEAs; lab modules reach ~0.8-0.95. Mammoth ran at roughly 4% of nameplate in H1 2026 (confounded by build-out and net accounting).

Fast cycles trade energy for productivity. Short cycles use only part of the equilibrium capacity, so sensible heat per tonne rises as 1/used capacity (OptiLex calc: 10.5 to 15.0 GJ/t when capacity use falls to 60% with an inert ratio of 3). On-stream fraction also falls when regeneration plus cooling approaches adsorption time (5+5 min gives 50%).

Sorbent-side kinetics at 400 ppm. Mass-transfer coefficients drop two orders of magnitude from 5.6% CO2 to 400 ppm (measured). Field uptake of 0.05-0.07 mol/kg/min is ~10-20x below the gas-film limit for a 100 um coating in 1 mm channels (OptiLex calc), so the amine layer, not the air side, is limiting.

Pressure drop above the film limit. A film-limited laminar channel needs only ~14-85 Pa; field laminates run 400-1,000 Pa and packed beds >2,000 Pa. Fan work is ~0.3 GJ_e/t per 100 Pa at 75% capture; NETL: 895 to 3,200 Pa adds 36% to cost, 895 to 200 Pa saves 8%.

Durability under real air and steam. Oxidation found at the air-inlet side after >3,000 field cycles (Climeworks/Svante); bench degradation after ~300 cycles from steam condensation (TDA/GE); PEI loss in Joule-heated foams. If degradation is time-based, faster cycling cuts sorbent cost per tonne (OptiLex calc: $384/t at 4 h cycles vs $32/t at 20 min, 0.6 mol/kg, $20/kg, 1-year life); if cycle-based, it does not. This is not settled.

Evidence gap for electrified heating. Joule, microwave and induction results are at milligram to 10 g scale; no kg-scale wall-plug GJ/t in humid air exists. They use electricity at COP 1, so they must beat heat pumps (COP ~3) by removing inert-mass heating or capex.
open_problems: Design a self-supporting, high-sorbent-fraction contactor (>80 wt% active, inert ratio <0.3 kg/kg including housing share) that still reaches >0.1 mol/kg/min uptake at 400 ppm and <200 Pa. Verifier: extend TVSACycle with inert_mass_ratio and used-capacity fraction (already done in scratch script contactor_levers.py) plus a linear-driving-force kinetic term.

Decouple the water swing from the CO2 swing: keep water adsorbed during regeneration (steam purge at matched water activity), add a hydrophobic or water-gating layer, or operate at a humidity where CO2 enhancement saturates (~40% RH) but multilayer water is avoided. Target: <2 mol H2O desorbed per mol CO2 at 50-70% RH, measured.

Recover latent heat instead of avoiding it: vapor recompression or a heat pump whose cold side is the product condenser (Carnot COP ~9 for a 60 to 100 C lift, OptiLex calc). Does a recompression loop on a cyclic bed work with realistic non-condensable (CO2) fractions?

Counter-current sensible-heat recovery between beds, imported from regenerative heat exchangers and desiccant wheels (moving or rotating sorbent, heat-transfer fluid loops). Simulations claim 21-57% thermal savings; no measurement exists. What recovery fraction survives sealing and leakage losses at scale?

Per-climate cycle optimisation as a pure computation product: find cycle times, purge and partial loading that minimise cost given hourly temperature, humidity and power price. Models show ~25% residual spread between sites and 17-26% productivity given up for energy; flexible short cycles also exploit cheap-power windows.

Close the 10-20x gap between field uptake rates and the gas-film limit without adding inert mass: hierarchical pores, thinner amine films, plasticising water at the right humidity, chaotic-advection geometries tested in humid air at 1-3 m/s (existing TPMS data are dry and at ~0.1 m/s).

Heat only the sorbent: can Joule, induction or microwave heating reach <3 GJ_e/t at kg scale in humid air including water evaporation? A decisive test is a wall-plug energy balance on a >1 kg module at 50% RH; none has been published.

Is amine degradation in structured contactors governed by oxygen exposure time or by cycle count? The answer decides whether fast cycling lowers or raises sorbent cost per tonne; a split test (same hours, different cycle counts) would settle it.

Use the co-produced water as a product (modelled 1.5-2.5 t water per t CO2 in moderate climates) or pair DAC with atmospheric water harvesting, so the water heat buys something. Needs a combined energy and value balance.

Passive contactors: find the contactor capex per tonne at which wind-driven operation beats fans given that fans cost only ~$4-15/t in energy. Requires wind-resource-weighted flux and capacity-factor modelling.

key_claims.claim: In NETL's 2025 independent techno-economic study of a generic monolith sorbent DAC plant, cutting the sorbent's CO2 desorption energy by 85% (2 to 0.3 GJ/t) lowers cost by only about 1% ($1,028 to $1,017/t net), because water desorption, vessel and material heating and capital (about 54% of cost) dominate; working capacity, water content, pressure drop and capacity factor move cost far more. A weaker-binding sorbent alone is therefore not a cost breakthrough.

Measured kg-scale sorbent DAC pilots use 14.5 MJ/kg CO2 (U Twente steam-assisted TVSA, 0.27 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day, 2024) to more than 22 MJ/kg (42 kg rotary wheel, 2026), which is 2.4-3.6 times the idealised 6 GJ/t cycle, with the excess traced mainly to sensible heat of sorbent, inert material and housing plus heat losses. Contactor thermal mass and water, not binding chemistry, set real energy use today.

surprises: An 85% cut in CO2 desorption enthalpy moves NETL's cost by about 1%, while a wetter product stream moves it 28% and a low working capacity 70%. Binding enthalpy is close to irrelevant once water and thermal mass are counted.

Structured contactors that fix mass transfer create the thermal-mass problem: TDA/GE's coated heat exchanger hit its kinetics and 6,500-cycle durability targets but the metal needed more heat than the sorbent, forcing a waste-heat-only design.

The paper claiming the highest productivity in the literature (Wu 2026) reports 0.235-0.352 kg CO2/kg/day, yet TEAs assume 0.76 to 2.5. Integrated-system productivity is 3-10x below what cost models take as given.
Measured water swing is about 8x the CO2 swing at only 45% RH (Georgia Tech fibres, 2026); the OptiLex reference cycle's 2:1 and NETL's 1:1 are both optimistic by a factor of 3-8.

The gas-film limit is generous: a laminar channel could capture 75% at 5 m/s for ~85 Pa (OptiLex calc), so fans and passive wind contact are minor levers. Real contactors sit 30-60x above that pressure drop because the sorbent layer is slow.

Faster cycling is not free energy-wise: using 60% of equilibrium capacity raises heat per tonne by about 45% when inert mass is present (OptiLex calc), so the productivity optimum and the energy optimum pull apart; models put the gap at 17-26% productivity.

Mammoth reported 675 t net in H1 2026 against a 36,000 t/yr nameplate, even after a more than five-fold improvement year on year. The cause is not public and is confounded by partial build-out and net accounting, so it should not be read as a sorbent limit.

Electrified-heating papers report attractive numbers (3.4-6.1 GJ/t) but at 20 mg to 13-fibre scale; no kg-scale wall-plug measurement exists, and a silver heating layer halved capacity per mass in one design.

Calculation scripts for these levers are at climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/contactor_levers.py and contactor_masstransfer.py (run with the OptiLex verifiers; no repo files were modified). WebSearch budget ran out early, so RSC, ACS and Climeworks pages that returned HTTP 403 were checked through repositories, Europe PMC, OSTI and news syndication instead.

verifs.claim: In NETL's 2025 independent techno-economic study of a generic monolith sorbent DAC plant, cutting the sorbent's CO2 desorption energy by 85% (2 to 0.3 GJ/t) lowers cost by only about 1% ($1,028 to $1,017/t net), because water desorption, vessel and material heating and capital (about 54% of cost) dominate; working capacity, water content, pressure drop and capacity factor move cost far more. A weaker-binding sorbent alone is therefore not a cost breakthrough.
verifs.corrected_claim: In NETL's "Direct Air Capture Case Studies: Sorbent System (Revision 1)" (DOE/NETL-2024/4526, 11 Feb 2025), a modelled (not measured) techno-economic study of a generic monolith sorbent DAC plant (100,000 t/yr net, 420 ppmv CO2, 15 C, 60% RH, May-2023 dollars, AACE Class 5 capital estimate +/-50%), the single-variable sensitivity on Case 1-NG (direct-steam TVSA at 0.4 bar, powered by an on-site natural-gas CHP with CANSOLV capture) shows that cutting the sorbent's CO2 desorption energy from 2 to 0.3 GJ/t lowers LCOC-net by only about 1% ($1,028 to $1,017/t net, excluding T&S). NETL's stated reason: the CO2-desorption steam falls 85%, but total DAC regeneration steam falls only 30% because steam for H2O desorption (2.4 GJ/t at 1 mol H2O/mol CO2), vessel and material heating and radiation losses is unchanged; the saving is too small to remove a combustion turbine, so it only shows up as 1.8 MW more power export (electricity sales $105 to $114/t). Case 1-NG cost is about 54% capital, 20% fixed, 11% variable, 15% fuel. Other parameters move cost more, but mostly on the downside: working capacity 0.8 to 2 mol/kg gives -7% ($939) while 0.2 mol/kg gives +70% ($1,749); pressure drop 895 to 200 Pa gives -8% ($949) while 3,200 Pa gives +36% ($1,406); desorbed-stream water 75 to 70 wt% gives -0.6% ($1,022) while 90 wt% gives +28% ($1,313); capture fraction 0.6 to 0.8 gives -7%, 0.2 gives +65%; sorbent price $148/kg gives +58%. Desorption energy itself is strongly asymmetric: raising it to 12 GJ/t gives +53% ($1,571). Capacity factor is shown to be highly impactful (cost rises rapidly below 50% CF), but that sensitivity is reported for the electric-boiler Case 1-EB. Within this thermal-swing, NG-CHP configuration, lowering CO2 binding enthalpy alone (all else held constant) is not a cost breakthrough.
verifs.caveats:
All headline numbers check out against the primary PDF (Section 5.3.3, Exhibit 5-31, Exhibit 2-x parameter table): 2 to 0.3 GJ/t, $1,028.3 to $1,017/t net, "roughly 1 percent", 85% CO2-regeneration steam cut, ~54% capital share. Corrections and context that change how the claim should be used:

1. Simulated, not measured. This is an Aspen-based TEA of a generic sorbent with literature-average parameters; NETL says the base cases "do not represent optimized systems" and some assumptions are optimistic. Capital uncertainty is +/-50%, so an $11/t difference is far inside the noise.

2. Causal wording is imprecise. Capital share is not NETL's stated reason. The mechanism is (a) non-CO2 heat loads unchanged, so total regen steam drops only 30%, and (b) a step-function: not enough to drop a combustion turbine in the 2-CT CHP plant, so the benefit appears only as extra electricity sales. This is configuration-specific.

3. Case-specific. The sorbent sensitivities were run only on NG cases. NETL explicitly notes energy-related factors "will have a greater impact on EB cases" (Case 1-EB is 31% power cost vs 15% fuel in 1-NG), so the ~1% figure should not be generalized to electrified or heat-pump-driven plants.

4. "Move cost far more" is true mainly on the downside. The upside from better working capacity or pressure drop is only -7% to -8%, and water content -0.6%; no single sorbent parameter gives a large reduction from this base case. NETL's best-case combined scenario is ~$630/t (about $430/t with 90% CF, $1/MMBtu gas and FCR 0.05). The capacity-factor sensitivity cited is from the EB case (Exhibit 5-36/ES-5), not the same Case 1-NG tornado.

5. The report itself still says improving "working capacity and regeneration energy can significantly reduce the LCOCnet" and that low-vacuum TVSA with reduced regeneration energy "provide a cost advantage" -- so NETL does not draw the strong "not a breakthrough" conclusion; that final sentence is the claimant's inference, not a source statement.

6. Scope limit relevant to a "release without heat" research direction: the sensitivity varies only the CO2 desorption enthalpy while keeping the steam-driven temperature/vacuum-swing process, 1 mol H2O/mol CO2 co-adsorption, sensible heating of sorbent and vessels, working capacity (0.8 mol/kg) and the CHP plant fixed. It therefore says nothing about non-thermal regeneration (moisture-swing, electro-swing, etc.) or sorbents that also cut water co-adsorption and sensible heat, which would attack the loads NETL identifies as dominant. Conversely, the model treats binding energy and working capacity as independent; in practice a 0.3 GJ/t (~13 kJ/mol, physisorption-range) sorbent would likely lose capacity at 420 ppm, which the model shows is far more costly (+70% at 0.2 mol/kg).

7. "Independent" is the report's own framing of the original 2022 study ("independently assess"); it is a DOE/NETL in-house study with support contractors, not vendor data. Costs exclude transport and storage and 45Q credits.

Source verified directly: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2520078 (166-page PDF, text extracted locally).

verifs.claim: Measured kg-scale sorbent DAC pilots use 14.5 MJ/kg CO2 (U Twente steam-assisted TVSA, 0.27 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day, 2024) to more than 22 MJ/kg (42 kg rotary wheel, 2026), which is 2.4-3.6 times the idealised 6 GJ/t cycle, with the excess traced mainly to sensible heat of sorbent, inert material and housing plus heat losses. Contactor thermal mass and water, not binding chemistry, set real energy use today.
verifs.corrected_claim:
Two lab-scale sorbent DAC pilots (n=2, both run on indoor lab air with elevated CO2) report energy use well above an idealised ~6 GJ/t cycle, for different reasons.

(1) U Twente (Schellevis & Brilman, React. Chem. Eng. 2024, 9, 910-924): 4 fixed beds x 1.2 kg = 4.8 kg Lewatit VP OC 1065, steam-assisted TVSA, 1.3 kg CO2/day = 0.27 kg CO2/kg sorbent/day, total energy duty 14.5 MJ/kg CO2 (11.9 thermal + 2.65 electrical, including blower and vacuum/compression of product to 5 bar). Conditions: ~20 C, ~20% RH, 476 ppm CO2, campaign of several weeks. The 14.5 figure is calculated bottom-up from measured flows/temperatures/pressures and explicitly NEGLECTS heat losses to surroundings. Sensible heat is 7.37 MJ/kg (51%): sorbent 2.84, reactor segment 2.96, heat-transfer water in the tubes 1.57. CO2 desorption heat is 1.7, co-adsorbed H2O 1.12 (estimated from equilibrium isotherm, not measured), steam purge 1.67, vacuum/compression 1.81, air blower 0.83.

(2) Shanghai Jiao Tong University rotary adsorber (Wu et al., Advanced Science 2026, DOI 10.1002/advs.202521499): 42 kg structured adsorbent (PEI/silica-sol coated glass-fibre honeycomb wheel), atmospheric steam-purge TSA (no vacuum), 0.235-0.352 kg CO2/kg adsorbent/day, THERMAL energy alone >22 MJ/kg CO2 (electricity extra). Conditions: 21-30 C, 49-88% RH, inlet CO2 ~450-600 ppm, 8 days x 8 h. The authors attribute the excess to heating metal piping, imperfect insulation, steam leaking through the rotary seal, and unrecovered steam heat sent to the condenser, not to sorbent/housing sensible heat.

So 14.5 total is ~2.4x and >22 thermal is >3.7x a 6 GJ/t benchmark (the benchmark is not from either paper; Twente thermal-only 11.9 is ~2.0x). In Twente the excess is dominated by contactor thermal mass (sorbent + reactor + heat-transfer fluid); in the rotary wheel by steam over-use, leakage and heat loss. Binding enthalpy is only ~12% of the Twente duty, but sorbent working capacity and H2O selectivity still scale the sensible-heat and water penalties directly.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against full text of both primary sources (Twente PDF via UT repository; SJTU paper via Europe PMC PMC13045267). The headline numbers (14.5 MJ/kg, 0.27 kg/kg/day, 42 kg, >22 MJ/kg) are all correct; the framing needs these corrections:

1. Heat losses are not in the Twente number. Quote: values are "calculated from experimental results, neglecting thermal energy losses to the surroundings". So 14.5 is a calculated duty from measured process data, not a metered consumption, and real consumption would be higher. "Plus heat losses" applies only to the rotary wheel.
2. Apples vs oranges: 14.5 is thermal + electrical (incl. compression to 5 bar); >22 is thermal only (steam generation enthalpy / CO2), a lower bound with no single measured value stated in the text. Process also differs: TVSA at ~75 mbar vs atmospheric steam TSA.
3. Rotary-wheel excess cause is misattributed: piping heat-up, insulation, seal steam leakage and uncondensed/unrecovered steam, not sorbent/inert/housing sensible heat. This is prototype engineering immaturity, arguably fixable; the authors' model gives 11.68 MJ/kg thermal without those losses and 7.41-9.64 total with heat recovery (simulated, not measured).
4. "Water" is weakly supported by measurement. Twente ran at 20% RH where H2O co-adsorption was only 1.12 MJ/kg (8%) and was not measured (equilibrium estimate). The authors project 5-10 MJ/kg for NW European climate and 3-5 for dry climates; that is a projection. Steam purge was 1.67 MJ/kg and without it duty fell only 5% (13.8).
5. Both pilots used indoor air with elevated CO2 (476 ppm; 450-600 ppm), which flatters productivity and energy versus ~425 ppm outdoor air. Neither is an outdoor, long-duration test: several weeks (Twente), 64 h over 8 days (SJTU). No cycle-stability claims beyond that.
6. Twente product purity was only 50-55% CO2 (air leaks), SJTU 70-99%; SJTU's 42 kg includes the honeycomb substrate, so per-kg productivity is per structured adsorbent. SJTU scale is ~10-15 kg CO2/day, Twente 1.3 kg/day.
7. "Not binding chemistry" is too strong for use as a research-direction premise. Reaction heat is small (1.7 MJ/kg), but Twente calls working capacity "a critical parameter" because sensible heat per kg CO2 scales inversely with it, and the reactor-to-sorbent heat-capacity ratio (1.05, or 1.59 with heat-transfer water) is the lever. Sorbent circulation would cut ~4.5 MJ/kg (~30%); listed optimisations give 8.1 and a heat pump 5.1 MJ/kg, all unmeasured projections. SJTU's model likewise projects 2.5-3.1 MJ/kg from adsorbent improvement. So sorbent properties (capacity, kinetics, H2O selectivity, heat capacity) matter a great deal; only the binding enthalpy itself is not the dominant term.
8. The "idealised 6 GJ/t cycle" is not defined in either paper; the 2.4-3.6x ratio depends entirely on that external benchmark and on whether it is thermal-only. Generalising from two bench pilots to "real energy use today" (commercial plants) is not supported by these sources.

Process note: web search quota was exhausted, so the 2026 paper was located via Crossref and read via Europe PMC; no independent third pilot was checked.

items.name: Open DAC 2023 'promising MOF' list vs independent recalculation (Jin, Garcia, Smit 2025)
items.mechanism: DFT (PBE-D3) screening of CoRE-MOF-2019 structures for CO2 adsorption energy stronger than -0.5 eV and stronger than H2O; then an independent re-run (PrISMa workflow, CP2K PBE-D3) that re-optimises the empty framework after removing the guest.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No uptake measured. ODAC23 paper: '135 of the 5,079 pristine MOFs bind CO2 strongly' and beat H2O (0 K DFT energies, single molecule, no humidity isotherm). The correspondence (which counts 5,961 pristine) reproduced only 1 of the 135 (ASEJOZ01). ODAC23 binding energies spanned about -100 to +75 kJ/mol; the recalculation gave -50 to -10 kJ/mol, the range of measured heats of adsorption. About 40% of the underlying CoRE-2019 structures were flagged as charged (missing H or counter-ions).
items.regeneration: Not addressed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed. No synthesis or measurement exists for ASEJOZ01 or the other 134 in either paper.
items.cost: ODAC23 used over 400 million core-hours for about 38 million DFT single points.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 1-2, computation only (2023-2025).
items.bottleneck: Hit list was dominated by method artifacts (empty framework stuck in a local minimum, bad input structures): 134 of 135 hits (99%) not reproduced. Confound: this is DFT against DFT with the same functional, so it shows the list was unreliable, not that the MOFs fail in the lab.

items.name: Open DAC 2025 dataset and eSEN / UMA models (Meta FAIR, Georgia Tech)
items.mechanism: About 60 million DFT single points for CO2, H2O, N2 and O2 in about 15,000 MOFs, including 3,920 amine-functionalised MOFs with explicit ammonium-carbamate and carbamic-acid placements, GCMC-derived configurations (2.7 million) and re-relaxed empty frameworks; machine-learned potentials trained on it.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No uptake measured and no new DAC candidates named. Model error against DFT: eSEN 0.077 eV overall, 0.061 eV for CO2 and 0.075 eV for H2O adsorption energy; UMA-Small 0.110 eV; the ODAC23 EquiformerV2-Large 0.155 eV. Fixes to ODAC23: about 7% of ODAC23 calculations had k-point errors above 0.2 eV; re-relaxing empty MOFs shifted median adsorption energy by more than 0.1 eV in every split.
items.regeneration: Not addressed (energies only, no free energies or cycle).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed. O2 results flagged by the authors as unreliable near redox-active metals (619 of 38,441 O2 configurations showed O-O stretching above 1.4 Å).
items.cost: Free: data CC BY 4.0 on Hugging Face (gated form), checkpoints esen_sm_odac25_full / filtered under the FAIR Chemistry licence; UMA has an 'odac' task (uma-s 6.6M active parameters, uma-m 50M). Needs a GPU, no cluster.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 1-2; dataset released August 2025. I found no published synthesis and measurement of any ODAC-selected MOF (search was limited, see caveat in surprises).
items.bottleneck: Model error against DFT (0.061 eV = 5.9 kJ/mol for CO2) is about 60% of the whole usable binding window (9.4 kJ/mol = 0.097 eV wide in the OptiLex Langmuir model). That error alone moves predicted 420 ppm site filling at -70 kJ/mol anywhere from 15% to 95%, and shifts regeneration temperature by about 31 C. DFT's own error against experiment comes on top.

items.name: The only experimental check of ODAC25 models: Henry coefficients in three MOFs
items.mechanism: Widom-insertion Henry coefficients from each potential compared with repeated published isotherms for UiO-66, HKUST-1 and MOF-5 (298 K, single gas, dry), error expressed in eV (proportional to log K_H).
items.uptake_and_conditions: Mean absolute error against experiment for CO2: UMA-Medium 0.0145 eV, eSEN-filtered 0.0234, eSEN-full 0.0250, UMA-Small 0.0274, classical UFF 0.0299, DAC-specialised MACE-DAC 0.0513. Lab-to-lab experimental spread: 0.016 eV for CO2, 0.009 eV for N2. For N2, UFF (0.0190) beats eSEN-full (0.0433) and both UMA models.
items.regeneration: Not applicable.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable.
items.cost: Reproducible by a small team with DAC-SIM-style Widom insertion and any ASE calculator.
items.trl_and_scale: Benchmark of 3 rigid, weakly binding, heavily studied MOFs; no humid data, no 400 ppm data, no strong-binding sites.
items.bottleneck: The validation set is 3 materials and excludes the chemistry that matters for DAC (strong sites, water, amines). On it, a 1990s generic force field is within 0.007 eV of the new model for CO2. Confound: this does not show UFF is adequate for DAC, since ODAC23 itself found UFF errors of 0.29 eV (CO2) and 0.39 eV (H2O) in the chemisorption regime.

items.name: Framework flexibility: rigid-framework screening error (Brabson, Medford, Sholl 2025)
items.mechanism: DFT test of adsorbate-induced framework deformation on 59 MOF+CO2/H2O systems from the ODAC23 test set, then benchmark of one classical and six machine-learned force fields against DFT.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 17 of 59 systems (29%) deform significantly (above 0.05 eV per cell, up to 0.757 eV); nearly 30% move more than 0.1 eV between rigid and flexible treatment. Adsorption-energy error against DFT: CHGNet 0.124 eV (best), MACE-MP-0 0.181, UFF4MOF 0.186, EquiformerV2-ODAC 0.191, eSEN 0.243, M3GNet 0.247, MACE-MPA-0 0.357. Chemisorption cases are worse: 0.217 to 0.575 eV.
items.regeneration: Not addressed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed.
items.trl_and_scale: Computation only; 59 systems. Tested models pre-date the ODAC25 checkpoints, so this is a lower bound on today's accuracy only if ODAC25 models have not improved on flexible cases (untested in this paper).
items.bottleneck: Authors' own bar is agreement with DFT within 0.1 eV; no tested model met it. 0.124 eV is 12 kJ/mol, a factor of about 125 in Henry coefficient at 25 C (my calculation).

items.name: Input-structure errors in MOF databases (LitMOF preprint 2025-26; CoRE MOF 2019 vs 2025)
items.mechanism: LLM multi-agent pipeline that repairs database structures against the original papers, then a DAC screen (4,256 MOFs, MACE-mh-1 heats of adsorption, criteria |Qst| above 40 kJ/mol and CO2/H2O selectivity above 1) run on original and corrected structures.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Original structures: 192 of 1,945 pass (9.9%); corrected: 282 of 1,446 pass (19.5%). Only 46 MOFs appear in both hit lists; 236 real candidates were missed and 146 were false positives. CO2 heat-of-adsorption correlation between original and corrected structures: Pearson 0.056; H2O MAE 30.2 kJ/mol; 97 MOFs gave infinite values. 9,227 invalid entries repaired (69.1% of not-computation-ready CoRE entries).
items.regeneration: Not addressed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed.
items.cost: LitMOF-DB lists 189,567 computation-ready structures; CoRE MOF 2025 (Matter, doi 10.1016/j.matt.2025.102140) is CC BY 4.0 with ML stability and heat-capacity predictors.
items.trl_and_scale: Preprint; ML potential rather than DFT energies, so magnitudes are indicative.
items.bottleneck: Hit-list overlap between raw and corrected structures is 46 of 192 (24%). Structure curation changes the answer more than the choice of potential does.

items.name: Reproducibility of the experimental ground truth (Sholl 2026)
items.mechanism: Literature audit of 130 randomly chosen MOFs for any repeat synthesis 11-17 years after first report, plus prior analysis of replicate isotherm measurements.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 83% of the 130 MOFs have no reported replicate synthesis (89% in the 2019 audit). About 1 in 6 replicate single-gas isotherm measurements are outliers. For roughly 2 in 3 MOFs the original report is the only evidence of structure or properties.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not addressed directly; implies stability claims are also mostly unreplicated.
items.trl_and_scale: Meta-analysis of published lab data.
items.bottleneck: Most database MOFs have never been made twice, so a screen over 8,000-15,000 'experimental' structures is mostly a screen over single unreplicated reports.

items.name: Closest predicted-then-made-then-measured cases for humid CO2: Cooper macrocycle prisms (2025), Boyd Al-PMOF (2019), PrISMa MIP-212 (2024)
items.mechanism: Bottom-up screen of CO2 versus H2O binding on 27,446 molecular fragments found bent aromatic 'clips' that favour CO2 by many weak pi contacts; two water- and acid-stable prisms were then synthesised. Boyd et al. mined 300,000+ hypothetical MOFs for 'adsorbaphore' pockets and made two Al MOFs.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Prism P4-am: 1.21 mmol/g CO2 at 298 K and 1 bar pure CO2; breakthrough working capacity 0.48 mmol/g in 15/85 CO2/N2, unchanged at 75% relative humidity. Zeolite 13X fell from 3.13 to 0.12 mmol/g under the same humid test. The triangular prism lost capacity when humid. None was measured at 400 ppm. Boyd Al-PMOF: capture 'not affected by water' at 313 K and 85% RH flue gas (abstract only; numbers not retrieved).
items.regeneration: Not reported in what I retrieved.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Prisms: 10 cycles without loss. Far short of the 2,000-20,000 cycles that set sorbent cost.
items.trl_and_scale: Gram-scale lab, TRL 3. All three are flue-gas (4-15% CO2) cases, not DAC.
items.bottleneck: The mechanism is weak physisorption (measured heats in the -10 to -50 kJ/mol range), which the OptiLex model puts at under 3% site filling at 420 ppm. Humidity tolerance was predicted correctly; DAC-level affinity was not the target and is not shown.

items.name: Generative MOF design with synthesis: MOFGen (2025)
items.mechanism: Agentic pipeline: LLM proposes compositions, diffusion model generates crystal structures, MACE and DFT filter them, ML scores linker synthesizability, then high-throughput synthesis.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No CO2 or water adsorption measured on any product. Funnel: 259,559 generated structures, about 180,000 after pore and relaxation filters, 3,000 DFT-optimised (r2SCAN-D4), 349 linkers shortlisted, 5 'AI-dreamt' MOFs made with PXRD or single-crystal structure matching prediction.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not measured.
items.trl_and_scale: Lab milligram-gram scale. All five are zinc MOFs; three are MOF-5-topology variants. The number of failed synthesis attempts is not disclosed.
items.bottleneck: Generation is no longer the limit; property validation is. Human experts agreed with only 40% of the linkers the ML called synthesizable. Zinc carboxylate MOF-5 analogues are a class known to be water-sensitive, so these are not DAC candidates as made.

items.name: Stability-aware screening: Kulik group water-stability models (2024) and 180-million-MOF multi-objective search (2026); QMOF-Thermo (2026)
items.mechanism: ML classifiers trained on literature-mined water, acid, thermal and activation stability labels, combined with a genetic algorithm (NSGA-III) over seven objectives (five stability, two DAC performance from adsorption simulation). QMOF-Thermo adds DFT energy-above-hull for 20,000+ MOFs as a synthesizability metric.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No measured uptake. Water-stability model: 911 newly labelled MOFs (WS24, over 400% more data), test ROC-AUC above 0.8. The 2026 search covers 'over 180 million' hypothetical MOFs and reports that coordinatively saturated metals and dispersion-dominated pockets favour humid CO2 uptake.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Predicted class labels only (stable / unstable), not cycle life.
items.cost: Models and data are public (web interface); usable on a laptop.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 1-2, computation only; abstract-level access to the 2026 paper.
items.bottleneck: ROC-AUC 0.8 on about 1,100 labels means a meaningful false-positive rate, and the label is binary water stability rather than capacity loss per cycle. No candidate from the 180-million search has a reported synthesis.

items.name: Amine binding-site screening without experiment: LANL 1.65-million-site screen (2025)
items.mechanism: B3LYP DFT binding enthalpies of CO2 on nitrogen sites in GDB-17 molecules, extended by an ML model, filtered by ML synthesizability scores; benchmark is branched PEI.
items.uptake_and_conditions: About 2,600 of 1.65 million sites (under 0.3%) bind CO2 more strongly than branched PEI with acceptable synthesizability (1,887 primary, 755 secondary amines). ML error: RMSE 0.13 eV overall (about 12.5 kJ/mol), 0.08 eV in the binding region; rank correlation 0.9. Dry, gas-phase, single site.
items.regeneration: Not addressed.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Oxidative and thermal stability explicitly left for future work.
items.cost: Data on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.17478899), code at github.com/lanl/binding_prediction.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 1-2; nothing synthesised.
items.bottleneck: Screens only the quantity that existing amines already satisfy (binding strength) and ignores the two that set cost: humidity behaviour and oxidative lifetime. A 12.5 kJ/mol error exceeds the 9.4 kJ/mol usable window.

items.name: Measured humid 400 ppm benchmarks any computed candidate must beat: TAEA@MIL-101(Cr) (2026), COF-999 (2024), diamine-appended MOF in humid air (2024)
items.mechanism: Amine chemisorption in a porous host (grafted or covalently bound amines); none of the three was found by computation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: TAEA@MIL-101(Cr): 3.12 mmol/g equilibrium at 400 ppm, 298 K; dynamic breakthrough 12.4 wt% dry and 9.7 wt% at 50% RH (78% retained). COF-999 (abstract): 0.96 mmol/g dry and 2.05 mmol/g at 50% RH from ambient air, half capacity in 18.8 min. ExxonMobil study (J. Chem. Phys. 2024): a diamine-appended MOF shows a step isotherm in dry air but an ordinary Langmuir isotherm in humid air.
items.regeneration: TAEA@MIL-101(Cr): complete at 50 C in about 100 min. COF-999: 60 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: TAEA@MIL-101(Cr): 10 cycles, 92.2% retention. COF-999: 100+ cycles reported in the paper (I retrieved the abstract only).
items.trl_and_scale: Lab gram scale, TRL 3-4.
items.bottleneck: Humidity changes capacity in opposite directions by chemistry (+114% for COF-999, -22% for TAEA@MIL-101(Cr)) and changes isotherm shape for cooperative MOFs. Water diffuses 7.2 to 8.7 times faster than dilute CO2 (50-80% RH). A CO2-versus-H2O binding-energy comparison cannot predict any of this. Cycle counts are 10-100, against 2,000-20,000 needed.

items.name: Public measured-data resource for amine sorbents (Wang et al., Scientific Data 2025)
items.mechanism: Manually curated literature dataset of amine-impregnated solid sorbents with 28 features per entry, from 0.04% CO2 to pure CO2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 1,336 data points from 52 articles, 29,857 filled cells. Units and terms harmonised by hand.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Only 216 data points (16%) carry any cycling-stability value; 53 carry weight-loss stability. Complete kinetic models in 7 of 52 articles; regeneration-energy data 'often absent'.
items.cost: Free (Figshare, XLSX); paper is CC BY-NC-ND.
items.trl_and_scale: Dataset of lab measurements.
items.bottleneck: The measured literature is too small and too uneven to train a lifetime or energy model: 84% of points have no cycling data.

items.name: Tools a small team can run now: universal ML potentials, DAC-SIM, PrISMa
items.mechanism: Pretrained general-purpose interatomic potentials used inside Widom insertion or Monte Carlo to get CO2 and H2O Henry coefficients and heats of adsorption; PrISMa links material data to process cost.
items.uptake_and_conditions: MOFSimBench (20 models): top universal potentials (eSEN-OAM, orb-v3, MatterSim) beat UFF+DDEC charges and the DAC-fine-tuned MACE-DAC-1 on CO2/H2O host-guest energies; heat capacity MAE 0.018 J/K/g (2.3%) on 231 frameworks; over 94% of frameworks stay intact in 50 ps MD. DAC-SIM (MIT licence) screened 8,000+ experimental MOFs. PrISMa: 1,200+ materials, 66 point-source case studies, data on Zenodo.
items.regeneration: PrISMa computes process energy and cost, but has no DAC case study.
items.stability_and_lifetime: A 2026 benchmark (arXiv 2604.25262) reports all five tested universal potentials show 'significant error' at high temperature, which matters for regeneration and degradation.
items.cost: Open source; one GPU. UMA and ODAC25 checkpoints need a Hugging Face access form.
items.trl_and_scale: Software, ready to use.
items.bottleneck: PrISMa finding: materials ranked top-10 on a material metric (for example Henry selectivity) can rank below 100 on cost; adding water raised capture cost by 8% (cement) to 22% (gas power). MOFSimBench did not test ODAC-trained models, and none of these tools predicts lifetime.
