items.name: Self-driving labs and high-throughput experimentation for DAC sorbents
items.mechanism: Robotic synthesis plus automated humid 400 ppm testing in a closed loop with a model.
items.uptake_and_conditions: I found no published closed-loop or robotic campaign that discovered a DAC sorbent and reported humid 400 ppm cycling data. The NIST-led 'sorbent materials foundry' (2022) is a proposal ('We envision'), with no results. Robotic MOF discovery exists for other targets (for example polyoxometalate MOFs, JACS 2024).
items.stability_and_lifetime: None reported.
items.trl_and_scale: Concept stage for DAC. Company signals: Orbital Materials' site now redirects to 'Orbital Industries' and describes GPU-cooling materials with no carbon-capture claim (checked October 2026); CuspAI's site gives no measured DAC result.
items.bottleneck: The missing instrument is a cheap, parallel, humid, 400 ppm, many-cycle test. Without it, no computational pipeline gets feedback. Caveat: my search was restricted (see surprises), so absence here is weaker evidence than a full search would give.

bottlenecks: Energy accuracy versus the usable window. In the OptiLex Langmuir model the binding enthalpy that gives 30-95% site filling at 420 ppm spans only 9.4 kJ/mol (0.097 eV). Best ODAC25 model error against DFT is 0.061 eV for CO2 (5.9 kJ/mol): a factor of 11 in Henry coefficient, predicted filling anywhere from 15% to 95%, regeneration temperature off by about 31 C. Best force field on flexible frameworks: 0.124 eV (factor 125). DFT-versus-experiment error is additional. Script: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/comp_error_propagation.py
Zero closed loops. 135 ODAC23 hits, 1 reproduced by independent DFT, 0 synthesised and measured in anything I could find. ODAC25's only experimental check is 3 rigid MOFs, dry, single gas.

Humidity. At 25 C and 50% RH water is 37 times more abundant than CO2 (1,584 Pa versus 42.6 Pa), so a site needs CO2 to bind about 9.0 kJ/mol more strongly in free energy than water just to be half-shared (computed). Measured humidity effects range from +114% (COF-999) to -22% (TAEA@MIL-101(Cr)) to loss of the cooperative step (diamine MOF); binding-energy screens predict none of these.

Input structures. About 40% of CoRE-2019 structures used by ODAC23 were flagged charged; correcting structures changed the DAC hit list so that only 46 of 192 original hits survived, and the hit rate rose from 9.9% to 19.5%.
Experimental ground truth. 83% of sampled MOFs were never re-synthesised; about 1 in 6 replicate isotherms is an outlier.

Lifetime is unscreened. No dataset or model found predicts capacity loss per cycle. Only 16% of points in the public amine-sorbent dataset have any cycling value, and benchmark papers report 10-100 cycles, while OptiLex's own numbers show sorbent cost falls from $218/t at 2,000 cycles to $22/t at 20,000.

Material metrics do not rank process cost. PrISMa: top-10 by Henry selectivity can be below rank 100 on cost; water adds 8-22% to point-source capture cost. No equivalent open DAC process ranking exists.
open_problems: Consensus re-screen on corrected inputs: run ODAC25 eSEN, UMA-odac and one universal potential on LitMOF-corrected / CoRE-2025 structures, keep only MOFs that pass in all pipelines and pass the water-stability and energy-above-hull filters, and report each candidate's probability of landing in the 66-76 kJ/mol window given the stated model error, rather than a point estimate. Cost: GPU time only.

Build the missing validation set: collect every published 400 ppm CO2 uptake with humidity and cycle count for MOFs, COFs, zeolites and amines, and score existing models against it. ODAC25 was checked on 3 MOFs; a 50-100 material humid benchmark would be new and directly useful to the field.

Predict the sign of the humidity effect. Water raises capacity for some amine sorbents and lowers it for others; a model (reactive ML potential or simple descriptor) that predicts which, checked against the dozen or so measured cases, would beat CO2-versus-H2O binding-energy filters.

Screen for lifetime instead of uptake: computed oxidation or urea-formation barriers for amine sites (Li et al. JACS 2024 show CO2 acid-catalyses PEI oxidation), ranked against the few measured degradation rates. Uptake is already adequate in existing amines; cycle life sets the $/t.

Free energy, not energy: ODAC-style screens rank 0 K adsorption energies. Adsorption entropy varies between sites, and the OptiLex window is defined in free energy. Finite-temperature Widom or thermodynamic-integration estimates on a shortlist would test whether the ranking survives.

Flexible and defective frameworks: 29% of DAC-relevant systems deform on adsorption and no general potential reaches 0.1 eV. A targeted fine-tune on deforming cases, validated against CALF-20 and MIL-120 measured isotherms, is a tractable project.

A cheap parallel humid-400-ppm cycling rig. No high-throughput or self-driving experimental loop for DAC sorbents was found. A design that tests tens of samples for hundreds of cycles is the instrument every computational effort lacks, and a natural basis for a lab partnership.

DAC version of PrISMa: couple shortlisted materials to the OptiLex TVSA cycle model so candidates are ranked by GJ/t and $/t (including water co-desorption and sorbent replacement), not by Henry coefficient.

key_claims.claim: Of the 135 MOFs the Open DAC 2023 paper flagged as promising for DAC, an independent DFT recalculation that re-optimised the empty frameworks reproduced only one (ASEJOZ01), and about 40% of the underlying structures were flagged as charged. I found no published synthesis and measurement of any ODAC-selected MOF (limited search).

The best Open DAC 2025 model reproduces DFT CO2 adsorption energies to 0.061 eV (5.9 kJ/mol), ODAC23 had errors above 0.2 eV in about 7% of calculations, and the only experimental check covers three rigid MOFs under dry single-gas conditions. The usable DAC binding window in the OptiLex model is 0.097 eV wide, so current screening cannot by itself tell a working sorbent from a non-working one.

surprises: On the only experimental benchmark in the ODAC25 paper, the generic classical force field UFF (0.0299 eV) beat the DAC-specialised ML potential MACE-DAC (0.0513 eV) for CO2 and beat eSEN-full and both UMA models for N2. Only UMA-Medium (0.0145 eV) got below the lab-to-lab experimental spread (0.016 eV). Confound: three rigid, weak-binding MOFs; says nothing about strong sites or water.

Fixing database structures doubled the DAC hit rate (9.9% to 19.5%) rather than shrinking it: structure errors hide more real candidates (236 missed) than they create false ones (146). A screen on corrected structures may find overlooked materials, which supports the 'sharp screen' option.
General-purpose ML potentials outperformed the one fine-tuned specifically for DAC host-guest interactions (MOFSimBench), and the authors conclude data quality matters more than architecture.

The ODAC23 failure is partly outdated: ODAC25 fixed the k-point and re-relaxation errors. What still applies is the absence of experimental validation, PBE-D3 limits at open metal sites, and flagged structures kept in the 'full' set. ODAC23's bad hit list should not be read as evidence against the ODAC25 models themselves.

Generative design reached the bench (5 of 5 reported AI-generated MOFs made, structures matching prediction), but all are zinc MOF-5-type frameworks and nobody measured adsorption. Generation is not the constraint.

Humidity helps as often as it hurts in measured amine sorbents (COF-999 capacity more than doubles at 50% RH), so 'CO2 must out-bind water', the criterion used by ODAC23 and most screens, is the wrong filter for chemisorbents.

Orbital Materials, which publicised an AI-designed carbon-capture sorbent in 2024, now redirects to 'Orbital Industries' with a GPU-cooling focus and no carbon-capture claim on its homepage (checked October 2026). Homepage observation only; I did not find a statement explaining the change.

Method caveat: the WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted, so I worked from the arXiv API, Europe PMC, Crossref and direct fetches of primary papers. Numbers were extracted from full text by the fetch tool's summariser; the two key claims were cross-checked in separate fetches. 'None found' statements (no synthesised ODAC candidate, no DAC self-driving lab) are therefore weaker than a full search would support. Not retrieved: DAC-SIM Matter paper results beyond its abstract, Kulik 2026 full text, Boyd 2019 numbers, the CCST 2026 paper 'Humid-air competitive adsorption invalidates conventional sorbent screening criteria'. ODAC23 says 135 of 5,079 pristine MOFs; the correspondence says 135 of 5,961.

verifs.claim: Of the 135 MOFs the Open DAC 2023 paper flagged as promising for DAC, an independent DFT recalculation that re-optimised the empty frameworks reproduced only one (ASEJOZ01), and about 40% of the underlying structures were flagged as charged. I found no published synthesis and measurement of any ODAC-selected MOF (limited search).
verifs.corrected_claim: The Open DAC 2023 paper flagged 135 pristine MOFs (of 5,079 converged pristine structures, plus 107 defective ones) as promising for DAC on a DFT-only criterion: CO2 adsorption energy stronger than -0.5 eV (about -50 kJ/mol) and stronger than that of H2O. An independent PBE-D3 recalculation (Jin, Garcia and Smit, ACS Cent. Sci. 2025, doi 10.1021/acscentsci.5c00255) that re-minimised the empty framework after removing the adsorbate reproduced none of the 135. It found only one MOF meeting the criterion, ASEJOZ01, and the authors state "This structure was not in OpenDAC's list of promising MOFs." About 40% of the CoRE MOF structures underlying the ODAC23 pristine set as a whole (not of the 135 specifically) were flagged as charged by MOFchecker and discarded before recalculation. The correspondence concludes that ODAC23's very strong binding energies are artifacts of local-minimum reference energies and that the released ML models should be retrained. I could not establish whether any ODAC-selected MOF has since been measured under DAC conditions (400 ppm, humid); the frameworks themselves are all previously synthesised CoRE MOF structures, so "no published synthesis" is the wrong framing.
verifs.caveats:
**Sources read:** the correspondence's open-access full text (PMC12203258), its Zenodo data (zenodo.org/records/14802658), the ODAC23 preprint (arXiv 2311.00341), the ODAC23 promising-MOF list on GitHub (Open-Catalyst-Project/odac-data), and the ODAC25 preprint (arXiv 2508.03162) via an automated summary.

**The main error.** ASEJOZ01 is not one of the 135. I confirmed this against ODAC23's own `promising_pristine_MOFs.csv` (135 entries, no ASEJOZ). The result is therefore 0 of the 135 reproduced, plus one new candidate, which is a stronger negative than the claim states.

**Scope of the recalculation (my own tally of the Zenodo files, not stated in the paper).**
- The recalculation was not run on all 135. It covered only neutral, closed-shell structures with fewer than 500 atoms and large enough cells, using CP2K with a DZVP basis (ODAC23 used VASP).
- `binding_energy.csv` holds 714 structures, of which only 15 are from the 135. None of those 15 passes.
- The rest of the 135 were discarded as charged or problematic, or fell outside the computational limits; they were not individually recomputed.
- ASEJOZ01 passes only marginally: CO2 about -51.4 kJ/mol against a 50 kJ/mol threshold, with H2O about -10.1 kJ/mol.

**The 40% figure.** It checks out as 2,052 of 5,168 checked structures (39.7%), and refers to the whole CoRE-MOF-derived pristine set. Among the 135 specifically, 60 (44%) are flagged charged and 68 (50%) are flagged charged or geometrically wrong. Every one of the nine CSD-coded entries in ODAC23's top-10 pristine table (Table S3) is flagged charged.

**Count discrepancy.** The correspondence says "135 out of 5961 pristine", while ODAC23 itself says "135 of the 5,079 pristine MOFs".

**Everything here is simulated.** The quantities are 0 K, single-molecule DFT adsorption energies. They are not capacities at 400 ppm, and involve no humidity isotherms, temperatures or cycling. The correspondence notes that its own method does not guarantee global minima either.

**What ODAC23 already conceded.**
- It ran a second-round empty-framework relaxation (lower-energy states found for 690 pristine and 625 defective MOFs).
- It warned about CoRE MOF cleaning errors and charged structures.
- It narrowed the list to 10 manually vetted MOFs for synthesis (Tables 2 and 3).
- Of those 10, the two that were recalculated both fail: ODIXEG at about -17.5 kJ/mol CO2 (ODAC23: -0.94 eV), and QOVSOL, which binds water more strongly than CO2. A third, QEFNAQ, is flagged charged by MOFchecker.

**ODAC25.** It acknowledges the re-relaxation problem and reports k-point errors above 0.2 eV in about 7% of ODAC23-setting calculations. It reports no experimental validation and no revised count of promising MOFs.

**Source type.** This is a Correspondence from a group with its own competing screening platform (PrISMa). A Crossref query turned up no published rebuttal.

**The synthesis sentence is unverified.** The web-search budget for this session was exhausted, so I ran no independent literature search. All ODAC23 candidates are previously synthesised frameworks. ODAC23 Table 2 cites pre-existing CO2 uptakes for some of them (for example 0.1 to 1.6 mmol/g at 150 mbar, 273 to 298 K), but none at DAC conditions (about 0.4 mbar CO2, humid).

verifs.claim: The best Open DAC 2025 model reproduces DFT CO2 adsorption energies to 0.061 eV (5.9 kJ/mol), ODAC23 had errors above 0.2 eV in about 7% of calculations, and the only experimental check covers three rigid MOFs under dry single-gas conditions. The usable DAC binding window in the OptiLex model is 0.097 eV wide, so current screening cannot by itself tell a working sorbent from a non-working one.
verifs.corrected_claim: In the Open DAC 2025 paper (arXiv 2508.03162v2), the best model for CO2 (eSEN trained on full ODAC25) has a CO2 adsorption-energy MAE of 0.061 eV (5.9 kJ/mol) against DFT. This is a single-point (S2EF, non-relaxed) error on the ODAC25 test split (Table 2). A 100-system sample of ODAC23 showed DFT k-point convergence errors above 0.2 eV in about 7% of calculations, which ODAC25 corrects. The only comparison with experiment is a Henry-coefficient benchmark on 16 physisorbing MOFs (15 with CO2 data, 11 with N2; Table S6), not three. The main text names only UiO-66, HKUST-1 and MOF-5 as examples. That benchmark uses single-component CO2 and N2 isotherms at 292-308 K and treats the frameworks as rigid. It has no humid, co-adsorption, chemisorption/amine or cycling validation. The 0.097 eV (9.4 kJ/mol) window is not part of the committed OptiLex verifier. It comes from a session scratch calculation: the dH range giving 30-95% site fill at 420 ppm and 298 K for a single-site Langmuir sorbent with dS fixed at -165 J/mol/K (-66.3 to -75.7 kJ/mol). Because the 0.061 eV MAE exceeds the window half-width (0.048 eV), a candidate predicted at the window centre has only about a 47% chance of truly lying inside it, assuming Gaussian errors. Screening with these models therefore cannot reliably separate working from non-working sorbents, though it can still rank candidates and reject ones far outside the window.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the arXiv v2 HTML (last revised 23 Sep 2025) and by re-running the OptiLex scratch script.

**What holds**
- **0.061 eV:** Table 2, eSEN (Full), CO2 column. 0.061 eV x 96.485 = 5.89 kJ/mol. It is measured against DFT (PBE-D3), not experiment.
- **7% above 0.2 eV:** quoted correctly, but it is a DFT k-point error in ODAC23 "as compared to K = 40 Å", from 100 randomly selected systems. It is not an ML-model error rate. The paper does not say whether it refers to total or adsorption energy.

**What is wrong**
- **"Three rigid MOFs":** Table S6 lists 16 MOFs and 44 MOF/gas/temperature points, including CALF-20, CAU-10, MIL-160, MIL-96 and UiO-66-NH2. "Rigid" is the Widom-insertion modelling assumption, not a measured property. The paper never says "dry"; that is implied by single-component isotherms.
- **"In the OptiLex model":** `climate/sorbent.py` defines no window. The figure comes from the uncommitted `scratchpad/sorbent/comp_error_propagation.py`, and I reproduced 9.4 kJ/mol = 0.097 eV from it.

**Context that changes how the numbers are used**
- **Worse elsewhere:** the same eSEN models score 0.077 eV across all adsorbates and 0.081 eV for CO2+H2O. On an independent 59-MOF deformation benchmark, eSEN-Full has MAE 0.125 eV with R² = -1.264 (worse than guessing the mean); eSEN-Filtered has 0.087 eV and R² = 0.542.
- **Experimental benchmark is off-target:** the best CO2 Henry-coefficient MAE is 0.0145 eV (UMA-Medium), with eSEN-Filtered at 0.0234 and the UFF baseline at 0.0299, against an experimental spread of 0.016 eV. These are weak physisorbents, whereas the 0.097 eV window sits in the amine-like chemisorption range near -70 kJ/mol, so the benchmark does not validate the regime the window is in.
- **Window definition is a choice:** the 30% and 95% fill thresholds are arbitrary. The session's other definition (at least 20% fill, unloading to 20% residual at 1 kPa by 120 °C) gives about 10.4 kJ/mol (0.108 eV) by my hand calculation, so "about 0.1 eV" is robust.
- **Window position depends on entropy:** it shifts by about T x ΔdS, so a 30 J/mol/K change in dS moves it by roughly one full width. The models predict 0 K electronic adsorption energies, not dH at 298 K, and give no dS.
- **Error against reality is larger:** DFT-versus-experiment error for chemisorption is not quantified in this paper and adds to the 0.061 eV. These points strengthen the qualitative conclusion, but it rests on the OptiLex Langmuir assumptions, not on anything the paper states.

items.name: Oxidation window at DAC conditions: 400 ppm CO2 in air accelerates PEI autoxidation at 55-90 C (the dominant, unmitigated failure mode)
items.mechanism: Radical autoxidation of the aminopolymer (alkyl/peroxyl radicals, hydroperoxide decomposition, C-N and C-C scission to carbonyl/imine/amide plus NH3 and volatile fragments). Chemisorbed CO2 (carbamic acid) acid-catalyses the C-N cleavage steps, while heavy CO2 loading (>=1% CO2) stiffens the polymer and slows radical propagation, so the CO2 effect is non-monotonic. Sorbed water raises chain mobility and O2 access on hydrophilic alumina supports.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Li et al., JACS 2024: branched PEI on gamma-Al2O3, dry 0.04/1/5% CO2 in air, 18 h, 30-150 C, TGA + in-situ IR. Guta et al., ACS AMI 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.3c08140): 45 wt% PEI/Al2O3, fresh capacity 1.34 mmol/g, 70 C, dry and humid 0.04% CO2-air, continuous and 30-cycle TGA tests.
items.regeneration: Desorption itself (N2 or vacuum, low O2) is not where the damage occurs in these tests; the damaging step is air contact while the bed is still warm (cool-down from 70 C to 30 C followed by 2 h adsorption).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Dry 0.04% CO2-air, 18 h: about 2% capacity loss at 55 C but 15% at 60 C (sharp onset, not Arrhenius: my two-point fit gives an unphysical 379 kJ/mol). Below about 80 C, 0.04% CO2 degrades faster than 1% or 5% CO2; trend reverses above about 90 C. At 70 C continuous 0.04% CO2-air: 17% loss after 3 h, 80% after 7 days, versus 2-3% under 0.04% CO2 in N2. Cyclic (30 cycles): 23-29% loss dry, 48-52% humid, i.e. roughly 1-2.4% per cycle for an unprotected sorbent, about 1000x faster than a commercial lifetime allows. Confound: unprotected low-MW PEI on alumina, long 2 h cycles with warm air exposure; engineered sorbents and plants do far better (see pilot items).
items.trl_and_scale: mg-scale TGA, TRL 2-3 mechanism work (Georgia Tech / LLNL), 2023-2024.
items.bottleneck: Every temperature-swing cycle crosses the 55-90 C window twice; any O2 present while the bed is above about 55 C costs capacity. Flue-gas stability data (high CO2 protects) and classic dry CO2-free tests do not transfer to DAC.
items.cost: Converted with the OptiLex verifier: 1-2.4%/cycle fade would cost more than $5,000/t in sorbent alone at $20/kg, so unprotected PEI is not viable; the value is in closing the window, not in the baseline.

items.name: Pilot durability data: Climeworks + Svante structured amine laminates, >10,000 field cycles in California (DOE DE-FE0031959)
items.mechanism: Vacuum-temperature swing with steam on amine-coated laminate beds (Gen2 humid-air sorbent, Gen3 weather-stable sorbent). Post-test autopsy by TGA, FTIR and SEM assigned the capacity loss to amine oxidation, larger on the evacuation side of the bed than on the steam-inlet side, with no loss of active material and intact mechanics.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Real outdoor air, Kiewit site California, June 2022-July 2023. Equilibrium cyclic capacity 0.8-1 (Gen2) and 1.1-1.6 (Gen3) mol CO2/kg laminate; fast-cycle capacity 0.5-0.7 and 0.8-1.0; uptake rate 0.05-0.07 and 0.08-0.1 mol/kg/min; productivity above 20 and 30 t CO2 per m2 frontal area per year; pressure drop 800-1000 Pa and 400-700 Pa.
items.regeneration: Steam-assisted vacuum-temperature swing (Climeworks process); cycles shortened for the life tests to accumulate cycle count.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Gen2: about 3,100 life-test cycles (Nov 2022-Feb 2023), 3,400 total; target below 10% cyclic capacity loss per roughly one year-equivalent was met only for certain climatic conditions. Gen3: about 5,200 cycles (Jan-Jul 2023); target below 5% per year was shown only in very short cycles. Exact percent losses are not published. Implied budget: 10% per 3,000 cycles is 3.5e-3 %/cycle; 5% is 1.7e-3 %/cycle (my conversion).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4 to 5, bench/pilot beds (36 cm class), 2020-2023; the laminate route is the basis of Climeworks' later structured-sorbent generation.
items.bottleneck: Even the leading commercial developer's best sorbent missed its 5%/year target except in short cycles; damage is spatially localised (evacuation side), pointing to residual or leaked O2 meeting hot sorbent rather than to bulk chemistry alone.
items.cost: Project TEA: about 2x lower cost than packed-bed reference at 1.3 Mt/yr and a projection of about $200/t pipeline-ready CO2 at 1 Gt/yr cumulative deployment (company-led projection, not measured).

items.name: Operating plants: Orca and Mammoth capture far below nameplate; one public data point on filter ageing
items.mechanism: Amine-functionalised filter beds in temperature-vacuum swing (Climeworks Gen 1/2 packed filters). Underperformance has mixed causes: mechanical problems, ice and snow, partial build-out, and filter degradation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Iceland, geothermal heat and power. Orca: design removal 3,000 t/yr (4,000 t/yr gross nameplate), of which 2,500 t/yr was achievable with the installed filter; best weekly run rate equivalent to 1,900 t/yr with a two-year-old filter; actual removal 487 t (2022) and about 1,000 t (2023). Measured plant energy from Climeworks data (Deutz and Bardow 2021, 4 kt/yr scale): 700 kWh electricity plus 11.9 GJ heat per tonne; target 500 kWh plus 5.4 GJ.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 1,900 versus 2,500 t/yr bounds two-year filter fade at 24% or less (weather and mechanics are confounded in that number). If Orca runs about 3,000 cycles/yr this is at most about 4.6e-3 %/cycle (my conversion, cycle count assumed). Filters therefore last at least 2 years in gentle, slow-cycle service.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8-9; Orca 4 kt/yr (2021), Mammoth 36 kt/yr nameplate (start May 2024, 12 of 72 collector units installed at launch). Mammoth captured 105 t in its first 10 months per Heimildin (15 May 2025, registry and accounts data, https://heimildin.is/grein/24581/) or 750 t per SwissInfo (22 May 2025); the two figures conflict and neither is audited here. Stratos (500 kt/yr liquid-solvent plant) was in wet commissioning in Aug 2025; I found no measured 2026 output.
items.bottleneck: Net delivery of 10-25% of nameplate; energy 5,000-6,000 kWh/t reported by Heimildin; current cost above roughly $900-1,000/t against a company target moved from $100 to about $300/t (SwissInfo).
items.cost: More than three times the $300/t target per SwissInfo (journalistic source); 106 of 498 staff cut in May 2025.

items.name: 6,500-cycle bench test of a tethered-amine coated heat-exchanger contactor (TDA Research / GE Vernova, DOE DE-FE0032261, report April 2026)
items.mechanism: Covalently tethered amine sorbent (TDA SSSA-7A) coated with a binder on fin-tube heat exchangers; indirect water heating and cooling under vacuum, so the sorbent never sees hot air.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 500 ppm CO2, 40-50% RH lab air, 20 C, 300 SLPM; 10-minute cycles (5 min adsorb with 15 C water, 5 min regenerate). Capacity only about 0.8 wt% of coating (about 0.18 mol/kg) at 19% capture efficiency; capacity rises about 50% at 70-80% RH.
items.regeneration: Vacuum at 1 psia with 90-100 C water in the tubes; 30 s vacuum purge before heating.
items.stability_and_lifetime: About 11% capacity loss over the first 5,000 cycles (2.2% per 1,000 cycles, 2.3e-3 %/cycle), 6,500 cycles total; milestone was below 5% per 1,000 cycles. Caveat: 5,000 ten-minute cycles is only about 35 days, so calendar ageing is not sampled. A separate bench rig lost performance after about 300 cycles because of steam condensation, not sorbent decay.
items.trl_and_scale: Sub-bench, 0.5-3 g CO2/h; bench 10-50 g/h; TRL 4; 2023-2025.
items.bottleneck: Extrapolation gap: the report's TEA and LCA assume a 4-year sorbent life, but its own measured fade leaves about 1% of capacity after 4 years of 10-minute cycles, or about 35% at 44-minute cycles (my calculation). Low working capacity per kg coating.
items.cost: Modelled $251/t (2019 USD, excluding transport and storage), $153/t in the optimistic case with $15/kg sorbent, $30/MWh, 90% capacity factor (simulation, NETL method).

items.name: What lifetime is worth: review claim plus OptiLex conversion of measured fade rates into $/t
items.mechanism: Sorbent replacement cost per tonne = price / (working capacity x cycles x 44 g/mol); fading capacity also inflates the capital charge per tonne because the same hardware captures less. Optimal replacement time balances the two.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Varni et al., Chem 2026 (LLNL, NREL, Georgia Tech), citing Holmes et al., Energy Environ. Sci. 2024: raising the optimal replacement interval from 3 months (their present state of the art for PEI-type sorbents) to 1 year would cut the levelized cost of net removal by more than 60%. I could not open the Holmes paper itself (publisher blocked); the review shares an author with it.
items.stability_and_lifetime: OptiLex calculation (reference amine cycle, 1.04 mol/kg, 30-minute cycles, capital $274/t with 60% scaling with productivity, heat $5.6/GJ): degradation penalty versus an ideal non-fading free sorbent is $65/t at 2.3e-3 %/cycle (TDA measured), $82/t at 3.5e-3 (Climeworks Gen2 target), $101/t at 5.1e-3 (LLNL TEA assumption), all at $20/kg; $109-175/t at $50/kg. Reaching 1.1e-3 %/cycle (20% fade at 20,000 cycles) leaves $43/t; 2.2e-4 %/cycle leaves $19/t.
items.bottleneck: State-of-the-art engineered sorbents sit 2-5x above the fade rate needed; the prize for closing that gap is roughly $25-60/t at $20/kg, larger for expensive sorbents (MOFs, structured laminates). Returns diminish below about 1e-3 %/cycle.
items.cost: Scripts: scratchpad/sorbent/deg_lifetime_econ.py and deg_tornado.py. Model is idealised (Langmuir site, fixed capital split), so treat deltas as ranking, not forecasts.

items.name: Which property moves cost most: NETL case studies (2022, Rev. 1 2025) and OptiLex one-at-a-time sensitivity
items.mechanism: Techno-economic models of a 100,000 t/yr net solid-sorbent plant with natural-gas CHP (NETL) and a simple levelized-cost model built on the OptiLex TVSA verifier.
items.uptake_and_conditions: NETL Rev. 1 Case 1-NG base: $1,028/t net, sorbent $9.27/kg, 1-year life, working capacity 0.8 mol/kg, capture fraction 0.6, CO2 desorption energy 2 GJ/t, pressure drop 895 Pa.
items.stability_and_lifetime: NETL Rev. 1: life 1 yr to 0.25 yr is +10% ($1,138/t); to 2 yr is -2%. Price $148/kg is +58% ($1,623/t). Working capacity 0.8 to 2 mol/kg is -7%; to 0.2 is +70%. Capture fraction 0.6 to 0.2 is +65%. Pressure drop to 3,200 Pa is +36%. Desorption energy 2 to 0.3 GJ/t is about -1%; to 12 GJ/t is +53%. Best-to-worst combined range $630 to above $15,800/t. NETL 2022: $702/t at $0.20/kg rises to $1,030/t at $15/kg and $2,910/t at $100/kg with 0.5-year life (about 22 kg sorbent consumed per tonne CO2).
items.bottleneck: With a cheap sorbent, lifetime is the weakest lever and capital dominates; lifetime becomes a first-order lever only when price/(capacity x cycles) is large. This is consistent with, not opposed to, the >60% claim above: the two studies assume very different sorbent costs and fade rates.
items.cost: OptiLex tornado from a $417/t base: 2x working capacity -$139/t; 2x faster cycle -$107 to -$132/t; 5x lower fade -$59/t; price $20 to $5/kg -$54/t; waste heat at $2/GJ -$22/t; no co-desorbed water -$11/t; 50% sensible-heat recovery -$7/t; binding enthalpy weakened from -70 to -65 kJ/mol +$570/t (capacity collapses). Heat levers grow about 3x if heat is bought as resistive electricity.
items.trl_and_scale: Paper studies; 100 kt/yr design basis.

items.name: Trace Cu and Fe at ppm level catalyse the radical initiation step
items.mechanism: Cu(II)/Cu(I) and Fe(III)/Fe(II) couples run Fenton-type cycles that decompose hydroperoxides and lower the barrier for radical initiation; Ni(II) is kinetically sluggish and has little effect.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Kuspangaliyeva, Lively, Jones, Environ. Sci. Technol. 2026: PEI in SBA-15 silica doped at PEI:metal molar ratios 1:1 to 100,000:1; aged in dry air (21% O2), 120 C, 4.5 h (also 80 and 160 C). Idealised: dry, CO2-free, hot.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Capacity retained after ageing: 72% for metal-free control; 63% with about 4 ppm Cu (10,000:1); 25-50% at 1,000:1 Cu or Fe. Commercial PEI is reported to carry 7-160 ppm Fe and up to 47 ppm Cu; commercial alumina up to 12 ppm Fe; boiler steam and mineral dust add more in service. Min et al., Nat. Commun. 2018 (flue-gas mix 3% O2, 15% CO2, 10% H2O, 110 C, 30 days): deactivation constant 0.123 per day for PEI/SiO2, about half that with either epoxybutane functionalisation or 2 wt% trisodium phosphate chelator alone, and 0.00258 per day with both (about 50x slower; 91.5% capacity retained versus total loss).
items.bottleneck: Chelators added at synthesis cannot bind metals that arrive later with steam or dust. The 50x result was obtained at 15% CO2, where CO2 protects; it has not been shown at 400 ppm CO2 in 21% O2.
items.regeneration: Steam regeneration is itself a metal source (entrained Cu, Fe, Zn from boilers).
items.trl_and_scale: Powder, mg to g scale, TRL 2-3.
items.cost: Chelator loading below 2 wt% had no measurable capacity penalty in Min et al.; cost impact negligible if it transfers.

items.name: Radical-trapping and hydroperoxide-decomposing additives
items.mechanism: Diarylamine radical traps (BDDPA) donate N-H hydrogen to peroxyl radicals and regenerate; hindered-amine stabilisers work through nitroxide (Denisov) cycling; thioether and disulfide additives decompose hydroperoxides. Phenols, quinones and ascorbic acid can instead accelerate amine oxidation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Guta et al., Energy Fuels 2025 (Georgia Tech / LLNL): 35 wt% PEI on gamma-Al2O3 with 2 mol% additive; aged 4.5 h at 120 C dry CO2-free air, plus humid (about 43% RH) and 0.04% CO2-air runs at 120 and 70 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Deactivation after 4.5 h at 120 C dry air: about 1% with BDDPA, 6% BTBPA, 8% BTMPS (hindered amine), 30% spin trap TTBNB, 35% unprotected. At 70 C in dry 0.04% CO2-air: near 0% with BDDPA versus about 15% unprotected. After 18 h at 120 C BDDPA still lost about half; in humid 0.04% CO2-air at 70 C over longer exposure radical formation overwhelmed it. 2 mol% was the optimum; 1 or 4 mol% did no better. Separately (Vu et al. 2019, via the Varni review): TEPA/SiO2 stored 15 months at room temperature kept 52% of capacity unprotected, 69-84% with sulfur additives, under 48% with BHT (capacity measured at 40 C in pure CO2, an idealised readout).
items.bottleneck: Additives are consumed, block some amine sites, and no test exceeds tens of hours or reports thousands of cycles; humidity plus 400 ppm CO2 erodes the benefit.
items.trl_and_scale: Powder, TRL 2-3.
items.cost: Not quantified; additive must be co-located with the polymer and cannot be topped up in service.

items.name: Backbone chemistry: propylene spacers, epoxide (hydroxyalkyl) functionalisation, amine type
items.mechanism: Three-carbon spacers (PPI) raise the barrier for bimolecular hydroperoxide decomposition by about 40 kJ/mol versus two-carbon analogues (computed). Epoxide ring-opening adds beta-hydroxyl groups that hydrogen-bond, cut chain mobility and suppress urea formation. Secondary amines are the least oxidation-stable class, primary and tertiary more stable.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Accelerated tests in dry air or 17-20% O2 at 110-120 C for 3-24 h on silica or alumina powders; uptake afterwards usually at 400 ppm CO2, 30-35 C.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Linear PEI on SBA-15 lost up to 82% of capacity after 24 h in air at 110 C versus up to 35% for linear PPI (Pang 2018). After 20% O2 at 120 C for 24 h, PEI/SiO2 kept 19% of working capacity versus 80-81% for epoxybutane-PEI (Min/Choi). Long-alkyl epoxide and glycidyl-ether PEIs lost under 15% amine efficiency in dry and humid oxidation versus 25-40% for PEI (Shaikh 2024). A 2025 preprint reports a solid amine network keeping over 75% after 7 days at 85 C versus over 50% loss for impregnated sorbents and commercial resins (unreviewed). Epoxide-modified DETA kept 97.8% after 24 h at 60 C in air and cycled 50 times in ambient air (ACS AMI 2026, abstract only).
items.regeneration: Epoxybutane-PEI has a lower calorimetric heat of adsorption (66.2 versus 80.5 kJ/mol, Min 2018, measured at flue-gas CO2 pressure).
items.bottleneck: Stability is bought with binding strength and amine density: in the OptiLex single-site model, -66 kJ/mol gives only 29% site filling at 420 ppm and 25 C versus 65% at -70 and 99% at -80. PPI is not a commodity polymer. No backbone variant has a published multi-thousand-cycle DAC dataset.
items.trl_and_scale: Powder, TRL 2-4; PEI still dominates deployed sorbents.
items.cost: Not quantified in sources; epoxide modification uses commodity reagents, PPI needs new monomer supply.

items.name: Non-oxidative losses: urea formation, evaporation and leaching, support attack
items.mechanism: Dry hot CO2 dehydrates carbamate to urea cross-links (irreversible when dry, suppressed or reversed by water vapour or steam). Low-MW amines evaporate at regeneration temperature and can leach during steam contact or condensation. Steam restructures some silica and alumina supports. Ester-containing polymer supports are aminolysed by PEI.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Thakkar et al., ACS Omega 2024 (LANL): PEI-silica pellets, about 40 wt% PEI, 1 mmol/g at 420 ppm; continuous exposure 24-100 h at 80/100/120 C in air, N2, dry CO2 or CO2 at 75% RH.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Capacity loss, 24 h in 21% O2: 33% (80 C), 86% (100 C), 92% (120 C). 100 h in N2: 21%, 21%, 26% (evaporation). 100 h dry CO2: 16%, 38%, 57% (urea). 100 h CO2 at 75% RH: 20%, 8%, 19%. Recommended regeneration window 80-100 C. Fibre sorbents (Wang et al., IECR 2025, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.5c00462): cellulose-acetate/silica/PEI lost 40-60% of working capacity in 20 cycles (400 ppm CO2, 35-40% RH, 90 C regeneration) through aminolysis of acetate esters; KOH-hydrolysed fibres kept over 85%, poly(ether sulfone) fibres 97%. Hot-water-cycled hollow fibres lost about 10% productivity in 10 cycles (IECR 2026). Molecular sorbents fare worse: K-sarcosine -14.5% and K-glycine -24.9% in 10 cycles, bis-iminoguanidines 26-32% loss in 3-10 cycles; Lewatit, PEI/silica and porous polyvinylamine under 1% over 20 cycles (NETL TCF report, Jan 2026).
items.regeneration: Steam or humid purge protects against urea but raises leaching and support-hydrolysis risk; direct liquid-water heating risks condensation-driven amine redistribution.
items.bottleneck: These modes are considered manageable (higher MW, tethering, hydroxyl groups, humid regeneration); the pilot autopsy found no loss of active material. The practical risk is choosing a support or binder that reacts with amines.
items.trl_and_scale: Pellets, fibres and modules at lab scale, TRL 3-4.

items.name: Calendar ageing at adsorption and storage temperature
items.mechanism: Slow oxidation plus non-oxidative thermal rearrangement at ambient to 40 C; a CO2-saturated polymer is protected.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Guta et al., ACS Omega 2026: 800 g/mol branched PEI on gamma-Al2O3 at 70% and 100% pore fill, stored in sealed vials under N2, O2, Ar, 0.04% CO2 in N2, pure CO2 or ambient air at -4, 23 and 40 C for up to 12 months; capacity by TGA. Static storage, not cycling.
items.stability_and_lifetime: At 23 C and -4 C: under 13% loss over 12 and 5 months in air or Ar. At 40 C: 62-66% loss in 2 months under N2 or ambient air, similar under pure O2 and N2 at 4 months (so not purely oxidative), but no measurable loss in 2 months under pure CO2. Earlier reports cited there: TEPA/SiO2 -48% in 15 months in room air; PEI and TEPA on alumina -15 to -20% in 6 months; linear PPI/SBA-15 about -20% in 1.5-2 years; an in-situ polymerised linear PEI in silica foam about -12% in 3 years.
items.bottleneck: A time-based loss term exists independently of cycling, so faster cycling does not automatically consume calendar life, and hot-climate siting or idle periods at 40 C may dominate. Which share of plant fade is per-cycle versus per-hour is unknown.
items.regeneration: Not applicable (storage).
items.trl_and_scale: Powder vials, TRL 2-3.
items.cost: A CO2 blanket during idle periods and storage is nearly free if it transfers to structured sorbents.

items.name: Validation gap: accelerated-ageing protocols are unvalidated and long-run field degradation data are not public
items.mechanism: Lifetimes are extrapolated from hours-long tests in hot dry air assuming Arrhenius behaviour, although CO2 and water effects are non-monotonic and several mechanisms run in parallel.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Not applicable (methods gap).
items.stability_and_lifetime: The 2025 Energy Environ. Sci. DACCS review states there is "no data in literature on how any DAC materials degrade" over extended pilot or commercial operation, and that no study apportions degradation among adsorption, regeneration and air re-exposure phases; moisture-swing sorbents have stability data for about 10 cycles only. The 2026 Chem review calls oxidative degradation an irreversible, unmitigated risk and asks for protocols that reproduce process-relevant CO2, water and O2 activities. The NETL-led multi-lab project to validate ageing protocols with Avnos and Oxy's DAC unit (2025) was cancelled before finishing its first budget period; only one material (Lewatit) completed a run beyond 500 cycles; most of eight surveyed DAC companies rated a validated protocol as essential. The Aircapture field campaign at the National Carbon Capture Center logged over 3,300 operating hours (2020-2024, TRL 5) but the public final report gives no degradation numbers.
items.bottleneck: Typical papers report 10-100 cycles against a need of 20,000 or more; resolving 1e-3 %/cycle requires detecting a 0.1% capacity change over 100 cycles, below normal TGA and weather noise.
items.trl_and_scale: Field data exist inside companies (Climeworks, Svante, Aircapture) but are not published.
items.cost: Lifetime uncertainty propagates directly into TEAs: assumed sorbent lives range from 0.25 to 5 years and prices from $1.95 to about $1,000/kg (NETL literature survey).

items.name: Trace atmospheric oxidants: ozone and NOx
items.mechanism: Ozone abstracts hydrogen from amine and methyl groups and adds to linker double bonds; exposure forms nitro species and lowers amine electron donation to MOF metal sites.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Jamdade, Cai, Sholl, J. Phys. Chem. C 2025: DFT kinetics for diamine-appended Mg2(dobpdc) at 25 C and about 10 ppb ozone. Experimental follow-up (Zorrilla-Valtierra et al., IECR 2026, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.6c01324): amine-grafted Mg2(dobpdc) and PEI in MIL-101(Cr) exposed 8 h to 50 ppm O3 with NOx in 2% O2 (equivalent to about 57 ppb-years), then 400 ppm CO2 uptake.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Computed upper bound 0.0002% amine loss per cycle, about 8% cumulative over 40,000 cycles. Experiment: all composites lost CO2 capacity after the 57 ppb-year dose (percentages only in figures); cooperative step pressure shifted for the men and dmen variants.
items.bottleneck: Second-order next to O2 autoxidation today (roughly 10x smaller than the best measured total fade), but it sets a floor of order 2e-4 %/cycle that no antioxidant aimed at O2 chemistry removes. SO2 and NO2 bind irreversibly at ppm level, relevant near geothermal sites.
items.trl_and_scale: Computation plus mg-scale exposure tests, TRL 2.

items.name: Cost targets versus modelled and reported costs
items.mechanism: Targets: DOE Carbon Negative Shot, under $100 per net tonne CO2 removed; Frontier buyers' criteria, a path to under $100/t, more than 0.5 Gt/yr and storage beyond 1,000 years.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Harmonised literature TEAs (Energy Environ. Sci. 2025 review, data from Young et al. 2023, 2024 USD, generic US site, nuclear power plus heat pump).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Not applicable.
items.cost: Solid-sorbent first-of-a-kind average $2,089/t gross captured with CAPEX 68% of cost; nth-of-a-kind at 1 Gt/yr deployed $288/t with CAPEX 24%. Liquid-solvent first-of-a-kind $462/t. Mineral looping $394 falling to $180/t. Most nth-of-a-kind points remain above the $100/t line. LLNL 2026 US siting study (Hunter-Sellars et al., https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c14628): $2,850/t net near-term to $250/t by 2050 at 0.5 Gt/yr, assuming 0.8 mol/kg, 20-minute cycles, 5.1e-3 %/cycle fade, 11.9 GJ/t steam learning to 7.0 GJ/t. Literature thermal energy for solid sorbents: 5-25 GJ/t, median 9, with no downward trend over time; electricity median 0.8 GJ/t.
items.bottleneck: Capital per tonne, set by productivity (capacity x cycle rate x uptime), is the main term; sorbent durability is necessary but cannot by itself reach $100/t.
items.trl_and_scale: Targets and paper studies. Frontier criteria read from frontierclimate.com on 2026-10-05; DOE target wording taken from DOE-funded project reports because the energy.gov Carbon Negative Shot page returned 404 on that date.

items.name: Durability evidence for alternative regeneration routes is thin
items.mechanism: Electric (Joule) swing on grafted-amine conductive aerogels, ambient-temperature regeneration of epoxide-modified small amines, moisture swing on quaternary-ammonium resins: all avoid or shorten the hot-air window, which should in principle slow autoxidation.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Nat. Commun. 2026 electric-swing sorbent: adsorption at 25 C and 80% RH, electrothermal desorption; claimed 3.4 GJ/t regeneration energy.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 3.7% uptake loss by cycle 100, then flat to 500 cycles, amine loading change under 2%. Epoxide-DETA: 50 ambient-air cycles. Moisture-swing sorbents: about 10 cycles in the literature per the 2025 review.
items.cost: Authors' own TEA: variable operating cost $48-62/t (their model for a 4,000 t/yr unit; not a full levelized cost and not independently checked).
items.bottleneck: 500 cycles is about 2.5% of a 20,000-cycle life; none of these routes has oxidation data under 400 ppm CO2, humidity and thousands of cycles.
items.trl_and_scale: Gram-scale lab, TRL 3.

bottlenecks: Fade-rate gap: the best measured multi-thousand-cycle results for engineered amine sorbents are about 2e-3 to 5e-3 % capacity loss per cycle (TDA/GE 11% over 5,000 cycles at 500 ppm CO2, 40% RH; Climeworks/Svante roughly 10% per 3,000-cycle year-equivalent, Gen3 5%/year target met only in very short cycles; Orca two-year filter at most 24% down). A 20,000-cycle life at 20% fade needs 1.1e-3 %/cycle or less; 100,000 cycles needs 2.2e-4. Gap: 2-5x for engineered sorbents, about 1000x for unprotected lab PEI (1-2.4 %/cycle in humid 400 ppm CO2 cyclic tests).

Cost of that gap (OptiLex model, 1.04 mol/kg, 30-minute cycles): degradation adds $65-100/t at $20/kg sorbent and $110-175/t at $50/kg at today's fade rates, i.e. about the size of the whole $100/t target. Closing to 1.1e-3 %/cycle leaves about $43/t; below that the return is under $25/t.

Capital dominates: first-of-a-kind solid-sorbent DAC averages $2,089/t with 68% CAPEX (2025 review); NETL 2025 base case $1,028/t. In the OptiLex sensitivity, doubling working capacity (-$139/t) or halving cycle time (-$107 to -$132/t) beats a 5x durability gain (-$59/t) or a 4x cheaper sorbent (-$54/t); heat levers are worth $7-22/t at low-grade heat prices. NETL finds lifetime the weakest lever at $9/kg sorbent (+10% for 1 yr to 0.25 yr) but price a strong one (+58% at $148/kg).

Thermal window: oxidation in 400 ppm CO2 air switches on between 55 and 60 C (2% versus 15% loss in 18 h), while regeneration runs at 80-120 C, so every cycle passes through the damaging range; humidity roughly doubles cyclic loss on alumina-supported PEI.

Binding-strength coupling: stabilising modifications lower binding enthalpy (epoxybutane-PEI 66 versus 80.5 kJ/mol); in the OptiLex model a 5 kJ/mol weakening from -70 cuts working capacity from 1.04 to 0.34 mol/kg and adds about $570/t, far more than durability saves.

Catalytic impurities: about 4 ppm Cu lowers retained capacity from 72% to 63% in a 4.5 h, 120 C air test; commercial PEI carries 7-160 ppm Fe and up to 47 ppm Cu, and steam and dust add metals during service where synthesis-stage chelators cannot reach them.

Measurement and validation: published tests run 10-500 cycles against 20,000+ needed; accelerated protocols are unvalidated; the one multi-lab validation project was cancelled in December 2025; company field data are unpublished.

Plant reality: Orca has delivered about 1,000 t/yr at best against 3,000-4,000 t/yr; Mammoth reported 105-750 t in its first ten months against a 36,000 t/yr nameplate with one sixth of collectors installed; cost above about $900-1,000/t.
open_problems: Apportion the damage by cycle phase. No published study separates fade into adsorption-phase (ambient, long), hot-regeneration (low O2) and warm air re-entry contributions. A kinetic model integrating measured rate data (Li 2024, Guta 2023, storage data at 23 and 40 C) over a real cycle temperature and gas profile is computable now and would say whether to fix the material or the process. The pilot autopsy (damage concentrated on the evacuation side) is a spatial clue to test against.

Import battery-style lifetime metrology. Batteries separate calendar from cycle ageing and detect ppm-per-cycle losses with high-precision coulometry. Analogue to test: per-cycle quantification of oxidation off-gases (NH3, formamide, acetamide; PTR-MS has already detected them) as a rate signal that resolves 1e-3 %/cycle within about 100 cycles instead of thousands. Needs prior-art search and a mass-balance check that NH3 release is stoichiometric with site loss.

Import polyolefin stabiliser packages. Polymer practice combines a regenerating radical trap, a hydroperoxide decomposer and a metal deactivator; DAC studies have tested each alone (BDDPA, thioethers, phosphate chelator). Test the three-part package, tethered rather than blended, under humid 400 ppm CO2 air at 60-70 C in cyclic mode, tracking capacity penalty per mol% additive.

CO2-blanket or oxygen-exclusion cool-down. Storage under CO2 stops ageing at 40 C and at least 1% CO2 slows oxidation below 80 C, so cooling the bed below about 55 C before air entry, under product CO2, steam flash or vacuum, should remove most cyclic damage. The verifier can price the lost working capacity from CO2 re-adsorption during cool-down against the fade avoided; evaporative vacuum cooling is known art, so the novelty would be in the quantified trade-off and bed-end design.

Sacrificial or graded protection at the evacuation end. If oxidation is localised where residual O2 meets hot sorbent, a thin oxygen-scavenging or antioxidant-rich zone there (imported from oxygen-scavenger packaging and guard-bed practice in catalysis) may protect the whole bed at small capacity cost.

Refurbish instead of replace. If the structured support and contactor carry most of the $/kg and the amine little, in-place stripping and re-impregnation (imported from ex-situ catalyst regeneration) changes the economics from sorbent price to amine price. Needs a cost split of structured sorbents and a test of whether oxidised polymer can be washed out of mesopores.

Oxidation-proof binding sites that keep -70 to -75 kJ/mol. Design question for screening: amine environments without labile alpha C-H or with hydroxyl hydrogen bonding that do not drop below the OptiLex binding window; every candidate must be checked for site filling at 420 ppm with the verifier before stability is considered.

Per-cycle versus per-hour fade. Whether faster cycling (the largest cost lever) shortens calendar life depends on this split; no dataset reports the same sorbent at two cycle rates for equal elapsed time.
Metal ingress in service: measure Fe and Cu accumulation from steam and dust over months and test scavengers that work after deployment (steam-side polishing, renewable chelating layers).

A lifetime-normalised screening metric, kg CO2 delivered per dollar of sorbent over life (capacity x cycles x 0.044 / price), should replace capacity as the headline number; today's engineered sorbents are near 20 kg CO2 per dollar at $20/kg and 10,000 cycles, and under $10/t needs above 100.

Resins and non-PEI networks: degradation of benzylamine resins (Lewatit, Purolite) is barely studied although they are used commercially; oxidative deactivation of Lewatit begins above about 70 C in air.

key_claims.claim: Under DAC gas composition the damage window is warm air contact, not hot regeneration: for PEI on alumina in dry 0.04% CO2 air, 18 h causes about 2% capacity loss at 55 C but 15% at 60 C, and 400 ppm CO2 accelerates oxidation relative to 1-5% CO2 below about 80-90 C. Stability results from flue-gas mixtures or dry CO2-free accelerated tests therefore do not transfer to DAC, and cooling below about 55 C before admitting air is the highest-leverage protective step to test.

The best public multi-thousand-cycle measurement for an engineered amine DAC sorbent is about 11% capacity loss over 5,000 cycles (2.3e-3 %/cycle; 500 ppm CO2, 40% RH, 20 C, 90-100 C vacuum regeneration, TDA/GE 2026), and the Climeworks/Svante pilot autopsy attributes its loss to oxidation rather than amine loss. A 20,000-cycle life needs about 1.1e-3 %/cycle, so the remaining gap is 2-5x and is worth roughly $25-60/t at $20/kg sorbent in the OptiLex model, less than a doubling of capacity or cycle rate.

surprises: Ambient CO2 concentration is itself a pro-oxidant: 400 ppm CO2 speeds PEI oxidation at 55-80 C while 1% or more protects. Much of the older stability literature, including the widely cited 50x improvement from epoxide plus chelator, was measured at 15% CO2 and 3% O2 and has not been reproduced at 400 ppm CO2 in 21% O2.

Oxidation has a sharp onset rather than smooth Arrhenius behaviour: 2% loss at 55 C versus 15% at 60 C over 18 h. A two-point Arrhenius fit gives an unphysical 379 kJ/mol, which argues against extrapolating hot accelerated tests down to service temperature.

In the Climeworks/Svante pilot the damage was localised on the evacuation side of the bed and no amine had been lost, so the problem looks like a process-geometry interaction (residual O2 meeting hot sorbent) as much as a chemistry problem.

PEI/alumina stored at 40 C lost 62-66% of capacity in two months even under nitrogen, yet lost nothing under pure CO2. A non-oxidative thermal pathway exists at hot-climate adsorption temperature, and a CO2 blanket is a nearly free protective measure.

NETL's 2025 study ranks sorbent lifetime as its weakest lever (1 year to 3 months adds 10%) while the 2026 Chem review says 3 months to 1 year cuts net cost by over 60%. They are not in conflict: NETL assumes a $9/kg sorbent in a $1,028/t capital-heavy plant, the other a costlier, faster-fading PEI system. Lifetime matters in proportion to price divided by capacity times cycles.
TDA's own TEA assumes a 4-year sorbent life although its measured 2.2% per 1,000 cycles implies about 1% capacity left after 4 years of 10-minute cycles (about 35% at 44-minute cycles).

The LLNL 2026 siting study's Table 1 does not reproduce: 5.1e-3 %/cycle and a 30% fade limit give 6,993 cycles, not the stated 15,363; 15,363 cycles matches a life-averaged capacity of about 69% (end-of-life capacity about 46%).

The DOE-funded project to validate accelerated-ageing protocols with industry partners was cancelled in December 2025 before finishing its first phase, although nearly all surveyed DAC companies called such a protocol essential.

Secondary amines are the least oxidation-stable amine class, yet epoxide functionalisation, which converts primary into hydroxyl-bearing secondary amines, improves stability; hydrogen bonding and reduced chain mobility outweigh the amine-class effect.

Common antioxidants can backfire: phenols, quinones and ascorbic acid accelerate amine oxidation, and BHT-doped TEPA/silica retained less capacity after 15 months than the best sulfur-additive samples by more than 30 points.

Failure of early plants is not evidence against newer sorbents in general (Orca uses first-generation packed filters and suffered mechanical and icing problems), but the specific mechanism does carry over: the 2023 autopsy shows oxidation still limits the newer Gen2 and Gen3 laminates.

Process notes. The WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted (0 of 200 left), so discovery used Crossref, Europe PMC and OSTI APIs plus direct fetches; I fetched two general search-engine result pages (Bing, Brave) before deciding that sidestepped the budget and stopping. Coverage of 2026 plant news is therefore thin: I found no measured 2026 output for Stratos or Mammoth. Publisher sites (RSC, Nature, Climeworks) blocked fetching, so Holmes et al. 2024 is cited via the Varni review and Climeworks' Generation 3 marketing figures were not verified and are omitted. One mistake to flag: while probing for an open-access copy I sent the user's email address as the contact parameter in a single request to api.unpaywall.org (response discarded); I did not repeat it. Scripts and extracted texts are in climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/ (deg_lifetime_econ.py, deg_tornado.py, deg_ebpei_check.py, deg_*.txt); nothing in the repository was modified.

verifs.claim: Under DAC gas composition the damage window is warm air contact, not hot regeneration: for PEI on alumina in dry 0.04% CO2 air, 18 h causes about 2% capacity loss at 55 C but 15% at 60 C, and 400 ppm CO2 accelerates oxidation relative to 1-5% CO2 below about 80-90 C. Stability results from flue-gas mixtures or dry CO2-free accelerated tests therefore do not transfer to DAC, and cooling below about 55 C before admitting air is the highest-leverage protective step to test.
verifs.corrected_claim: Measured (Li, Guta et al., JACS 2024, 146, 28201; doi 10.1021/jacs.4c08126): for 45 wt% branched PEI (800 g/mol) on mesoporous gamma-Al2O3, one continuous 18 h isothermal exposure to dry 0.04% CO2 in air (21% O2) in a TGA (~29 mg sample) caused about 2% loss of CO2 capacity at 55 C versus 15% at 60 C (capacity measured afterwards at 400 ppm CO2, 30 C, dry). At 60 C, oxidation products appeared in in-situ IR only after about 180-200 min. Deactivation in 0.04% CO2-air was consistently higher than in 1% or 5% CO2-air below 80 C (abstract: below 90 C); the order reverses above about 90 C versus 1% CO2 and above about 100 C versus 5% CO2. CO2 at any tested level (up to 5%) accelerated deactivation relative to CO2-free air at all temperatures. So flue-gas-mixture results (which the authors say "do not directly translate to DAC conditions") and dry CO2-free air tests should not be assumed to transfer to DAC; CO2-free tests understate oxidation for this sorbent. The paper does NOT show that the damage window is "warm air contact, not hot regeneration", and it does not recommend cooling below 55 C before admitting air. Those are inferences by the claim's author. Keeping this sorbent at or below about 55 C whenever it contacts air is a reasonable hypothesis to test, not a finding, and nothing in the paper ranks it as the highest-leverage step.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the full text via Europe PMC (the PMC page itself was behind a CAPTCHA). The figures were not viewable, so I have no values beyond those stated in the text.

- **Numbers confirmed.** The 2% at 55 C, 15% at 60 C, 18 h, dry 0.04% CO2-air and the below-80/90 C ordering are all stated in the text and are experimental (TGA capacity plus in-situ ATR-IR). The mechanism (acid-catalysed C-N cleavage versus reduced chain mobility) comes from metadynamics and ML-MD simulation, supported by 1H relaxometry.
- **"Not hot regeneration" is unsupported.** The paper only exposed sorbent to 21% O2 air at 30-150 C; it never tested regeneration atmospheres (vacuum, steam, low or ppm O2). Deactivation in 0.04% CO2-air keeps rising overall with temperature, with a local maximum at 80 C and a local minimum at 100 C. The introduction cites a separate study on a benzylamine sorbent where ppm O2 during regeneration did more damage than high O2 at 56-70 C, which cuts against the framing.
- **The 55 C threshold is protocol-specific.** It comes from one 18 h continuous exposure of fresh sorbent, not from cycling. Because onset at 60 C took about 3 h, "safe at 55 C for 18 h" does not establish safety over thousands of hours of cumulative air contact, nor does it show that brief warm-air contact during cooldown is damaging.
- **All tests were dry.** Real DAC air is humid. The paper cites a prior report that humidity accelerates bPEI oxidation, and its own simulation finds water lowers the C-N cleavage barrier by 8 kJ/mol. The paper's dry results therefore also do not transfer directly to field DAC, the same limitation the claim assigns to other tests.
- **Single sorbent, milligram scale.** One PEI molecular weight, one loading (about 100% pore fill), one support. The authors note that support chemistry (their alumina versus SBA-15 silica) and O2 partial pressure change the CO2 effect. Thresholds should not be generalised to other amines, supports, MOFs or structured contactors.
- **The authors' own mitigation suggestions are material-side.** They propose functional groups, additives or supports that reduce side-chain mobility or neutralise acids. Process implications are mentioned only generically.

verifs.claim: The best public multi-thousand-cycle measurement for an engineered amine DAC sorbent is about 11% capacity loss over 5,000 cycles (2.3e-3 %/cycle; 500 ppm CO2, 40% RH, 20 C, 90-100 C vacuum regeneration, TDA/GE 2026), and the Climeworks/Svante pilot autopsy attributes its loss to oxidation rather than amine loss. A 20,000-cycle life needs about 1.1e-3 %/cycle, so the remaining gap is 2-5x and is worth roughly $25-60/t at $20/kg sorbent in the OptiLex model, less than a doubling of capacity or cycle rate.
verifs.corrected_claim: A quantified public multi-thousand-cycle measurement for an engineered amine DAC sorbent (TDA Research / GE Vernova final report DOE DE-FE0032261, OSTI 3029720, April 2026) gives an estimated ~11% working-capacity loss over the first 5,000 cycles, which the report states as ~2.2% per 1,000 cycles (2.2e-3 %/cycle linear; 2.3e-3 if compounded). It is measured, not simulated, but under accelerated and benign conditions: sub-bench scale (four coated fin contactors, ~3 g CO2/h), 10-minute cycles (5 min adsorb / 5 min regen, so 5,000 cycles is only ~35 days on stream), compressed air at 500 ppmv CO2 and 40% RH (20 C, 15 C coolant), regeneration at 1 psia with 90-100 C water, and a working capacity of only ~0.8 wt% (~0.18 mol/kg coating). Whether it is the "best public" result cannot be established. The oxidation finding comes from a different source, the Electricore/Climeworks/Svante final report (DE-FE0031959, OSTI 2267573, Dec 2023): autopsies after ~3,400 (Gen2) and ~5,200 (Gen3) cycles on a 30 kg/day outdoor field unit attributed capacity loss to oxidation by FTIR, and inferred from SEM images only that it was not loss of active material; no capacity-loss percentage is published. The 1.1e-3 %/cycle target for 20,000 cycles holds only for an 80%-capacity end-of-life criterion, giving a ~2x gap (about 4.4x for a 90% criterion). In the repo model (climate/sorbent.py, $20/kg, 1.04 mol/kg working capacity) a 2x gap is worth ~$24/t (about $46/t at ~9,600 cycles versus $22/t at 20,000) and a 5x gap ~$87/t, so "$25-60/t" matches a 2-3.8x gap, not 2-5x. This dollar figure is a model output, not a measurement, and it assumes a working capacity ~6x higher than the one in the TDA durability test.
verifs.caveats:
Primary sources read in full text: OSTI 3029720 (PDF, 27 pp) and OSTI 2267573. Web search budget was exhausted, so the "best public" superlative was not checked against the wider literature.

What is confirmed (OSTI 3029720, Task 6.1, Fig. 12):
- "around 11% over the initial 5,000 cycles ... ~2.2% capacity fade over 1,000 cycles"; the test ran to 6,500 cycles with capacity above 0.7 wt%.
- Conditions: 500 ppmv CO2, 40% RH (20 C), 300 SLPM, regeneration at 1 psia with 90 C water (baseline section says 100 C).
- Sorbent: TDA tethered-TEPA-on-silica (TDASSSA-7A) with GE binder, coated on aluminium fin heat exchangers. Measured, TRL 3 to 4.

Context that changes how the number can be used:
1. Cycle count is not lifetime. The cycles were 10 minutes, so 5,000 cycles is ~833 h (~35 days) and 20,000 such cycles is ~139 days. The same report's LCA assumes a 4-year sorbent life. If oxidation depends on time at temperature rather than cycle count, the per-cycle rate does not transfer to a commercial cycle, and the real gap could be far larger than 2-5x.
2. The 11% is the report's own "estimated" trend from a noisy trace. Cycles ~800-1,500 were disturbed by a heat-exchanger fluid leak, and capacity recovered at ~1,600.
3. Benign air. The executive summary says the 5,000-cycle test ran on compressed air, not outdoor air; 500 ppm is above ambient and 40% RH is moderate. Regeneration was vacuum with hot water, not steam.
4. Capacity mismatch with the model. The test's working capacity was ~0.8 wt% (~0.18 mol/kg coating, 19% capture efficiency) against 1.04 mol/kg in the OptiLex reference cycle. At the tested capacity and fade, $20/kg sorbent costs on the order of $280/t at 80% end-of-life, not ~$46/t. The $25-60/t figure therefore depends on pairing a short-cycle fade rate with a full-swing capacity that the test did not demonstrate.
5. The bench-scale (10-50 g/h) GE test in the same report degraded after ~300 cycles, attributed to steam condensation rather than the sorbent, so multi-thousand-cycle durability is shown only at sub-bench scale.
6. Other long-cycle claims exist. The same report cites TDA's earlier Navy project as "stable sorbent operation for 10,000 cycles" (unquantified), and the Climeworks/Svante unit logged more than 10,000 cycles in total in real outdoor air with steam regeneration.
7. Climeworks/Svante autopsy: the cited URL does not contain it. The cycling there was also accelerated; the Gen3 target of under 5% loss in ~1 year was met "only in very short cycles"; capacity loss was higher on the evacuation side; the evidence against amine loss is SEM surface appearance only (condensate showed low ammonium/total N).
8. TDA's own TEA target for sorbent cost is $15/kg; the $20/kg and the comparison with doubling capacity or cycle rate are OptiLex model assumptions and were not verifiable against a primary source.

items.name: Proton-trap amine aerogel with Joule-heated electric swing (N5-dGA)
items.mechanism: Pentamine loaded on a defect-engineered conductive graphene aerogel. Point defects act as proton acceptors, so one amine binds one CO2 (instead of the usual 2:1), and the conductive support is heated directly by current. It does not weaken binding; it raises capacity so that sensible heat per tonne collapses.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 6.57 mmol/g from 400 ppm CO2 at 25 C, 80% RH, gas velocity 1 m/s; 2.93 mmol/g dry (0% RH). 12.6 mmol/g in pure CO2 at 66.6 wt% amine loading. Nat Commun 2026, milligram-to-gram samples.
items.regeneration: Joule heating to 80 C at 0.6 A; reported minimum heat duty 3.4 GJ/t CO2 (electrical, for 95% release); release 48% faster than conventional heating. OptiLex check: at 6.2 mol/kg working capacity sensible heat is only 0.30 GJ/t (vs 1.80 GJ/t at 1.04 mol/kg), so 3.4 GJ/t is physically plausible and leaves room for about 1.5 mol water per mol CO2. As electricity it is 944 kWh/t, more than the reference cycle supplied by a COP-3 heat pump (559 kWh/t).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Uptake down 3.7% after 100 cycles (adsorb 25 C/80% RH, desorb 0.6 A); a 500-cycle figure is shown; stable across 0-80% RH swings. No oxidative ageing at year scale, no outdoor air.
items.cost: Authors' techno-economic projection: operating cost $48-62/t with renewable electricity (projection, not measured). Support needs 1600 C graphitisation plus plasma treatment, so sorbent price is unknown; OptiLex calc: at $50/kg, 500 cycles gives $364/t, 5,000 cycles $36/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4; bench packed bed, single group, not independently replicated.
items.bottleneck: Single-lab result 28.8% above the previous capacity record; sorbent manufacturing cost and lifetime beyond 500 cycles unproven; electricity used as low-grade heat (second-law efficiency about 14% vs the 0.47 GJ/t floor).

items.name: Cooperative (step-isotherm) diamine-appended MOFs under humid air
items.mechanism: CO2 inserts into metal-amine bonds and forms ammonium carbamate chains, giving a switch-like step isotherm (the closest synthetic analogue of allosteric/haemoglobin-style binding). A step lets a small temperature swing unload nearly the full capacity.
items.uptake_and_conditions: mmen-Mg2(dobpdc): 1.5 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 25 C (dry); about 1.7 mmol/g CO2 plus 3 mmol/g H2O under humid CO2 at 50% RH; water isotherm rises abruptly at 40-50% RH to 40 mmol/g at 90% RH (Chem Sci 2023, full text). Separate breakthrough study (J Chem Phys 2024, doi 10.1063/5.0228985, abstract only): adsorbed water shifts cooperative chains to non-cooperative binding, i.e. step isotherm in dry air, ordinary Langmuir isotherm in humid air.
items.regeneration: Best regeneration 120 C under dynamic vacuum or 150 C under N2 (Chem Sci 2023). OptiLex Hill-isotherm calc (dS -165 J/mol/K, unload 90% to 10% at 1 kPa CO2): Langmuir needs 126 C and 3.83 GJ/t (reaction + sensible, no water); Hill n=4 needs 78 C and 2.72 GJ/t; infinitely sharp step 63 C. Cooperativity removes the isotherm-width term only; the pressure-ratio term remains (142 C for pure CO2 at 1 atm).
items.stability_and_lifetime: Stable only up to 50% RH at 25-40 C; 15% drop in total uptake over 10 cycles at 45-50% RH; 90% capacity kept over 15-20 cycles with 150 C N2 regeneration; amine lost under harsh conditions (uptake 1.5 to 0.07 mmol/g). Ozone/NOx exposure oxidises the amines and lowers the step pressure (Ind Eng Chem Res 2026, doi 10.1021/acs.iecr.6c01324).
items.cost: Not reported. Water co-desorption dominates: OptiLex calc 1.0 GJ/t per mol H2O per mol CO2; 2 mol/mol at 50% RH adds 2.0 GJ/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4 for DAC (gram-scale TGA/breakthrough).
items.bottleneck: The cooperative step, worth about 1.1 GJ/t of sensible heat in the ideal calc, disappears in humid air, and the hydrophilic framework takes up to 27 mol water per mol CO2 at 90% RH.

items.name: Phase-change molecular triamine solid (TriH)
items.mechanism: A framework-free crystalline triamine, 1,3,5-tris(aminomethyl)benzene, converts in humid air to a porous ammonium carbamate network solid. Switch-like uptake similar to cooperative MOFs but with no dead framework mass; water lowers the activation barrier instead of blocking sites.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 3.3 to 8.9 mmol/g from 400 ppm CO2 across 10-40 C and 20-80% RH (breakthrough; JACS 2025). No uptake in dry 400 ppm at 20-40 C; dry uptake needs 50-60 C (4.6 mmol/g at 60 C). At 20 C, 60% RH: 6.1 vs 8.3 mmol/g depending on flow rate (kinetically limited).
items.regeneration: Water removed at 70 C and CO2 at 100-110 C under flowing N2 (about 13 min at 110 C in cycling); about 84% of absorbed CO2 released in the first 50 min at 100 C. Inert purge was used, so pure-CO2 regeneration temperature is not established.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Cycling with 420 ppm CO2, 21% O2, 80% RH, 20 C: 6.0 mmol/g in run 1; later cycles absorb up to 4.5 and desorb 3.3-4.4 mmol/g over about 9-10 cycles. TriH melts at 50-52 C and volatilises on prolonged heating at 100-120 C; deliquescence observed. Oxidatively robust in the reported tests.
items.cost: Not reported; commodity-type small molecule. OptiLex calc: at $20/kg, 6 mol/kg and 1,000 cycles sorbent cost is $76/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2-3; milligram-to-gram samples.
items.bottleneck: Volatility and melting of the free amine during regeneration limit lifetime to about 10 demonstrated cycles; regeneration shown only under N2 purge.

items.name: Photo-swing liquids: photobase and photoacid pH swing
items.mechanism: Light switches the pKa of a dissolved photoswitch, moving solution pH so an amino acid or peptide binds CO2 (photobase on) or bicarbonate releases it (photoacid on). Binding strength is set by light instead of heat.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Photobase PyDIG + glycylglycine (JACS 2026): pKa shift 2.8 units under UV; cyclic capacity 0.21-0.26 mol CO2 per mol at 1 mM in water open to ambient air, 24 h loading. Pyranine photoacid in bicarbonate buffer (JACS 2024, doi 10.1021/jacs.4c07278): 0.48 mmol/h release from a 15% CO2 feed at 200 W/m2 visible light, 0.125 CO2 per photon; only 3 micromol over 2 h from air-saturated solution. Indazole photoacid (Angew 2023, doi 10.1002/anie.202304957): 55-78% of inorganic carbon released.
items.regeneration: PyDIG: release in the dark at room temperature over 5 days (2 days at 80 C). Quantum yield 4.01%; authors' theoretical minimum 338-386 kJ/mol = 7.7-8.8 GJ/t of UV light even at unit quantum yield. OptiLex photon calc: one 450 nm photon per CO2 is 6.0 GJ/t; at the measured 0.125 CO2/photon 48 GJ/t of light; at 4% UV quantum yield 186 GJ/t.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 6 cycles (PyDIG), 3 cycles with diminishing yield (indazole photoacid), 7 days/168 cycles without degradation for pyranine at 15% CO2.
items.cost: Not reported. OptiLex area calc: 27 m2-yr of collector per tonne for a pyranine-like system and 517 m2-yr/t for a UV photobase, vs 1.2-4.5 m2-yr/t for photovoltaics driving a conventional cycle.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 2; millilitre scale, millimolar concentrations.
items.bottleneck: Photon economy: each CO2 costs at least one 230-330 kJ photon against a 20.5 kJ/mol floor (under 9% efficiency even at unit quantum yield); real quantum yields 1-12%, concentrations 1 mM to 0.1 M, cycle times of days.

items.name: Moisture-swing sorbents (quaternary ammonium resins, hydrogels, graphene)
items.mechanism: Quaternary ammonium sites with carbonate/bicarbonate/phosphate counter-ions bind CO2 when dry and release it when wet; the free energy comes from water evaporating into dry air, so no heat is purchased. Binding strength is decoupled from fuel use but coupled to water use.
items.uptake_and_conditions: IRA-900 carbonate resin: 1.92 mmol/g at 20% RH, 25 C, falling as RH rises; theoretical maximum working capacity 1.27 mmol/g for a 20% to 50% RH swing at 25 C with inert purge; 0.97 mmol/g after 6 h breakthrough (ACS Sustain Chem Eng 2025, full text). Quaternised LCST hydrogel PDMH: 1.06 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 40 C, 30% RH (Adv Mater 2026, doi 10.1002/adma.74495, abstract). Quaternised graphene: 3.24 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 20% RH (Small 2024, doi 10.1002/smll.202401303, abstract).
items.regeneration: Humid gas above 85% RH at 25 C for resins; PDMH regenerates 92% at 90% RH and 79% at 80% RH at 25 C (diurnal 40 C dry / 25 C humid cycle). OptiLex calc: reversible minimum is 3.2 mol H2O per mol CO2 at 30% RH to deliver a 2 kPa CO2 product (1.3 t water/t) and 10.8 mol/mol at 70% RH; practical 10-100 mol/mol is 4-41 t water per t CO2; product is dilute and needs about 0.32 GJ/t further compression from 2 kPa.
items.stability_and_lifetime: PDMH: working capacity 0.97-1.05 mmol/g over 40 cycles. The 2025 Energy Environ Sci review notes almost no stability data beyond 10 lab cycles. Quaternary ammonium resin degrades at moderate temperature, so it cannot be combined with a normal thermal swing (ACS AMI 2025, doi 10.1021/acsami.5c12939).
items.cost: Not measured. OptiLex calc: $10/kg resin at 1 mol/kg costs $757/t if it lasts 300 diurnal cycles and $76/t at 3,000 cycles.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-5 for materials; one life-cycle study assumed 378 kWh/t electricity and zero heat for a 0.365 kt/yr design (not measured).
items.bottleneck: Works only where air is dry and water is available; one cycle per day gives 0.044 kg CO2/kg/day at 1 mol/kg (62 kg sorbent per t/yr); dilute product; competitive water uptake at high humidity.

items.name: Outdoor moisture-swing pilot: 300-day durability record
items.mechanism: Anion-exchange resin beads in mesh-tube packets capture CO2 passively from wind-driven air and release it when immersed in alkaline algae medium; moisture is the only trigger.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Small outdoor pilot delivering about 100 g CO2/day into a 4.2 m2, 840 L raceway pond; bench unit about 1 g/day (Environ Sci Technol 2026; companion paper doi 10.1021/acs.est.5c18177). Abstract-level numbers only.
items.regeneration: Wet/dry cycling by immersion; no heat or vacuum. CO2 is delivered as dissolved carbon, not as a pure gas stream.
items.stability_and_lifetime: Over 300 days of outdoor wet/dry cycling across four seasons: release capacity and kinetics fell from nitrate competition and biofouling (partly restored by washing); beads lost mechanical strength and quaternary ammonium groups, attributed to cumulative UV damage.
items.cost: Techno-economics reported only for a biofuel/protein co-product case and assume sorbent performance is retained (it was not).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5; 100 g/day outdoor.
items.bottleneck: First long outdoor record shows chemical loss of functional groups within one year; at one cycle per day that is about 300 cycles, where OptiLex's lifetime calc gives $757/t for a $10/kg, 1 mol/kg resin.

items.name: Humidity-plus-heat hybrid: vapour-promoted desorption with co-harvested water
items.mechanism: A desiccant bed (silica gel) and an amine resin bed capture water and CO2 from the same air. On heating, the released water vapour acts as an in-situ purge that lowers CO2 partial pressure, replacing the vacuum pump and steam boiler, and yields fresh water.
items.uptake_and_conditions: Amine resin 1.11 mmol/g at 20 C, 400 ppm; working capacity 0.85-1.0 mmol/g from air at 27 C, 35-60% RH (Nat Commun 2024, 180 mL resin + 180 mL silica gel).
items.regeneration: About 100-105 C at ambient pressure; 97.7% pure CO2 without vacuum; solar-heated prototype recovered 98% of CO2 in 50 min at 600 W/m2. Measured thermal energy 10.3-10.4 GJ/t CO2, compared with 12-15 GJ/t reported for vacuum and steam-assisted swings with the same resin.
items.stability_and_lifetime: 9 cycles stable at about 1.0 mmol/g; the same resin lost over 20% capacity in 6 cycles when desorbed at 110 C in air and none at 70 C.
items.cost: Authors: $29-144/t for the thermal energy at $0.01-0.05/kWh heat. No capital estimate.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4; bench and small outdoor solar prototype (Tianjin).
items.bottleneck: Measured heat is still 10.3 GJ/t, 1.7 times OptiLex's idealised 6.04 GJ/t reference; amine oxidation above about 100 C in air caps the temperature.

items.name: Avnos hybrid DAC (moisture-responsive sorbent with water co-production)
items.mechanism: Commercial hybrid that uses humidity-responsive sorbents and low-grade heat to co-produce CO2 and water.
items.uptake_and_conditions: No sorbent capacity or humidity window published on the company site.
items.regeneration: Company describes moisture-driven release assisted by waste heat; no GJ/t figure published.
items.stability_and_lifetime: No public data.
items.cost: No public data.
items.trl_and_scale: Bakersfield pilot 2023, listed at TRL 6 in the 2025 Energy Environ Sci review. Company claim for Project Cedar: 3,000 t CO2 and more than 6,000 t water per year.
items.bottleneck: No independently measured energy, capacity or lifetime numbers; the claimed 2 t water per t CO2 is consistent in sign with co-harvesting but cannot be checked.

items.name: Charged-sorbents: hydroxide-loaded activated carbon with Joule heating
items.mechanism: Battery-style charging inserts hydroxide ions into activated-carbon pores; the ions bind CO2 as (bi)carbonate and the conductive carbon is regenerated by direct resistive heating at 90-100 C instead of the 900 C needed for bulk carbonates.
items.uptake_and_conditions: 0.26 +/- 0.06 mmol/g at 0.4 mbar CO2, 25 C (isotherm); about 0.2 mmol/g from dry 400 ppm at 30 C; under DAC conditions capacity falls from about 0.14 to 0.08 mmol/g as RH rises from 11% to 38% (Nature 2024). Adsorption heat from -137 kJ/mol at zero coverage to -33 kJ/mol at 0.8 mmol/g.
items.regeneration: Joule heating to about 90 C in about 1 min under N2. Authors' minimum electrical energy for sorbent heating: 6.5 GJ/t at 11% RH and 11.4 GJ/t at 38% RH (1,800 and 3,200 kWh/t). OptiLex reproduces both numbers as pure sensible heat (cp 620 J/kg/K, 65 K rise, working capacity 0.14 and 0.08 mol/kg).
items.stability_and_lifetime: 150 cycles stable at 30% CO2 (dry, 30/100 C); survives 12 h in air at 150 C; capacity loss after 14 months storage; humidity loss is reversible site blocking.
items.cost: Low-cost carbon cloth, price not given. OptiLex calc: at $5/kg, 0.1 mol/kg and 5,000 cycles the sorbent cost is $227/t.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3; 30-120 mg samples.
items.bottleneck: Capacity 0.08-0.26 mmol/g is 4-12 times too low: energy is dominated by heating the carbon, and humid air halves the capacity.

items.name: Redox-switchable CO2 carriers under air (thiadiazole, quinones)
items.mechanism: An electrode-bound organic molecule binds CO2 when electrochemically reduced and releases it when oxidised, so binding strength is switched by voltage at constant temperature. A gas-permeation layer admits CO2 and restricts O2.
items.uptake_and_conditions: BPT thiadiazole carrier with ether-rich gas-permeation layer: 3.3 +/- 0.2 mmol per g of carrier (about 1.1 kg CO2 per m3 of electrode) from about 400 ppm CO2 with 21% O2 (Nat Commun 2026); ionic-liquid electrolyte with 1 M LiTFSI.
